MY LAD AT THE HELM. 6 , Be is but a lad, sirs, and„theugh I'm a man, ; The courage of both's in my bright little brat! Imdanger my limbs have been aye in the van, I But measure our hearts—he is monarch in that: We sail out together; my lad's at the helm, With berry-brown skin, and his crisp curls of gold; My lad! that I fear lest a wave should o'erwhelm. Ay, fear! yet his eyes are in wonderment bold! The spray lifts athwitrt of our frail little crafto • 'l've met its wild fury with teeth set and dread! My. bright little lad at the crashing has laughed, ' -Delightingly shaking his proud little head! The waved and I many a tussle hive had thus in their vengeance they strike a return. But, is it in love that they play round my lad? •Or is it a danger his big heart can purns? , Astern on the bulwarks he'll sit, and he'll dream Of some afar land that his future may know; And!, at the oars, through my tear?ut eyes gleam • On future when lof the twain am laid low— • A toiler the less, by the world's ocean crust-fed: My stranded barque warns him where danger-waves break. i see in my hones—and life's-tempests are hushed— My lad at the helm for his mother's dear sake! In darkness and terrors, that queileth the heart, His eyes are my sunshine, his laugh is my faith! You'd think him the man, sirs, for when we're apart I struggle half-hearted as one with a wraith. Be's brave for us both, for when dangers aped, • Be laughs, yet I fear lest the waves should o'er- whelm. rn think that my fears are, but prawns, after all, That God may-watch over my lad at the helm. 5, Bow-lane, Preston: JAMES Canirste-Erwanne.

"thoseele eon have 1 but one client between you, make the most of him." ; ATi Ca-uncle 'WITH THE Isnteers.—When I eetered, the Service had just commenced, and se crowded was the church, that I had some little difficulty in finding n vaelent gent in one of the pews. The congregation, was composed exclusively of Indians and half.breeds, the females sitting together on the left side of the aisle, and the men and boys on the opposite side. The women all had shawls, of a more Or less Sombre hue, pinned over their heads. As there was no clergyman at York Factory at the time ef my visit, the service WO conducted by a Cree Indian in a very reverent and apparently earnest manner, and, of course, in the Core tongue. The hymns were sung in a wailing kind of monotonous cadence, resembling a funereal dirge, and producing a very curious effect. The hymns and chants were led entirely by the man who was Officiating. Altogether I was much impreSsed with the decorous way in which the service was carried out, and with tele hearty and sincere manner in which, the conereention joined.--Commodore A. IL Nark:horn. R.N., i. Good Words..: FITIIINFSS WITH TITE YOTYINTI. Nothing, impresses chi/dren more than (inlet Tower; nothing so utterly demoralises them as a nervous, spasModic excitableness. A friend, whose life is over, and in whose nature there r was more real majesty than in any person I ever met, Mice told me an incident which exactly illustrates this rare faculty: The family %vett in an oid Queen Anne house a few miles out of London. Down each of the four corners of it there ran a fringe of moulded brick- work, with ornamentation jutting out 'sufficiently to make -a barely safe foothold lor a light climber. The youngest son of the house (had he been reading the •‘Hunclibeck of Notre Dame " ? ) took it into his head to descend from the topeef the building to the bottom by this improvised staircase, and, having succeeded in his attempt, was presently summoned into the presence of his mother. What was .that benignant and , sagacious woman's method of preventing the repetition of a-feat which was useless and alarming? She did not weep nor scold, not express either horror, admiration, or surprise. She contented herself with remarking that as he had done it once, and thereby made it clear that he was able to do it, there was no particular advanteee to be gained by his doing it again. He did not do it again.— Geed lrords for March. ' - A Become or Tesee.—ln a pleasant, airy, up-hill country, it was my fortune when I was young to make the acquaintance Of a certain beggar. I call him beggar, though he usually allowed his coat and his shoes (which were open-mouthed, indeed) to beg for him. De was the wreck of an athletic man, tall, gaunt and.hronzed ; far gone in consumption, with that disquieting smile of the mortally stricken oe his face; but still active afoot,' still with the brisk military carriage, the ready military salute. Three ways led through this piece of country; and as I was inconstant in my choice, I believe he must often have awaited me in vain. But often enough. he caught me; often enough, from some place of ambush by the roadside, he would spring soddenly forth in the regulation attitude, and launching at once into his inconsequential talk, fall into step with me upon nev further course. " A fine morning sir, though perhaps a trifle inclining to, rain. I hope I see you well, sir. Why, no, sir. I don't feel as hearty myself as I could wish, but I am keeping about my ordinary. tam pleased to meet you on the road, sir. assure you / quite look forward to one pf our little etm- versations." He loved the sound of his own voice inor- dinately, and though (with something too offhand to Call servility) he would always hasten to agree with anything, you said, yet he could never suffer you to say 'it to an end. By what transition he slid to his favourite subject I have no memory; but eye had never been lring, together on the way before he was dealing, in a very' Military manner, with the English poets. "Shelley was a fine poet, sir, though a trifle atheistical in'his opinions. His Queen Mab, sir, is quite an atheistical work. ficett. sir, is not so poetical a writer. With the works of Shakespeare I am not so well acquainted, but he was a fine poet. Keats—John Keats,' sir —he was a very fine poet." With "such refer- ences, such trivial critieism,such loving parade of his own knowledge, he would beguile the road, striding forward up-hill, his staff now clapped to the ribs of his deep, resonant chest, now swinging in the air with the remembered jauntiness of the private soldier; and all the while his toes looking out of his beets, and his shirt looking out of his elbows, and death looking out of his smile, and his big, crazy frame shaken by accesses of cough. He would often go the whole way home with tee ; often to borrow a book, and that book always a poet. Oft he would march, to continue his mendicant rounds, with the volume slipped into the

poqket of his ragged coat; and although he would sometimes keep it quite a while, vet it came alwave beck again at tst, not much the worse for its travels into beggardom. And in this way, doubtless, his know- ledge grew and his glib, random criticism took a wider Tenge.—Begears, ho7?obert L 01123 Steren.ton, in Scrtbner's Mega^ine for March. THE SMALLEST PEOPLE OF THE Wonm—Professor Flower, C. 8., director of the Natural History Museum, hes given a description of the two skeletons of Akka, lately obtained in the Monbuttu country, Central Africa, by Ernin lasha. The tribe was discovered 'by Schwein- furth in 1870. The two skeletons are those of fully grown up people, a male and female. They are both of them smaller than any other normal skeleton known, smaller certainly than the smallest l3ushman's skeleton in any museum in this country, and smaller than any Out of the 29 skeletons of the diminutive inhabitants:of the Andaman Islands. The height of neither of them exceeds four feet, while a living female Akka, of whom Emin Pasha has sent careful 4easuremente, is 3ft. 10in. The results previously obtained from the measurements of about half a dozen living Akkas are not quite so low as these, and give an average for both sexes of 4ft. Biin. But the numbers measured are not sufficient for estab- lishing the true average of the race, especially as it is not certain that they were all purebred examples. Ac- cording to Topinaid's list, there are only two known races which have a mean height below 1.500 metres (4 ft. lffiin.), viz., the Negritor of the Andaman Islands (1478) and the Bushmen of South Africa (1404). Of the real height of the former we have abundant and exact evi- dence. both from living individuals and from skeletons, whith dearly proves that they considerably exceed the Akkas in 'stature. That this is also the case with the Bushmen • there ie little doubt, although the measurements of this diminutive race are less nu- merous and carefully made. The point of com- parative size being settled, it remains to consider' to what races the Akkas are most nearly allied. They belong in all their essential characteristics_to the black or 'Negroid branch of the human species there can be nti doubt, having all the essential characteristics of that branch even to exaggeration. The form of the head is somewhat more rounded than usual, but it has been shown that in Equatorial Africa, extending from the west coast far into the interior, are scattered tribes of negroes, distinguished from the majority of the in- 12sbitants of the continent by this special cranial cha- Teeter, as wfll as by their smaller stature, to which the name of ":\egtillo" has been applied by Hamy. It is to this race of the great Negroid branch that the Akkas belong, and they are not by any means closely allied, either to the Bushmen or the Negritor of Lhe Indian Ocean, except in so far as they are members of the same great branch, distinguished among the general character eby their closely curled or frizzly hair. It is possible that the Negrillo people gave origin to the stories of pygmies, So 'eetrunon in the writings of the Greek poets and his- torians. and whose habitations were often placed near the sources of the Nile. The name Akka, by which Schweinfurth says the tribe now call themselves, has singularly enough been read by Marietta Pasha by the side of the portrait of a dwarf in a Monument of the ancient Egyptian Empire. PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE. VIII.-COURTSHIP.

•----—-- - - - - - ' The courtship of most people is looked back upon as the happiest time of their lives. Something • after the fashion of the boy who is caught stealing the jam; the spanking is excessively painful, but it cannot eradicate the sweet remembrance of the jam. No! when a man and his wife have told each other, to the fullest 'extent; how they have been "put on," it seems natural that they should fall back upon the remembrance of the, time when they didn't tell each other their opinion so pointedly. I know a man who remembers his court- ship so fondly that an allusion to it is the only thing by which you can possibly win a smile out of him, and his eyes sparkle as he listens to any anecdote ' labout courting. I don't suppose from this that he ever took. his girl to a confectioner's, and, after an expensive raid on the good things, found \that he hadn't money enough te pay for them. Recollections of this sort have a tendency to make a smile thin. I believe if that man had his time to. live over again, he would, .court ' right down to Isis • grave. But, no! he wouldn't; the l• other half of the contract would watch him for that. , . a Now, it may strike you to inquire what an old fossil like me wants talking about courtship ;to which I , humbly reply that, having been there myself, I am anxious:to set up a lighthouse for others, as the old 1 woman said (I don't know what old woman it was, by , the way), "Them wod's bin up th' loyn knows th' way," and ergo, I don't want to see anybody row upon the rocks of matrimony in the dark. There have been many reasons given why men don't Marry, but I don't accept any of them, as I think that thornby herb, the old bachelor, has either considered nobody good enough for him, or else it has been a case of solemn vice versa. My theory is that they go with the stream, and if you find a few old sticklebacks for ever swimming about among the roots of tlis same tree with ugly dignity, it doesn't upset the theory altogether. . . when a young man and a young woman first get engaged, they seem to get the idea that they are the first pair that ever were so. If the subject is mentimed to the young lady, she blushes like a' rose; if to- the young man, he blushes like—like a thousand of bricks. As if they were doing something unnatural! They don't seem to consider that that Sort of thing • has been going on at compound interest since the time of Adam and Eve. . As I informed you that I had "been there" myself, which is extremely true, I don't see why I shouldn't go in for advocating a general reform in courtship. There are points that strike me very forcibly now, that I didn't at all notice once, and this leads me to the subject of love letters.

We sometimes read of rich men dying and leaving so much money that the writer thinks we cannot grasp the enormity of the figures, and consequently he illustrates it by saying if so many dollars were placed side by side they would cover so many hundred mites; but if this example was followed up in love-letters, there wouldn't be an inch of vegetation upon the whole earth, even if you only take one year's production. "But," you say, "What's the use of trying to show this ?" Well, don't interrupt a man in the middle of an important calcula- tion. lam showing that love-letters may be of great importance, and the point I want to get at-is this. The Government ought to pass a law compelling every couple that get married to deliver up all love-letters interchanged during their courtship, to be manufactured into cardboard coffins for old bachelors, or burnt by the common hangman. If all love-letters were treated in either of these ways, a man wouldn't be constantly. having to face some old letter of perhaps' fifteen years back, and charged with inconsistency. I don't care to explain this matter further, as it is of a painful nature. Of course you can recollect how you used to walk out in the rain when you were courting; hOw you held the umbrella over your partner while your own clothes shone as if they had been black-leaded; what manly efforts you made to keep your teeth from chattering with the cold; and how you tried to smile andlook corn- fortable when you came in the light of a lamp. If you could see the reflection of that smile on that face now, you would go clean out of your mind. But, there isn't much chance of your seeing it. Mind you I don't mean to infer that you wouldn't get wet sow to hold the um- brella over your partner, but somehow there is a dif- ference between duty and pleasure that I- don't exactly know how to split. Perhaps I ought to apoligise to the good young man who has really formed projects that shall never, no never change; the young man who knows that he will make just as many and just as expensive presents to his partner after he has married her as he did before; who is prepared to have his pants re-seated four or five times in order to buy a bracelet. Well, I apologise to that. young man, but I shall tank what he may think an undignified expression to the apology-4 Experience makes fools wise."

We have all heard a good deal about "popping the question." Here is another fit subject for reform.. don't know why a man should be supposed to get nervous and stammer and sweat over a job of this sort, when the girl has been fretting and fuming over his delay for months. My advice to young men is td nip all nervousness in the bud, as. from a philosophical pdint of view it is patent that the girl wants you, or she wouldn't have let you court her so long. You just say to her, "Mary Jane, .I'm about sick of fooling around like this. You know that I estOem you above any woman on earth or I shouldn't have caught so much rheumatism slinking about on wet nights. My salSry is so much (say two shillings less than the amount for tobacco and extras) ; I'm about the same now that I always shall be, with the exception of going bald and that sort of thing. When shall we get married?" I don't say that these ought to be the exact words, out I lay them out as a guide to all practical young men. I would suggest that you make no allusion to "soft eyes" and "auburn hair," because if at any future time you jocularly let fall any remark about "squinting" or "a red bead" you will become suddenly await that re- tentive memories are not all on the wane.

I thhalr I ought to say a few words about Leap Year while we are on this subject of courtship. Leap Year is noted for two things. Its second month I)as twenty.. nine days' and its twelve months are devoted to masculine deafness to feminine hints of matrimony. The young men of this perverse generation will pro- bably sneer at the advice i give them, but as they don't have many rows during courtship they cannot appre- ciate its weight. To show, however, that "true love doesn't always run smooth," I shall tell you what hap- pened to ruffle the smoothness in the case of a young couple who used to visit the house of a man I knew. The young man, whose name was Josiah, but vrhb was generally known as Josh, had a fair sprinkling of firmness in his character, and his girl Matilda— for shortness—was about as stubborn as Josh himself. One evening they were sat in the house men- tioned, one at each side of the fireplace, when a mouse jumped over the fender, and cleared out through the back kitchen door. There were two holes in the masonry of the fireplace, each large enough to allow the exit of a mouse, and Josh calumny mentioned that he saw the mouse "come eawt o' thad hoyle," pointing to the une on the right hand side. " Tha'rt mistekken,' said 'Tilda, "Id coom eawt o' this hoyle." "Nod id," said Josh. "Aw see id as plain as dayleet come eawt o' this hoyle." And words ran so high that the word "liar" came in very often, and the upshot was tbat Josh and 'Tilda "fell out," and didn't speak for several weeks. The next time they met was at a party amongst a let of their friends, and they were quickly reconciled to each other. • Jost), of course, took qilda. home, and on the way he laughingly said, "'Tilde tha were a bit. stoopid abeawt thad meawse comin' eawt 'o' thad hoyle." ^ "Nod aw," replied 'Tilda, "id were thee as were stoopid ; if id hedn'd ha' come eawt o,' thad hoyle wod aw spd, aw wouldn't ha' keered." • "Well," said Josh, "tha non know as id coom eawt th' hoyle as aw sed, 'cause aw watched id." They con- tradict.d each other until they reached 'Tilcia's doer when she told him neverto speak to her again. After a three months' sulk, they were again brought together,

RHYMES IN THE DIALEPT. A POW UT TWICE. Aw've just heeard a "buzz" o'er a barber, A bit ov a wag in his way ; Bud nod quite as sharp as a razor, As geet sucked in reight t other day. It's gam when a " cutter " geds dropt on, While grinnin' away 'D'er his jooak, Un finds eawt he's bod a snuft candle— A. Turn Foo' lased' for o th' fooak. toe Latherboy allus wur nooate4 For bein' a good 'un for gam • Bud med a mistake when he tackled . •• A fawse chap like owd Joiner Sam. Ther's summat abeawt Sam decavin' ; . He looks rayther gasymless un green"; For o thad, ther's anus a sparkle 0' merriment leetin' his een. Joe's pride stuck eawt clooase bi' his windo', 'Twur th' pow, wi' a gowd knob ut top, He's oft bin sin, smilin' wi pleashur, When things wur bud Blackish th' shop. Admirin' th' grand twistin's o' colour As curved like a snake ot' way deawn, Un many a time hes he booasted Ther wornd sich another i' th' teawn. rother neet, while th' wind blew varra ruffiy, Un snow-aces coom thickly fro' t' sky. A lot set i' th' barber's shop, campin', Un tawkin' o'er marlocks gone by, ' Joe wur busy wi' th' corn ion big sithors, Powin' Nan o' th' Book's lad's bristly yure, When Joiner Sam, partly-wod fuddled, .Wi' his bass, cluttered inside o'tle door. "Hello, Sam! Wod's up neaw ?" wur Joe's greetin', As th' tool bass wur dropt on to t' floor; Sam anserd, "Mi thatch wants a thinnin', Un aw want a good pow, to be sure !" Joe. just ut his campers winked slyly, Un they o watched wod marlock he'd do; They cud see hi Joe's ways he wur actin' As iv he'd melt scinbry foo'. Sam set into th' cheer plump un gradely, ' Tin "Let's hey a good crop !" he cried; Bud Joe, while his mates grinned un tittered, Powed Sam bare as a booard o' one side, When he'd done thad he hair-oiled him smartly, Un brushed th' uncut side on to th' bare; ' Sam happened to look into th' wo glass. Then his een glittered keenly un quare. "Am aw reight, Joe,?" axed Sammy. "Ay, Joiner, Tha'rt finished un done up to Dick !" Sed Joe, as he geet howd o' th' tuppence, Welly brastin' wi' mirth o'er his trick. • Sam gript ut his bass. an then trundled Thro' t' door, wi' a hearty "Good fleet:" Un as soon as he'd zone, hey, wod laffin' Rung eawt, a roodr, then a skreet.., , • Sam hedn'd bin gone monny minutes, When a raspin' noise reached o tiler ears. " Wod's thad—hesta rats?" wur tie sharp questions. Nowe !" Th' noise wossend; soon dud ther fears. Joe leoked reawnd, then pept eawt o' th' doorhoyle, Un ay !—true enuff I 'twur no sham! A chap up a ladder wur sawin' , His pow, un thad fella wur Sam " Howd on theer !" Jae sheawted, " Tha wastrel! Tha's sawn away th' hawf o' ml pow ! "Well, well, wod hi thad ?" Sammy ansered, " Tha's done t' same wi me, stop thi row; Dosta think as aw want fooak rdisguidin'? Nowe.nowe, its reet neaw, ther's no deaivt, For them uts henof powerl inside, wi' thee Man tek th' bawl eanotside,—or do beawt. No mon ever geet sich tantrums Or pied use o' langwidge like Joe; He welly went wild, when fooak skitted ; He's threatened to put Sam to law.' • Iv yo' chance to want powin! erlshavin' •• Wi' Joe, keep yo'r meawtbs shut, neaw do; For nobry knows wod deed mut happen If yo' bed sed a word abeawt th' pow. • JACK WA's.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDCiN. TIIMISDAY - NIGHT. It is too soon yet to speak with confidence of the working of the New Rules of Vrocedure in the House of Commons. But it may be said that, as far as experience has yet tested them, they prove most lesirable reforms calculated to lengthem some valu- able lives. Atthe same time, it must be admitted that the happy results already obtained depend entirely on the attitude of the Opposition. Sup.- posing the Conservatives sat on the other side of the House, and supposing Ireland were not pacified and hopeful in the certainty of presently having justice dnne: the record of business done in the House of Commons would be very different. How ' the Rules might work was incidentally shown on Monday night. The debate on the Army Estimates collapsed half an hour befofe the appointed time, Lord Randolph Churchill refusing to imperil the symmetry of his speech by following the course laid down for ordinary members, beginning his die.- course, breaking its thread at midnight, and recom- mencing on the day fixed for resumption of the debate. There being an unexpected half hour to ' spare, Sir John Gerst, who was happily in his place, was obliged to rise and make a statement on moving a Bill dealing with so unimportant a place as India. When the hands of the clock touched 12 the conversation was peremptorily intprrupted, and for all practical purposes the half hour was wasted. If the Opposition were obstructive something like this might happen every night. Of course it could be met, and in the end overcome, by the:steadt, ap- plication of the Closure. But that is a very jerky , mode of getting along compared with the smooth progr.is of business, loyally assisted as it is just now by all shades of the Opposition. What clouds bave arisen over the Ministerial horizon come directly from their own friends. On Monday night the Army Estimates were brought on, and. ,it was fondly hoped, even•officially an- nounced, that before the House rose the customary vote for men would be agreed to. • Towards accom- plishing this end the Minister for War is assisted by a device of quite modern application., A very short time ago it was the time-honoured custom for the ginister of War, and the First Lord of the Admiralty to occupy a considerable portion of the first sitting on the estimates by the delivery of a long speech ex- 11 plaining them. tiow the Minister in either depart- ment prepires in advance a more or less .lucid state- ment which is printed and circulated with the votes. 1 Here is at least two hours saved on the motion to go into Committee of Supply. But it did not avail on. Monday Itgainst the machinations of Lord Salisbury's candid friend. Lord Randolph had been busy for a whole week in getting up a little cabal against his old colleagues. Buzzing about the library, the reading room, the smoking room, and the Carlton, he had put together a mixed and very effective com- pany of marksmen intended to bring down unhappy Mr. Stanhope. Mr. Smith might flatter himself that the debate wotild .be over in a single night. Lord Randolph took care that it should extend at least over two nights. To that end he declined to Speak on Monday, moving the adjournment, and so secur- ing a prominent place in this evening's proceed- ings. This is one of those situations particularly tempt- ing to a factious opposition. If. the Opposition, mindfuronly of the opportunity of inflicting a Mow upon the Government, were to whip up their men and carry them into the lobby with Sir W. Bartlelot, the Ministerial majority would be criti- call.y reduced. But that is not a view of their duty which the Liberal leaders have taken. They have studiously refrained from embarrassing the Govern- ment in dealing with so serious a matter as the war estimates, and the enemies of the Government

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1888.

, have exclusively been those of their own house- told. . . . 'Count Herbert Bismarck has been over here for the last few days in frequent, censultation with Lord Salisbury. It is shrewdly suspected that his visit is not altogether unconnected with what looks like a coming crisis in affairs in Bulgaria. Thaultan once more pl eying Rusia's game, hes formally notified to the Government at Sofia that the presence of Prince Ferdinand in ' Bulgaria is illegal, inasmuch as his election has not been accepted by the Signa- tory Powers of the Berlin Treaty, or sanctioned by the Porte. What the sultan has to say on any sub- iect is not in Itself of prime importance. But there is no doubt that in this matter Vie is.moving in con- juction, if not immediately at the instance of Ger- many, and that his action is the precursor of a definite and critical step to be taken by the Powera in concert. The position of the *Signatories to the Berlin Treaty will be ridiculous if, after having warped Prince Ferdinand of the illegality of his position, they dO.not take steps to justify the law. ' rince Ferdinand says be will stay and right. But e snay think better of it,. . , . The news from Berlin of the health Of thel Emperor has' ncldenly become critical. It is pro- • bable that before these lines are in print the end will have come. Recent experience in respect of the Crown Prince at San Remo affords an opportunity of judging the value of official bulletins when Royal personages lie sick. The reports fsom Berlin to hand as I write still talk of • hope. But clearly there is none. Similarly gleams of hope have fit- fully waved from San Remo about the Crown Prince; who, unless his doctors are terribly mistaken, is fatally stricken. In these circumstances a matter of prime importance is the health of Prince Bis- marck, who, if Prince William comes to the Throne, will be even more Emperor de facto than he has been through the reign of Father William. I hear item r one who had occasion to see a good deal of him the last few months that he is in wonderfully rugged health. He still works terribly hard. But it seems to agree with him, as do his peculiar habits. He never goes to bed till two o'clock in the morning, , and, dining early, as Germans do, eats ,a fearsome meal about midnight.' Going to bed late he does not Make up for it by getting up early in the moehing, rarely rising heft:4.e noon. The Imperial Chancellor has other affairs than those of Eutope to attend to. V he had not beer a 'statesman he would have been either a famous distiller or a mighty man in the sawmill line. As it is he finds odd moments to direct two large businesses in these walks ef life. In B Tlin he is reputed to drays, over £20,000 a year from his sawmill and his distilleries, which is a set- off against the comparative smallness of his official salary. . • , . The German ChancellOr is much more 'successful in the direction of his private affairs than Mr. I Gladstone has been in at least oiled his adventures. ' • For ordinary people who have blundered into bid investments there must be a melancholy kind of pleasure in knowing that Mr. 'GI i idstbne s sa large holder of stock in the Metropolitan District Rail - Way Company. Not only is he himself a Consider- able shareholder, but the various members of his family have large holdings. It would be difficult to imagide any moderately respectable security that has proved more unremunerative than this. In 1880, , its high water mark of prosperity in 'recent years, it paid in ' the first' half-Year 11 per cent., with i per cent in the second half. The next year it paid. 11 per cent, in the first half-year, and nothing in the second. In 183'2 it paid i per cent, on the first half year, and since then the shareholders of .ordi- nary stock have not received a penny, whilst the capital valneNif their shares has woefully decreased. If Prince Bismarck has time to look over.the last report'of the Metropolitan District Railway, with a knowledge of Mr.. Gladstone's private concerns, he would be more than human if he does not.chuckle over the ptofits from his tat distilleries and pis , booming saw mills: Ordinarily, Wednesday night is a quaint time in Palace-yard, and in summer sevenings the pigeons have it all to themselVes. For three hours last night the scene was changed; all the approaches being. blocked with carriages, and a constant stream pass- ing in and out of Speaker's Court. It was the occa- . sion of Mr. Peel's se,cond reception of the session. The first, given a fortnight ago, was attended by the Conservatives. Last niarlit the Liberal Party were the honoured guests, and as the most brilliant Lon- don season is not starred by a more attractive as- , sembly, the crush was enormous. But the Speaker's rooms are spacious, and only for a bad (limner of an . hour about eleven o'clock was there any inconveni- ent crowd. Mr. Gladstone, who had dined with the Speaker, remained till after eleven gaily chatting. • There were many familiar faces it the crowded room. But one was struck more forcibly than even • in the House of Commons with the enormous pro- portion of new people who constitute the present • House. Whilst, as I have said, the guests were for the most( part Liberals, there was a sprinkling of Conservatives, Ministers and their wives being in- vited to both parties. The youngest member of the House, Mr. Darling, just returned for Deptford, made his first appearay.ce in response to the Speaker's summons, and helped in these unusuallypleasant cir- cumstances to "make a House." Last year a good many of the trees in Kensington Gardens showed signs of premature decay. In some cases the Scripture recipe was literally applied. They were digged round and watered. And the digging was well and permanently done, so that it is to be hoped that the evil day has been put 'off. London tree life has latterly suffered from more than average mortality, and not in Kensington Gardens only. Several of the elms clustered rould the Temple fountain have had to be lopped sparingly. These are the very trees in which the robliks used to build their nests in Goldsmith's time, and which . he has described in one of the most charmieg of his essays. The lopping has in each case been severe ; but further delay would have imperilled the life of the tree. In Kensington Gardens too, the authori- ties have this winter done a little subsoil drainage. Parts of the ground, were in wet weather rather marshy, and this has been corrected. Ndt that any part of either the park or the gardens shows now the least sign of marshiness. Not for year's has there been so long a winter drought; and London is at last beginning to show signs of it. The price of vegetables within the week has gone up to fancy figures. We are living largely on our • foreign supplies, which, of course, unaided, are quite in- sufficient. A

div.head: LOVE AND LEARNING.
div.p: LOVE AND LEARNING.

A well-known, elderly nobleman, of large wealth, wooed and won, a few years ago, a young and very beautiful girl. ' Their life has been as happy as it is pos- sible for married • life to be, when 14ecember is united to May. His lordship is .distinguished in scientific circles and possesses high literary attainments. Sometime after his marriage he was foMish enough to think that his lovely 1 wife was not sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of 1 reading for her. A month.later he inquired about her progress. 1 and found that she had notopened a book. He set up his eye- ' brows after the manner or old husbands when their 'young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said : " I was made to bes loved, not to be learned." She won the day, of course. What is learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye ? Would not a husband rather be met with a smile ad a kiss, than b a ' wife who assured him that she " kaew her lesson ?" Wisn is all very well, but winning ways. go further. Laughing eyes beat Greek roots all to nothing.. A woman's lovely tress, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are ,more precious in a husband's eyes than eyer so mph learning in- side of it. Therefore, all women should endeavour to preserve their attractions, and welcome their liege lords with loving lobks, pleasant smiles, and towing silken tresses, for after all a beautiful head of hair is the crowning charm of a woman, a charm which all may posse,, lly using Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or faded hair to its original color, thud make it 'soft, silky, wavy and luxuriant. It may be had of, any chemist or perfumer.

.THE NEW " SUNLIGHT " SOAP WORKS.

About 150 gentlemen assembled on Saturday afternoon at the head of Bromborough Pool to wit- ness the cutting of the first sod of an extensive in- dustrial undertaking which in a short time will give employment to some hundreds of persons, and thus be the means of adding considerably to the popula- tion of the district. Hitherto the " Sunlight " soap works have been located at Warrington, but owing to want of room in which to extend their works, and from other causes, Messrs. Lever Brothers, the enterprising proprietors, were obliged to seek another locality where they could carry on the manufacture of their famous soap. They accordingly ourcbased upwards of 50 acres of land, which stretches from the head of Bromborough Pool to the line of the Birkenhead and Chester railway, on which to es- tablish their works. The site is an admire* one, as by means of Bromborough Pool access is. easily obtained by small vessels to the Mersey. The new soap works will be close to Price's Patent Candle Works, which give employment to nearly GOO hands, the estate consisting of „about .62 acres. The main buildings, which will form an irregular square, I will cover an area of 13,64.5 square yards; or nearly three acres, and will comprise the following departments : Soapery, 228 ft. long by 601 t. wide, three storeys in height, with floor area 4,275 square yards. Frame room, drying room, and stamping room, 225 ft. by 2281 t., with, floor area of 5,700 square yards ; out of this department a space of 90ft. by 801 t., giving 800 square yards of floor space, will be taken up by the temporary offices and dining rooms for the workpeople, which will afterwards I be located in a spacious isolated building. The offices I will consist of counting house 80ft. by 341 t., three large I private rooms, and laboratory,, together with public: space and cloakrooms and lavatones; men'spnc.l women's dining rooms, each 80ft. by 18ft.; card box-making room 2281 t by 54ft., with floor space of 1,361 square yards; box-making room, 180 feet by 51ift., with floor space of 1,00 square yards ; engine Wane, 51.i1t. by 20ft. ; melting-out shed, 121 ft. by 51ift., with 692 Square yards of floor space ; boiler ghed, 100 ft. by 48ft., with 533 square yards of floor space; mechanics' shops, joiners' shop, well room, and room for electric lighting. Engine and dynamo will be arranged in a building 110 ft. by 481 t. with a•floor space of 586 square yards. Railway shed and loading stage, 228 feet by 20 feet, with 506 square yards floor space ; and a building for glycerine and other plant, 175 feet by 64 feet, having 1,330 square yards of .floor space. At one angle of the soapery a tower will rise to a height of 90 feet, being 20 feet square, and in the top of this will be the water tank supplying the sprinklers for the purpose of extinguishing fires. On the top of 'the soapery will be two tanks for water storage, of wrought iron' . and holding 65,000 gallons. The soapery building will be fireproof throughout, and will bp fitted with hoist to each floor, and stone stairscommumcating. The walls will be of red bricks, and will have white stone dre,ssings. The buildings have been designed and will be carried out under the'charge of Mr. William Owen, A.R.1.8.A., of Warrinfton. •

div.head: INITIAL .CEREMONY.
div.p: THE INITIAL .CEREMONY.

The gentlemen invited to be present at the ceremony of cutting the first sod assembled on the .Liverpool Landing-stage at one o'clock, and were conveyed" to New Ferry in the steamer Firefly. From the landing-stage at New Ferry they were transferred to the steam barge Warrington. Leaving New Ferry, the barge steamed to- wards Bromborough Pool, atid entered an estuary of the Mersey seldom explored by any except those connected with Price's candleworks. Passing these works on the. south side, the barge proceeded under the bridge that spans the pool, and which forms part of the Birkenhead and Chester turnpike road. Steaming a short distance higher up, the party cameto*" Port Sunlight," named in honour of Messrs. Lever's new' "Sunlight" estate. A landing having been effected, the company proceeded to that part of the estate where the great tower in connec- tion with the wdrks will be erected. It was here that the first sod was cut. A square piece of land was en- closed, and inside the barrier were Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Lever, Mr. William Owen, who has designed the inten- ded new buildings, Mr. Lever, sen., ,Mr. R. L. Wilson, chairman, and Mr..dlopkinson, surveyor to the Lower Bebington Local Board, and others. After considerable cheering, . . _

Mr. William Owen. the architect, said he had been re- quested by Messrs. Lever Brothers to open the proceed- ings with a few words. There was no doribt that the introduction of "Sunlight" into the district would do it good. (Hear, hear.) He could not help thinking, as they came down the river, that it seemed like an in- vasion of Cheshire by Lancashire ; but he hoped it would beregarded as the extension of the right hand of fellowship by commerce, of which Lancashire was the typical county, to agriculture, of which Cheshire was the representative. (Hear, hear.) If it were an invasion, it was at any rate an invasion with an implement of peace, which was always a forerunner of success, and he had great pleasure in presenting, a spade to Mrs. W. H. Lever, and asking her to cut with it the first sod. He then presented to Mrs. W. H. Lever a handsome silver spade, with a silver-mounted oak handle, and which bore the following inscription ::--"•Presented to Mrs. W. H. Lever, by Messrs. Lever Brothers, on the occasion of her cutting the first sod of their new works at Port Sunlight, March 3rd, 1888." The spade wal supplied by Messrs. Elkington and Co., ,of Liverpool. Mrs. Lever; having performed the ceremony of cutting the sod, amidst cheering, said : The work I have done to-day has given me the greatest pleasure. In cutting this first sod, I wish you all success—success to the new works, success to the firm, and success to alllnterested in the sale and marwfacture of "Sunlight Soap." (Loud cheers.) . CELEBRATION DINNER.

On returning to Liverpool, the party wore entertained by Messrs. Lever Brothers at the Bear's Paw, Lord. street, to an excellent dinner. Mr. W. 11. Lever presi- ded, and at.the principal table were Mrs. W. H. Lever, Mr. and Mrs. J. D. Lever, Mr. James Laver, sen., Mr. and Mrs. John Makin, Mrs. Robert Smith, Mr. and Mrs. Taylor, Messrs. J. S. Salaman, E. S. Mamma, W. P. Thompson, A. Bigland, W. land, J. S. Ferguson, W. F. Tillotson, J. L. Tillotson, T. Harivooda. Greenhalgh, P. Winser, E. V. Salarnan, and W. Gray. The toast of "The Queen and the Royal Family" hav- ing been duly honoured, Mr. JAMES LEVIIR, senior, pro- posed the health of Mr. William Owen, the architect, who, in acknowledging the cordial way in which it was drunk, said that the success of "Sunlight soap" was not due to luck, but to the energy and perseverance of two men. His only regret was that they were leaving his native town of Warrington; but what was Warring-. ton's loss would be Bebington's gain. (Hear, hear.) Mr. P. WIESER, in proposing "Success to the Firm," said they had in an incredibly short space of time estab- lished one of the largest businesses in the country, and, having already filled a• pretty large works, were now obliged to overflow; as it were, into another county. (Applause.) • The toast was drunk with enthusiasm. The CHAIRMAN, who, on rising, was received with pro- longed applause. responded. On behalf of himself and his brother, he said they felt that the occasion wa.s a very important one. That they were now succeeding be thought might be taken for certain. (Applause.) They had had the gbod luck to obtain a piece of land .which from its situation was eminently suited for the new works. In the first place, they were sufficiently up the river to be out of the reach Of the Liverpool dock and harbour dues, which on a cargo of tallow would amount to so.methinglike 4s 10d a ton. They would be able to bring caro4 oppositcP Bromborough Pool,. send their flats alongside, and tranship and discharge it at the works, thus avoiding the payment of master porterage, cartage, dock and town dues' and everything. As com- pared'swith Warrington, this Would mean a saving of something like 8s 7d to 9s a ton. (Applause.) Another point of advantage was that they would be quite inde- pendent of railways. With all these advantages, they would be able to produce soap at a cost below which no one couldto. (Applause.) It was contemplated toerect upon a portion of the land which had been acquired at Bebington cottages for the workmen employed at the factory—semi-detached houses, with gardens back and i front, n which they would be comfortable and would ! learn that there was more enjoyment' in life than the mere going to and returning from work and looking for- ward to drawjng their wages on the Saturday. (Loud applause). Believing that cleanliness was next to godli- ness, his brother and himself proposed that each house should have a bath ; and in order that the workmen and the girls—of whom there were at present 250 employed—might go home clean from their daily toil, lavatories would be provided in connection with the new works. (Applause.) He thanked the company for the kind manner in which they had drunk the toast, and he hoped that, with the assistance of those whom he saw around him, without

..... „ ....-... which their own efforts would be all in vain, the firm of Lever Brothers woulcLbe more successful than ever. (Loud applause.) In conclusion, he proposed the health of "The Travellers," than whom, he said, no firm in the United Kingdom had more able body of representatives. (Applause.) \The toast having been drunk, was responded to by Mr. White, the oldest traveller iri the employ, and by repre- sentatives from London, Edinburgh, Manchester, New- castle, Carlisle, Belfa-st, Bristol OiNird, North and South Wales. The healths of the staffs at Warringeon and London and of the advertising staff were next proposed, and responded to by the heads of the various departments after which the proceedings terminated.

div.head: CHAPTER VIII. A RULING POWER.
div.p: CHAPTER VIII. A RULING POWER.

Geoffrey Stanhope's painting room in Eaton-square had once been the,nursery ; it was called ,so still, though it had long been converted into O. joint stock recreation room for both Geoffrey and Irene. ty Naturally Ferdinand might have claimed his share in it had he chosen, but Ms pursuits were not their pursuits, and he seldom joined the group of which. Phyllis more frequently than not made up the trio. She knew nothing of art but what the other two taught her; but she had a keen sense of appre- ciation, and never grew tired of sitting as Geoffrey's model, while Irene played on an old piano, which had certainly seen its best days, or warbled forth to her own accompaniment on the guitar. some melody of the South. They are sitting now in the well- accustomed room, Geoffery in a holland blouse, painting,, as it seems, assiduously, Phyllis half reclining on a divan of 'cushions, which he has arranged for her, watching him in a sort of speech- less ecstacy,/ while Irene- lounges,/ dreaming, in an armchair by the window,the piano closed by her side. For at least a quarter-of-an-hour not a sound has been uttered. Something has evidently stagnated the happiness of that usualtly merry, contented group. Perhaps it is the heat,for the' thermometer is at 84deg. —but no, they are scarcely old enough to object to the dog-days • their silence has a stronger and deeper cause. Geoffrey is the first to break it.., . "It is impossible to paint," he cries; "everything is wrong to day. Your raspberry coloured gown, Phylits, against those 'crimson cushions, jars till it drives me nearly mad." • 1" lam sorry, she says, rising; and walking across the room she takes an Eastern-looking cover off a table and throws it over the cushions, and then, half- seating herself upon them,again asks, "Is that better, ' Geoff ? ' He bows his head in acquiescence, while such • a glowing light of love shines on her from his dark eyes that hers sink abashed before it. "You are lovely, darling ; more lovely than ever to-day; so beautiful I cannot hope to do you justice. I wonder what lies made my little Phyllis so much more beautiful of late," lie murmurs, as, instead of taking up his brash again, he seats himself on the cushions beside her. _ . •

"If I look better, Geoffrey, it is because I am so happy in the knowledge that you really love me." ' He looked very intently into her face and said, "Yet there is something of sadness mixed, up with this new lease of beauty you have taken." She turned from him, and her cheek paled just a tinoe . "What it it, -my love? Tell me. Jam to beyour husband, you know, and should have full confession of your worries as well as of your joys." "I have no—well, no absolute Worries, Geoffrey ; still I cannot help looking into the future with dread.' This great Secret id our love brings to me such immense happiness that it frightens me. What will happen v'hen it is no longer a secret, and Lady Fedora and Mr. Stanhope knew 'it—and my father. Oh, Geoffrey, I sometimes think I shall ; never live through that time, but shall run away and hide or drown myself." "Good gracious, Phyllis, I ahrays believed you to be a brave little person. lam sure I have seen' you dare many a mighty jump; befole which most girls would have 'quailed." "Jumps when' we were at play or used to scour the country for amusement. are not like jumps in life," 'said Phyllis, solemnly. "You ought to have left me, Geoff, to my jumps in father's wood-yard. I feel certain if you try to make a lady of me some terrible thing will happen." "And this is what you call your immense happi- ness in my love ! Really, Phyllis, lam surprised at you. If you are so afraid of what our relations will say and do, let us ,run away and get married, and then it will not much matter what happens." " 0, no, no ! Geoffrey. I would not do such a thing for worlds. Lady Fedora has trusted me to be with you and Irene. How base it would be for me to be- have like that 1" "You think of everyone hut me; Phyllis," be said, rather tartly ' • "perhaps, after all, you would prefer to marry that individual who glared at you at the rail- way station." ' Phyllis's very 'lips grew white as she muttered in very low tons—" 0 Geoffrey, it is unkind to try me so."

Her words did not, however, tend to make him more kind ; on the contrary, his brow contracted, and he, too looked at her with something of the glare to which he had jusi alluded ; in fact their conversation had every appearance Of ending in a quarrel, since Geoffrey was by no means satisfied that there was not the shadow of an old flirtation with Tom Chilton between him and his love. Phyllis always 'denied it, but her man= never IFtierned to endorse the assur- ance of her words, • Irene, however, at this juncture, started up from her dreaming posture. "Merciful goodness!" she exclaimed, "I wonder if mamma is at home!" .

"My mother at home! Why, what do you mean? asked Geoffrey, joining her at the window from which she stood gazing, her face whiter than the artistically clinging virginal robe she wore; yet Irene was ever pale. " There is Prince Lenskoff driving across the square I I know he is earning here." • Geoffrey looked at her,and tie shadows on his brow deepened. "Poor little aister, is your d oorn, too, st aled so soon?" And a something passed over him which he could not define, but he felt that he dreaded all that the future had in store for Irene. . She, however, sought to regain • her usually bright spirits. " Hush! Geoff. No nasty ominous remarks, if you please. Just crane your head out of he window, and see if 'the Prince comes Geoff did as he was bid, and at'the risk of a sun- stroke ascertained that the Prince had been admitted and was probably at this moment on the way to the drawing-room. "I wonder if mamma will send for me? was Irene's next query. "Shan't you go down unless she does ? " asked Phyllis. No, certainly not! I would .not appear too in- terested in Lenskoff for millions." "Yet, though you have only seen him once, I be- lieve you Ivould give us all up, and follow his for- tunes to Russia, observed Geoffrey, laughing rather Oh, Geoff, I never thought of such a thing,." "And I hope fervently you never will." "Why, Geoff? You have never seen Prince Lenskoff." "No, Mit I have heard of him, Irene; his has been a dark life, one in which no young and simple girl like yourself can have any place." " Place ? No! Perhaps he does not wish me to have a place there; but it is the' very strangeness and mystery of his life that interest me. lam only seventeen,but I am bored to death by the monotonous sameness of all the other men I have met. All their *vices and all their pleasures are alike." • " What do, you know about men's vices, little. sister?" " Well, there's, Ferdinand, he is a fair average specimen of a man in a fast set. All the others are about the same pattern—you, dear old Geoff, arequite out of the question." "And you think you will find Something newer and more to your taste in the life of this Russian Prince? Oh, Irene, I trust you will not be dis- appointed." Dear old croaking Geoff. Hush, what is that ? " He had no time to answer her, or even to look round, before Lady Fedora, accompanied by Prince Lenskoff, was in the room., That strangers should intrude on the privacy of this apartment was an un- heard-of thing, and Geoffrey at all events was very much inclined to resent the arrival of this Prince. Lady Fedora Aid not, however, offer an)' explanation for bringing him there; she had chosen to do so, and that she considered, quite a sufficient reason for her children. Her white brow rfackered when she saw Phyllis, of whose presence in the hoise she was un- aware. Lady Fedora's white 'brow had taken to puckering of late when Phyllis was brought under her immediate notice and yet, as far as Geoffrey was concerned, she suspected nothing.. Prince Lenskoff shook hands with Irene and made a courteous speech about the pleasure he felt in being permitted to penetrate intothe sanctum of the house, accompanying his words by such an ardent gaze 9f admiration that the blood came coursing in full flow into her pale cheeks, and, in truth, tingled through her frame till she almost cried aloud from the plea. sirable sensation that was so nearly allied to pain. Another moment and Lenskoff had turned his glance towards Phyllis. Hers was a beauty of another and ruddier type; for beautiful he decided that she was, though scarcely fitted to be a Princess as WU

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock.• • THE PROCEDURE RULF-ci. A persistent effort was made when the consideration of the procedure rules was resumed, to obtain tile appoint- ment of a Grand Committee to deal with bills relating, to Wales. Some amusement was caused by Mr. Osbdrne Pdorgan's remark that the Welsh had a language and literature, but the Scotch had only an accent. It was , contended by many hon. pembers that Wales, like Scot- land, had little desire for Horne Rule; but that the Gov- ernment might reasonably grant the request in Mr. Rathbone's amendment for a Grand 'Committee, which should include the members for Wales and Monmouthshire —Mr. RAIRES, replying for the Govern- ment, seemed to imagine that the Welsh members were all descendants of Shaksperds Mellen, for, discovering beneath the proposal a restless disposition towards the dis-establishment of the Church, he said most emphatic- ally that the Government were not going to let Welsh- men set fire to their house and permit the flames to ex- tend elsewhere. Even if such a Committee were granted, no Welsh member ought to sit upon,, it unless he could speak the Welsh language; and he added, amid laughter, that though hon. members had speken of the splendid and peceher literature of Wares, it was never- theless a fact thaT outside the Principality Welsh litera- ture was unknown, though he believed there was one bard in the House—Mr. Osborne Morgan—who had been made a sort of acolyte in the Welsh hierarchy. The House divided, and there were for Mr. Rathbone's amendment 113, against 135 • majority 22. Another amendment,, proposed by dr. Rule 13, relating to the constitution of Standing Committees, was then agreed to, and the new procedure completed. OUR MILITARY SYSTEM. • Lord RANDOLPH Cans:emu. resufned the debate on Sr Walter 13arttelot's motion for a Royal Commission to in- quire into the military and naval requirements. for the protection of the empire. It was, his lordship said, prac- tically a loud cry Of intense disgust at our present military position which was deplorably unsatisfactory notwithstan- ding the increased expenditure. "Reform your system" was his remedy, and if they did that the money now spent would be more than ample to maintain the army in a state of thorough efficiency.. There was as much wisdom in allowing the civil element to have so much power in our military system as there would be in ap- pointing Mr. Bmdlaugh head, of the Cinirch and Arch- bishop of Canterbury.—Mr. STANHOPE replied to Lord Randolph's criticisms, and saki such a Commission as was suggested would occupy years, would make public everything connectol with the military resources of the country, and destroy the re- sponsibility and freedom of action of the Government.— The motion for a Commission was negatived without a division, and the SPEAKER put the question that the House should go into Committee of Supply.—Mr. SMITH Moved that the que,stionlbe now put, and the House di- vided, when there *ere—for the closure 250, against 75. —The Irish members challenged a division on the motion to go into Committee, and the figures were—for the . motion 268, against 63. The twenty-first annual meeting of the Wairing- ton,Permanent Benefit Building Society was held in Cairo-street School-room on Friday evening week, under the presidency of Mr. A. Kenworthy, when there was a good attendance. Amongst the gentlemen who supported' the Chairman on , the platform were the Rev. A. Kenworthy, ma Messrs. J. Chitchley„T. Critchley, Wm. Dick, E. W. Gaskell, Jos. Kay, F. Massey, C. Twiss (managers), P.' C. Price (one of the stewards), Robert Davie. and Kirkoonnell (solicitors), and Robeit Proud (secre- tary.)—The SECRETARY (Mr. Proud) read the state- ment of accounts, and the managers' report, the latter of which read as follows :—" The managers have pleasure in laying before the members the twenty- first annual statement of account, showing the amount of business done for the past year. The total receipts are £9BOl 2s 7d. The advances made to borrowers are smlllebeing £707 14s Bd, against £5,224 '3s 5d repaid, leaving the balance of the inorlegd account £54,044 4s Od. The amount subscribed by investors is £1,822 7s 6d, against £6,254 Os 5d withdrawn, leaving the lbalance of that account £51,320 17s sd. The entrance fee is now 2s per share. The profits, after de- ll ducting working expenses, aro £2,214 3s 10dhout of, 'which the managers declare a dividend at the rate of £4 Ilper cent, which absorbs £2,028 Os 64, leaving a balance of £lB6 3s 4d, which is carried to the contingent fund. There are 558 members upon the books, of which 482 are investors, and 76 borrowers.—The CHANNuyi in propos- ing the adoption of the report of the bal'lnce sheet, oke in terms of encouragement of the future prosperity of the society. There was, he said, no probability of the managers asking the members to accept less than four per cent, dividend, and he was happy to say that they were looking forward lto an increased rate of intereskin time to come.—Mr. Com seconded the proposition.—ln the course of an able speeck in support of the resolution,. Mr. R. DAVIES said that it had become a somewhat serious matter for people to learn where to put their Money so that it wouldproduce anything like what they trbEd to consider an adequate return. Five per cent: used to be a normal rate. He had seen that reduced gradually to 4 per cent., it had now got down to 3i per cent. They now aaw in the papers that the Chancellor of the Exchequer was credited with the idea of reducing the interest of the 3 per cent. Consols. Ho thought that they should be extremely thankful to get the 4 percent. dividend as things now were. He should be farely well satisfied if a good and safe dividend at 4 per cent, could be looked forward to, which, in the opinion of the managers, they might reasonably expect. Altogether,' he thought that he might sincertly congratulate the shareholder% on What he considprod to be the good', sound financial position of the society.—The resolution was then adopted.—The following officers for the ensuing year were then elected —Managers:: Messrs: James Kenworthy (chairman), John Critchley, Thomas Chritchley, William Dick, Edwin, W. div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE EITROPEAN SITUATION.AUSTRT- A . PREPARING FOR WAR. VIENNA, SUNDAY NIGHT.—The Government dies not intend to wait for the expiration of the present Army Law, which extends up to the end of 1889, but will in- Amduce bills in the two Parliaments of Austria and Hungary immediately after Easter in favour of increas- ing the war footing of the regular army of the Empire from eight hundred thousand to probably one million men. The bill is to take effect immediately after being passed. As this increase of the Austro-Hungarian troops by about 25 per cent:, of existing numbers will neces- sitate a corresponding addition to the stores for the army, such as rifles, uniforms, and other articled of equip- ment, as well as of 'an enormous quantity of provisions, and as, moreover, the Delegations meet as a rule only once a year, an extraordinary vote will be asked for. The amount will hardly be'leßs than ne hundred million florins; The Delegatioes will meet to consider these pro- posals at Pestli early in May. There is very little doubt Cs to the acceptance bath of the Military Bill by the two Parliaments and of the extraordinary credit by the Dele- gations : Such an enormous sacrifice on the NA of • a comparatively poor empire like Austria-Hungary, with its constant deficits in .both sections of the monarchy. furnishes the hest evidence how serious the international situation is considered to be. VIENNA, Mom:Av.—The Pres,me hears from Sofia, on good authority, that a revolutionary movement is notice- I able in Eastern Rourneliai in which province 40 army officers were recently arrested on a charge of high , treason. It is'said that the proclamation of the Republic was intended. This news had to be sent by post, as a telegram was stopted by the Bulgarian Government. PARIS. MONDAY.—According to diplomatic news re- ceived here the Porte is disposed to send to Sofia a declaration of its belief in the illegality of Prince Ferdi- nand's positiop, without waiting for the Powers to arrive at.a unanimous decision in the matter. • ' ' THE GERMAN CROWN PRINCE.—CONTRA, DICTORY REPORTS.—THE AGED 'EM- PEROR. i • SAN REMO, SUNDAY Nionr.-:-Profes.sor, Walflmever's arrival yesterday caused a had • impression here. Although the Prince's entourage appear to be in compara- tively good spirits, all hopes 'of an early recovery is entirely given up. Professor Waldmeyer spent the greater part of the morning with Sir Morel' examining. the preparations submitted to him, but the result of the examination is unknown. It is sta,ted that in no case -will Professor Waldmeyer's decision be made known in San Remo before being communicated to the Emperor. All interest is now centred in the result of this examina- tion, which is awaited with the greatest anxiety, not unaccompanied with universally expressed hope of a favourable conclusion. . SAN Remo, MONDAY Nmotr.—The physicians maintain complete silence on the case, and an ireptession is gain- ing ground that the result of Dr. Waldmeyer's examina- tions will notabe made known, whether satisfactory or not. Such a decision will not tend to alleviate the general anxiety. Meanwhile it is satisfactov to note that the general condition of the Prince is slightly im- proving. It is announoed that Prince William took with him to San Remo an anto_Tranh letter trona the Emperor to the Crown. Prince, in which his Majesty expreesed the wish that his son should return to Berlin. Effect will, it is said, be given to the Fitnneroes desire at the • end of March, and preparations for the Prince's recep- Alen_are being made in the Royal Palace here. TO° Councillors are, to be attached to Prince William, with a the duty of reporting to his Royal Highness on State affairs. It is believed that Protessor Gneist will be one of them. A General, whose task it will be to advise on military Matters, is also to be placed in special attend- ance upon his 'Royal Highness. The Ministerial order, Which empowers' Prince William to sign Royal decrees and ordinances, shoeld occasion arise, dates from the end of November last. BERLIN, MoNnAr.—The Emperor is Puffering from a slight cold. During the first part of last night his sleep ,eas broken. ~FRANCE.—GENERAL BOULANGER.—MILI- TARY PREPARATIONS:—AN EXPRESS IN , DANGER. Pants, MoNnAr.-LGeneral Boulanger has addressed a letter to the War Minister, dated "Clermont Ferrand, Zrd inst.," in which he says :—" Pressing solicitation has been made to me in regard to the eleetions being held •t his month. My clear duty from the potitiOn which I occupy, and more particularly from the period which we are piassing through, being to devote myself gxeltisively to my military duties:l have the honotir to ask you, with the object of putting an end to t,he manifestations which have just occurred, and which are being again attempted in connection with my name, to be good enough either to publish the present letter or to authorise me to publish a letter, in which I should beg my friends , not to waste upon myself votes which I cannot accept." j PARTS, MosmAy.—The Chamber of Deputies to-day concluded the debate upon the Budget of Public Works, and commenced the discussinn of the War Estimates.— The Marquis de la. Ferronnays, of the Right, asked if the War Minister proposed to call out the whole contingqnt this year.—General Logerot replied, regretting his inability to give a precise •reply to such a question so , long beforehand.—The discussion was resumed at a later sitting, when M. Kellar said the constant Ministerial changes and reductions in the War Budget tended greatly to prejudice the military position of the country. The Minister of War replied that 19,000 men weuld this year be restored to the ranks whose sefvices were lost ,

div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.
MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Sunday sermons in aid of Wesleyan Home Missions were preached in Bold-street and Bewsey- road Wesleyan Chapels by the Rev. W. Brooks and the Rev. E. H. Jackson. On Monday evening a meet- ing in furtherance Of the same object was held in Bold-street Chapel. Alderman John Crosfield pre- sided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. H. T. Smart, of Manchester, who attended as a depu- tation, G. E. Young, W. Brooks, and E. H. Jackson; and Mr. Barlow. There was a good attendance. Alderman CROSFIBLD, who was received with ap- plause, said he was very glad to be there that night if his presenee could do anything to further the good work of home mission, but he felt that perhaps some one else might have been got more suitable to take the chair than himself. He supposed the reason why he was asked wes that he was neither a Churchman nor a Dissenter. (Laughter.) He was brought up, as a good many of them knew, a mem- ber of the Society. of Friends. He belonged to that body till ho was four-and-twenty years of no, and he left them because of their rules of disetline, which he thought were not suitable to the age, and since then they had been entirely altered. But the principle of the Society of ,Friends remained in his blood;and bone, and would never be obliterated as long as-long as he lived. He looked upon their principles as the simplest and loftiest that any. sect could have, because they took the plain teaching of the New Testament, and they acted as closely as they could up to the teaching of Jesus Christ. There was no doubt that 'every one of then inside that building, and every Englishman and Englishwoman, to-dat enjoyed religious liberty far more than would hive been the case if there had not been a Society of Friends. (Hear, hear.) They had always upheld religious 'liberty, and many of them would know that they had sacrificed themselves—they were im- prisoned to death, they were burned at the stake, and it hall been tried to stamp them out, but as was always tffe case when itwastruth that was preached, the more it was tried to stamp it out the stronger it grew. (Hear, hear.) He had far more sympathy with home missions than with foreign missions—al- though he would be the last to`say a word against such men as Livingstone and Moffatt, who in their conscience believed it was their duty to go into, foreign lands td preach the gospel, but he thought ' Chat they had got an immense mass of heathenism in their own towns and cities, and that they ought to deal with the evil that is at home before they spent their energies abroad. (Hear, hear.) The two greatest curses in England are war and drink----(hear, hear,)—and it ought, in his opinion, to be'the duty in every Sunday school and in every day school to inculcate into the minds of the children the blessings of peace and the evils of war. Nothing to his mind was more melan- choly than to see a nation like this, which called itself a nation ef Christians, carried away like madmen at the time of war. (Hear,- hear.) Haying referred to. the Crimean war as an .instance of the evil he alluded to, he said he was anxious that the rising generation should be well taught the principles of peace as they were taught in the New Testament. (Applause.) ,He defied any man to defend war out of the New Testament. What was the word in the New Testament used by Christ more than anrother ? It was the word "peace." (Hear, hear.) They were told in the New Testament that blessed were the peacemakers. (Hear, hear.) It was not many years ago when to his utter astonishment, and horror he might say, there was one of the most 'eloquent bishops Of the Church of England positively declaring publicly that it was right to spread Christianity by means of the sword and the cannon. Well, he thought that any clergyman —bishop or whatever else he might be•-ought to have been put from his office for declaring a thing like that, as it was totally contrary to the teaching of scripture. (Hear, hear.) He thought they would all agree with him that war and drink were the two great evils, and he should hope that the object of their missions and the missions connected with all other sects was to teach and to preach the gospel of pears. (Applause.) The Rev. E. H. JACKSON next submitted the annual report. He remarked that although he had been in War- rington only' between five and six months, he had repeatedly heard of their chairman's liberality towards works such as that. (Hear, hear.) The chairman had referred to the two great evils of war and drink, and lie (Mr. Jackson) was more and more convinced that the greatest evil Jesus Christ had to contend with *as the drink. • (Hear, hear.) As be went down Buttermarket- • street the previous day, he passed a public-house and it appeared to him from the noise that was made that some forty people were there, while other poor men were staggering up the street and tumbling through the door, being drunk on the Lord's Day. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Jackson then read the report, from • which it appeared thatithe number of circuits receiving grants for the support of home missionary ministers is 51. Several of these, founded and cherished by the fund, were rapidly approaching the position of self-supporting circuits. The number of ministers whose names appear as home missionary ministers in the minutes of the con- ference is 84. Of these three are connexional evangel- ists, and 17 district missioners. In addition to these 12 ministers are appointed to labour for the benefit of Wes- leyan Methodists in the Army and Royal Navy in Great Britain. The number of circuits assisted by the fund exne4s 300; 44 missions have been conducted during the yeir by the connexional evangelists, generally witho Marked success. The income for the year now closed had been £35,826 8s 3d. The income of .the year pre- ceding was £33,465 4s Bd. The expenditure has amounted to £36,195 lOs sd, being £1,715 16s 7d more than that of last year. Toward § tile income Warrington had contributed ,as follows :—Yearly collection, £20"; Congregational ditto, £25 13s 8d; public meeting, £8 8s 9d; juvenile association, £l2 6s't Mr. W. Bennett, 5s : Mr. R. Garnett. QV; Mr. T. S. Smith, £1 is; total. £6B 14s sd: . The Rey. W. BROOKES, in an Adress, reAerred to the grosing indifference of the working classes of this coun try or religion. He had no doubt that drink had. great deal to do with the matter, but there were other causes that would help to account for what was a very solemn fact. (Hear, hear). The Rev. H. T. SMART next delivered an interesting I address relative to Wesleyan Home Mis.iion work. .Mr. Bani,ow moved, and the Rev. WI Ihrooxas secon- • ded a vote of thanksto the chairman tor presiding, and this was heartily accorded. In responding, Mr. CROSFIRLD said he did not want it to be understood when he said that he was neither a Churchman nor a. Dissenter that he did not belong to any sect at all. (Laughter.) He wanted just to tell them that he be- longed to the sect called Christians. (Hear, hear.) He Perfectly agreed with Mr. Smart that this work amongst the poor was not bound in the narrow borders of any sect. It was a work that called upon every Christian Englishman to do what he coprd to raise the poor out of the ditch. (Hear, hear.) Rtferring to Bank Quay Mission, Mr. Crosfield said a splendid work *as being done there by working-men. They had snatched many a one out of the fire and drawn them by persuasion to come to chapel instead of going to the pub- lic-house. There were den now at Bank Quay who had been on the verge of destruction, but whohadnow clean, happy, and comfortable homes, and their children were well-dressed and well fed. That was the sort of thing that wanted doing, if possible, thrOughout the country. (Hear, hear.) He should just like to say that his views on religion were so broad that it did not matter' to him what sect people belonged to. He did not care so long as men's hearts were in the right place. What he wan- ted to see in this country was more liberality in religious feeling between Church people and Dissenters, and he Should like to see the Archbishop of Canterbury preach in that pulpit and some Methodist minister preach in Canterbury Cathedral. (Laughter and applause.) That Would be the way to produce a strong and health,y, feeling between the different sects in this • country. ' (Loud applause). The singing of the doxology brought the meeting to E close.

div.head: NAVY ESTIMATER,
div.p: THE NAVY ESTIMATER,

The• Navy Estimate; for 1888.89, with the official memoranda of Lord'George Hamiltou, First Lord of the Admiralty, and Mr. A. B. Forwood, Parliamentary Sem- taryKif the Atmiralty, were issued on Monday. From Mr. Forwood's statement it appears that if the Navy is to be maintained at its existing strength, a sum of £2,070,389 should be expended in new construction in the coming year, exclusive of armament. The net esti- mates for the coming year amount to £13,082,800, as compared with £13,988.381 for the expiriag year, a de- crease of £905481. •Lord George HaMiltonstates that our organisation for war has much improved during the last year, and satisfactory progress has been made in work- ing out and fitting together the complementary parts of a scheme for a full utilisation, in time of emergency, of the naval resources of the country. The determination of the Government to effectively arm the coaling stations abroad and the home ports must largely increase our offensive naval power. The Estimates make provision for all immediate requirements. The numeral strength of the Navy provided for is 62,11.06" officers, men, and marines. The entire cost of maintaining the personnel of the Navy anacunts to £8,331,000. FINANCIAL REFORM MEETING. The annual conference of the Financial Reform Asso; elation was held in Glasgow on Monday, Mr. E. K. Mtn- pratt, Liverpool (President), in. the chair.—A letter of apology was read from Sir George Trevelyan, M.P., who said that he should have been very much interested in attending, the meeting, for herecognised the wcirk which the association was doing. He believed that the ex- travaga nees and irregularities of our expenditure and tile personal interests which depended on them were the main, motives for retaining a great deal of what as bad in our politicaransi administrative system.—The Chair- man, in meving the adoption of the report, stated that although the association had not attained all that they desired in, the way of the Abolition of duties on com- modities during the forty years of its existence, good work had been done in the way of controverting the principles of Fair Traders.—Air..Tacklion (Liverpool) moved, "That unless Provision be made in the Budget for the repeal of the .dury upon tea, coffee, chicory, dried fruits, gold and silver plate. Spd the tax upon carriages, the sense of tint House ought to be taken as to the abolition of such duties, and the substitution of a tax upon land values." —Mr. Kenneth Cochrahe (Galashielli) next moved, "Tleft this meeting views with satisfaction the appointment by the Government of Special Committees to examine the various Estimates before these are submitted to the house of Commons, and congratulates financial' re- formers upon the 'adoption of a principle which they have for forty years advocated."—Mr. J. M. Cherrie next proposed, "That this meeting deprecates any attempt being,,made in the forthcoming Local Government Bill to transfer taxation from proearty. to industry."—All the resolutions were adopted.
