div.head: GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: GOVERNMENT BILL.

_ There is reason to believe, writes the London cor- respondent of a Manchester paper, that the Cabinet on Saturday did not close the draft of the Local Govern- * inent Bill, that• Lord Hartington has expiessed.his wish to consult Mr.. Chamberlain on certain points of the greatest importance, and that in fact the bill will remain . . unsettled *until next week, when Mr. Chamberlain. returned to London, wiR drop his diplomatic and re- assume his political character. On the 19th instant Mr. Ritchie will have a statement of unusual length and complexity to place before the House, and it is most. Kobable lhat•the debate on the motion for leave to bring in the bill wilt occupy a couple of sittings. 'There is a rumour that the Government will ask for prece- dence for the successive stages of the bill, as they have already done for the new rules, and there is no doubt that a section of the House who are amtiotts to see legislation pressed forward would favour this course. But, on the other hand, it would be stoutly resisted by a large number of private members, both on the Conservative and Liberal benches, who have bills and motionvon.the paper. A member of the Govern-, ment, I. am :told, confessed on Friday to some doubt ichether thw. measure would find its way into law at all this session in view of the tnutitudinous diversities of opinion*which are certain/to arise on its details. '

IRELAND. A warder named Daly has been dismissed from Sligo' Gaol for, it is stated, surreptitiously supplying a copy ol United Ireland to Mr. Sheehy, M.P. - On Monday, Mr. Sexton. M.P., who while he was ill was elected Lord Mayor of Dublin, appeared for the first ' time in his official capacity at a meeting of the Corpora- tion. He looked rather pale, and seemed now to be almost as strong aslefore he became ill. On taking the Chair he was very warmly received, the occupants of the gallery cheering him with great vigonr. The London correspondent of the Dublin Express says: "The further time asked for by Mr. Parnell, of the 'active section *in America, is rani* expiring, and the Parnell- Rae want some new sensation. The Sullivan-Sexton -scandal disturbs their domestic harmony, and the Gaelic Society feud will soon appear on the surface. The plaister which temporarily covered the wound was not the manufacture of Archbishop Croke or Mr. Davitt, but from New• York." Mr. Devitt writes to the Freeman's Journal to say that 600 families, numbering 3,000 persons, on Arran Islands, off Galway, are completely destitute, and that unless seed, potatoes, and food are given they must die in hundreds of starvation. Mr. Devitt adds thaethe Local Government Board know the condition of affairs, but merely reply that urgent cases will be relieved in the usual way. That is very poor relief, the nearest work- house being in Galway, 30 miles distant. During the hearing of a. case at the police-court, at Belfast, on Saturday, an extraordinary charge was pre- fermi against two constables 4 Several witnesses deposed that the policemen, while under the influence of drink, entered, the house of Mrs. Latimer, and after demanding porter. which was refused, one of them violently assa NI a girl named Donelly, end afterwards threw a child on the fire. The neighbours, hearing screams, broke open the door, and Donelly was rescued through a win- dow. The case was adjourned for inquiries. ANOTHER ENGLISII DELEGATE ARRESTED. Mr. Snelling,, delegate to Ireland from the English Hotne Rule Associatien, has been afreitted at Newmarket, county I,,imerick, for a speech recently delivered at Six- mile Bridge. THE PROSEQUTION OF MR. GILHOOLY, M.P. The further hearing of the .charge against Mr. Gil- hooly, M.P., was resumed at Schull,•on Monday.—Michael Hegarty, for intimidating whom Mr. Gilhooly has been prosecuted: was examined, and said he was, boycotted for supplying cars to the police. Since the meeting at which Mr. Gilhooly speke, his emplov§s had left him, and no one would buy his butter. Fie attributed this more to local sDleen than anything which occurred at the meeting. SENTENCE ON MR. GILHOOLY, M.P. The trial of Mr. Gilhooly, M.P., concluded at Schull, on, Tuesday. Mr. Gilhooly declined to make a legal defeece, and said he regarded the Court with the greatest con- tempt, and did not care what ribnishment was inflicted. The magistrates, after deli berathin. sentenced him to two months' imprisonment, without hard labour. An appeal was lodged. Mr. Gilhooly was re-arrested immediately after leaving the Court, on a charge of assaulting In- svector Hayes, at &lull, on the 2nd inst.
RELEASE OF MR. WILFRID BLUNT.

On Tuesday, shortly before nine o'clock, Mr. Wilfrid Blunt was released from Kilmainham Prison, whither he had been transferred from Galway Prison, for conveni- ence in attending the trial of his action against Divisional Magistrate Byrne and Mr. Balfour. He was received by Lady Anne Blunt, Aid. Dillon, and several friends, besides a small crowd, who raised a cheer. Mi. Blurt drove, with Lady Anne Blunt, to Aid. Dillon's residence.

Mr. Blunt was pale, but otherwise no change in his appearance was noticeable. He bowed to the crowd, which included representatives from nearly all branches of the National League in Dublin, one of which—the Brian Boroo— presented him with an address, welcoming him back from prison, and assuring him of their high admiration of his chivalrous conduct in aid of their cause' by which he and his English compatriots had begotten and solidi- fied a union between the democracies of England, Scotland. and Ireland, that must be potent for the good of all. Mr. Blunt did not reply.

CILLKEERLAIN.—At, meeting of the Birmingham Town Council, on Tuesday, it was decided to tonfer the honorary freedom of the borough upon Mr. Chamberlain on his return from the United States, and also to present to him a congratula- tory address. Early on Monday mbrning, flames broke out in a book- ing office at Ascot Station. The stationmaster, Mr. Grieg, obtained assistance, and the flames were extin- guished, but not before the contents of the booking office were destroyed. The origin of the conflagration is unknown. Bank notes to the value of £l,lOO stolen from the British Linen Company's Bank, Coldstream, Berwick- shire, three days ago have been discovered by Supt. Moir_, of the Berwiskshire police, concealed in a corn- stack of a farmer named Kerr. Robert Kerr, son of the latter, has been arrested on suspicion. He was a junior clerk in the bank. .

The dead bodies of two sisters, both of whom had been missing from their home at Stanningley, near Leeds. for a month, have been found, one in the Leeds and Liverpool Canal at moss Bridge, Rodley, and the other in the river at Apperley Bridge. Nothing is known as to the cause of the girls leaving home. Deceased were twin sister., 23 years of nee. MOTHER AND MDR DIE TOGETISPR.—At Peace Oft, Sheffield, on Monday moraine, Maria limund. wifeof a furnaceman out of emplovtrient, was found dead in bed with her youneest child Icing beside her also dead. Two other children sleeping in the same bed were uninjured, and no foul play is suspected, the woman having been ill for some time.

In consequence of the alarming incrnase in the num- ber of street mendicants in London. the police have commenced a vigorous series of prosecutions against this class of the community. Upon several miserably-clad individuals who have been arrested within the past few days, large sums of money have been found, one man being in possession of over £3O.

A fire broke nut at Ditchatn House, three miles from Petersfield, on Sunder. Thr property was recently pur- chased by Mr. Cave fitr £B,OOO, and the house was in the hands of the contractors, who were making each room fireproof. Mr. Cave was to have gone into possession this spring. The, entire house and contents were reduced to ashes. The CRIMP of the fire is unknown, but the damage exceeds £200,000,

THE ASSAULT ON LORD HOWARD DR WILLDM—On the •opening of the Middlesex Sessions, on Monday, the Assis• tant Judge referred to the charge against Major Burrowes•of assaulting Lord Howard de Walden, and said there appeared no doubt that his lordships face bore marks of considerable violence. it must also be • rememtfered that th(re was no suggeslion of the defen- dant having acted in self-defecce. Tilj ury returned a true bill: •

-A DISHONEST Casa' FR.—At Bradford, on Monday. Peter Philemon Jaques WAS sentence:F.-to four months' im- prisonment for emberzlement. He had been in his employer's servire for twenty years as cashier and con- fidential clerk, but had to leave. It was then found that there was a deficiency of £1.158. Jaques had sneculated in'shippinz' and had been led to embezzle. The books were not falsified. He Pleaded guilty, after giving him- self up to the police.

At Sheffield, on Monday, Thomas Oxley and Benkunin Lambert, travellers, were charged.with assaulting Alfred Russel Fox, wholesale chemist. The prosecutor was walking down one of the principal streets of the town when, without provocation, it is alleged the prisoners attacked him, striking him over the head and mouth with sticks, knocking, out the whole of one row of teeth, and then made off in a cab. The prisoners were remanded in custody. On Monday, at Wigan, Wm. Ashurst, collier, was charged with smutting. James Hill, underlooker. at Findley. Both parties worked at Pearson and Knowles's colliery. On Tuesday last, Ashurst attacked Hill in. the •road with an iron bar, knocking. him downseveral times, and inflicting serious injuries, requiring medical attend- ance fusd necessitating his absence from work for another fortnight The complainant said there was not the slightest provocation for the assault The prisoner was committed for trial at the Lancas'er Assizes.

THE RECrturriNGFßETurtNs.,--The Annual report of the Inspector-General of Recruits to the Commander-in- Chief has been presented to both Houses of Parliament. The total number of recruits who joined the regular army during 1887 was 31,225, but, although this fell short of th,e number raised in 1886 by 8,184. yet as many were raised as were reguired,• the number voted by Parliament havinz been fully maintained during the Igst six months of the year. Of the numbers enlisted /343 were for long service. gnd 29,682 for short service.

EXTRAMDINABY CASIG-At intervals during the )at few months, 20 needles, one about three inches in. length and others about an inch and a-half, have been extracted from the body of an inmate of the Guisborough Work- house, named .Mary A. Butler, who suffers from epileptic fits. She states that some years ago she had a severe illness. and had mustard blisters placed all over her body, which were fastened tightly round with needles. and she thinks that a quantity of these must have penetrated her body. Although such a large number of needles have been extracted, there are indications that a further number are coming. - -

THE MURDER BY A POACHRI2.—The brother of the deceased man Copley made the following important statement on the night of the njleged murder. He said that the deceased had given hitt the following account of the affray :—The poachers went away. Illingworth sent me one way and he went the other. When I came in sight of them again they were struggling together. The young fellow Pilmore took and laid the gun on the grass and then went to assist his mate. When I got within a few yards of them the young fellow saw me. and we both made for the gun. He succeeded in getting to it first, and as I rushed At him the gun went off as he was picking it up before I knew where I was. SMUGOI.4IO TN LADTRS' IMPROVRRS."—At QUINTTISTAWD, on Sunday, a novel case of smuggling was detected. Two young girls, passengers per the Royal mail steam- ship Celtic, from New York, after landing at the deep- water quay, fashionably dressed, and adorned with rather large improvers, were directed to enter the female searcher's room by the Customs officers, the result being that the improvers were found filled with cakes of cavendish tobacco. The girls protested their innocence. but the official informed both that they were guilty of smuggling, and consequently should pay treble duty and single value on the contraband goods and forfeit the tobacco and improvers. The penalty was complied with.

A DESCENDANT OF MR. Picxmot.--During the Hearing of a case in the High Courtpf Justice on Saturday, be- fore Mr. Baron Huddlestone' and a jury. Mr. Pickets, a son of the famous novelist, counsel for the defendant. said he should call•as a witness:a Mr. Pickwick.—Baron Hmidlestone: Pickwick is a very appropriate witness to be called by Dickens. (Laughter.)—Mr. Dickens: I fully believe that the sole reasbn why I was instructed in this -case was that I might call Mr. Pickwick. (Laughter.) And it may interest ynur. Lordship to learn that this gentleman is a descendant—the grand-nephew, I believe of Mr. Moses Pickwick, who kept a coach at Bath; and I have very good reason to believe that it was from this Mr. Moses Pickwick that the name of the immortal Pick- wick was taken. • THE SALFORD GAS SCANDAL: TRIAL REMOVED.— To the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, an appli- cation was made by Sir Hy. James, on behalf of Samuel Hunter, the late manager of the Salford Gasworks, who now stands to take his trial at the Lancaster Assizes, upon charges of perjury and forgery, far an order directing the venue to be removed from Landaster to the Central Criminal Court, London. The ground of the • application was that the defendant would he more likely to obtain a. fair trial in London than in Lancashire, where the circumstances of the case are so notorious. Sir Chas. Russell, who represented the Salford Corpora- tion, the prosecutors, did not offer any oPposition, and the application was therefore granted.

ALIVE OU DRAp 2 A GRAVEDIGGER'S HALLUCINATIOS. The Leeds coroner, by direction of the Home Secre- tary, held an inquest, on Monday, on the body of Arabella Elizabeth Tetley, 23, wife of Mr. W. Tetley, schoolmaster, Beckwithshaw, near Harrogate. who, it was stated, had been buried alive at Woodhouse Cemetery, Leeds, on the 14th uit, after a fortnight's illness following her con- finement. —Mr. Scattergood, surgeon, who had examined the corpse after the body had been exhumed, cave evi- dence that nothing had been moved in the coffin, and that. there was not the. slightest indication of the deceased having been buried alive. The evidence of the grave- digger who raised the alarm was that he had heard rattling in the coffin. This, -however, it was shown bad resulted from some earth falling upon it.. After bearing evidence as to the cause of death, the jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

TWELVE DAYS AT TEE PUMPS: TIMELY REStIIR. —The Glasgow steamer Sidonian has rescued in a timely manner the captain and crew of the barque St. Olaves. The crew when fallen in with had been twelve days at the pumps, and were then in an exhausted state. The St. °laves as going from Cork to St. John, N. 8., and had on board about 600 tons of railway iron. She encoun- tered very heavy weather, and sprang a Teak. She ad- mitted water very freely, And to keep her afloat the pumps were put ißto 9pP..ration. The crew worked con- . tinuously at the 'imps, otherwise their vessel would have sunk beneath them. Day after day for.twelve days the men worked energetically, but the .water, notwith- standing, gained upon them until when the Sideman hove in sight there were Bft. of water in the vessel's hold. The poor fellows were then nearly done no with the arduous and incessant work, and the appearance of the Sidonian was providential. All of the crew were taken on board the Sidonian, which was going from Messina and Palermo, and landed at New Orleans on the Bth.ult. The St. °laves doubtless foundered soon after

' WARRINGTON RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. • A quarterly meeting of the members of this Assovltlion was held on Thursday evening.in the IVorkmtih's Club, Warrington. The chair was taken by Mr. J. Smethurst, and there were also on the platform Messrs. S. Davies, Jones, H, Thornton, and Walker (assistant secretary). There was a fair aftendance.

The CHAIRMAN remarked that they had called that meeting together, as they thought that some of their members might wish to know what had been done by the committee. Although they had not placarded the town, but simply put an an- nouncement of that meeting in the papers, they thought there might have been more present than there were.
THE DEPOTS AND INFECTIOUS DISEASES DE7TATIONS.TO

LONDON, Stc. The Assistant Secretary read the minutes of a special meeting of the Committee held on February 29th. In these minutes it was stated that the secretary had read a letter from Mr. F. Monks, J.P., intimating his inability to be present at the meeting, and urging that steps should be taken to ascertain the true state of affairs in the Longford matter, and the desirability of half-a-dozen members of the Council banding together for the pur- pose of insisting that reports and other information asked for should be 'presented to the Council, and, through them, to the ratepayers in due course. The letter was received with lively satisfac,tion. It was sqggested that in future contested elections, the eindi- date receiving the support of that Association should contribute a small sum to the 'funds, but no definite amount was settled upon. The Chairman of the Com- mittee (Mr. James Smethurst) afterwards brought for- ward the matter of a deputation from the Corporation going to London for the pose of getting an analysis of the manure manufactured at Longford, an on this subject a very strong feeling was exhibited, and it was decided that one of the Association's representatives in the Council Should ask the question as to the necessity of this kind of expenditure. On the motion of Mr. John Toft, it was decided to ascertain whether the Infectious Diseases hospital was at the present time full of patients, and from what part or parts of the town the cases arose, with a view tol_ finding OUlb whether the neighbourhood of the intercepting de- pots were responsihle for an unreasonable share of fever or other cases of sickness. A vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. James Morris was passed. A discussion tobk place with regard to income tax assess- ment, and it was resolved that inquiries should be made of similar societiesin other towns as to what assistance they gave their members in appealing against • over- charges.—A report was also read aa_to the progress the association had made since its institution. In thi; re- port it was remarked that " it could not, of course; 'be expected that in such a short time the representatives of the association should have succeeded in overcoming all those obstacles which they were so anxious to see re- moved ; at the same time the committee were satisfied that in course of time much good would result from the banding together of the ratepayers in an association of that kind, and they 'confidently appealed to those who had not already done so to join at once so as to give their representatives in the Council that moral support which would enable them to prevent careless or extrava- gant expenditure of the public monies. It was also men- tioned that there were two vacancies on the committee. —The Crumarax said that inquiries had been made as to the districts from which the patients in the hospital had come.—The ASSISTANT SISCRETABY said they had informa- tion that there were 24 cases in the hospital, chiefly scarlet fever, and lie mentionedthatthey understoodthat some of these had come from Napier-street, Hill-street, , Sharp-street, off Battersby-lane, Wakefield-street, and Bank Quay district. He (the secretary) had received Iseveral letters of apology for non-attendance.—Mr. T. FLOOD moved that the report be adopted. He said that after the occurrences of Tuesday night that in regard to a portion at least of the promises made at the inaugura- tion of that Association, there had been no attempt made to carry them out. • (Hear, hear.) That was much to be regretted, and it was to be hoped that a little experience would show the members of the com- mittee *Ho were members of the Council that they could not either treat the Association with indifference or act independently of it. (Applause.) —Mr S. Dawns seconded the proposal, and the reports were adopted.
THE VACANCIES ON THE COMMITTEE. It was unanimously agreed that Mr. T. Flood and Mr. H. F. Greenough should be • appointed to fill the vacan- cies on the committee of the Associatipn.

The CHAIRMAN referred to the lamented death of Coun- cilor Brown, which they regretted very much because they believed he had been a very faithful servant of the ratepayers of the borough. (Hear • hear.) There was i consequently a vacancy n the ward which Mr. Brqwn represented, and they as a Ratepayers' Association were not disposed to let any opportunity pass them when they thought they had a right to interfere. The Chairman then referred in eulogistic terms to the qualifications of Mr. F. Monks, and he moved that that gentleman be 'waited upon by a deputation from that association and asked to become a candidate. (Applause.)—Mr. THORN- TON, in sqconding the proposal, said that if they had Mr. Monks in the Council Chamber they would have a man with a mind of his own. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. FLOOD said it was a matter of general regret through all circles of society when Mr. Monks left the Council before.—After a short discussion the proposal was agreed to unaai- mously, and four gentlemen were apppinted as a deputa- tion to wait upon Mr. Monks. THE VACANCY ON THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The CHAIRMAN mentioned that through the death of I Mr. Brown there would be a vacancy on the Board of Guardians, and he moved that Mr, T. Jones be the can- didate of the Association for that office.—Mr. McgoLtom Seconded this proposal, which was agreqd to:

THE INCOME TAX. Some talk took place with regard to the "lode of assessing the income tax in 'Warrington, against which several of those present complained very strongly. It was urged that the matter should be taken up tly the Association, on behalf of its members, but no definite steps were resolved upon apart from those recommended in the committee's report.

If these had voted he believed the nramit would have been the other way. In his calculation, from the way the markets had turned; the slate, company would clear from £6OO to £l,ooo.—ln answer to. a question, it was stated that there were about 200 members in the association.— Some conversation also took place with regard to asking the committee to consider the advisability of calling a public meeting, after which the meeting terminated.

A HUTTON TRADESMAN FOUND HROWNED.--OD Sunday morning, at a quarter to -twelve o'clock, the body of Thomas Travis, plumber, of Blue Bell-lane, Huyton, was found ipt a large marl pit, in a field belonging to Wood- fall Hall, Huyton, in the occupation of -Mr. W. Haim. It appears that the dean sod, who was forty-two years Of age, left his home at eight o'clock on Saturday night to visit his mother, at Knowsley. On parting from her he said that he *ish'ed to got back quick and would' cross the fields as a short cut'. The night being very dark, he appears to have missed his way and fallen into the pit, which was slightly frozen over, the bank at the spot being six feet high and precipitous.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
qATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1888.

THE people of Scotland and of Wales, as well as of Ireland, are more and more showing themselves in favour of Home Rule for those countries. Ilhe • significancy. of a movement of this kind does not seem to be fully realised, and it is noteworthy that, •as yet, there is no organisation in this country for • lime Rule ih England pure and simple. Mr. W. linch-um is chairman of the committee of what is,

, called the Scottish Party, and he has been in com- munication with Mr. GLADSTONE with a view to \ "ascertaining whether he is favtrurable to the "rapidly-spreading demand' for Home Rule" on the part of Scotland. Mr. GnersTortz's reply is brief, but it is important. He says :- 1 I have rdad for the first time the words you use ' respecting Lord Elgin, but I have on various occa- sions explained myself as to the position of Scotland Under the Act of Union, to the effect that in my opinion it will now be very carefully considered by the Scottish people, and will be treated' in such manner as they, on full consideratioxi, may desire. It will be seen that the leader of the Liberal party is guarded in his statement. He takes up the .Position with regard to the demand for Home Rule for Scotland that Lord HARTINGTON toqk, when questioned in Scotland, as to the disestablishment of the Church. It was a matter, he said, for the People of that couritiy to decide. This was taken as meaning that his lordship would be ready for disestablishment when they.themselves had demon- strated that the'time had arrived for affecting the severance between Church and State. An attitude

df this kind implies that there is no objection to the principle of the course proposed; and this is Mr. GLADSTONEI positidn' with regard to Home Rule. It has. become a pressing necessity for Ire- land; 'and as to Scotland, it will be "carefully con- sidered by the Scottish people, and will be treated in such a manner as they, on full consideration, may desire." The logical issue of this utterance is that Wales and England may have Home Rule too, 1 if.-they do but sufficiently demonstrate their desire it. We cannot but express ourselves'as gratified to find that M. GLADSTOKE has taken up this un- assailable position. Comparatively few, even of the ' Irberal party, have recognised that Hone Rule for eland might mean Home Rule for the other L• ree countries of the United Kingdom. They slowly and painfully reached tthe conclusion Oiat it is inevitable for Ireland; but they do not,

ex•yet, perceive that there is a possibility of the application of the principle be.ing extended. But extended 4 will be, if we read arijght the signs o the times, until there are four Home Rule Parlia- xuents. It may be many years before this evolu- tion is accomplished, but we do not see any ether Ultimate and satisfactory way out of the difficulties by which we shall be beset, even after granting Rome Rule for Ireland. Let it be conceded that Ireland, with a Parlia- iuent on College Given, will still be represented at Westminster.* In that case, we shall either have Irishmen taking part in, and in some degree con- trolling, the domeiitic aflairs of England, Scotland, and Wales; or they will be excluded from debating, Or voting upon, any matters except those, of a Strictly imperial character. 'With regard to the first supposition—that Ireland's representatives at Westminster would take part in all business—we
cannot but think that it would soon be utterly die-

tasteful to English, Scotch, and Welsh electors, Who would naturally say—" Let. Irishmen be.con- tent to manage their own domestic affairs, and leare us to manage ours in our own way." As to the . second idea—that the Irish members should be

compelled to confine their attention to imperial niattere— that would involve a division of the business of Parliament. Imperial affairs would . require to be dealt with in a body, either at the be- ginning or towards the end of a session; for R ,ould hardly be expected that the representatives , of Ireland would remain constantly in attendance ---to be called in as imperial business might arise. In any 'case, the Government of the day would c'eoupy a.peculiar, not to say - unsatisfactory posi- tion. They would never be sure of remaining in °fhee, if they had not a majority so large as to be, Practically independent of the Irish vote. They lAight be strong and triumphant as to domestic legislation ; but—as Lord SALISBURY puts it— when the Irish tap was 'turned on they•would run the risk'of being enfeebled and defeated. Let it be BuPpoied, for instance, that a Tory GI-ovemment, after having .their own way pretty much as to 4emestic legislation, were turned out-of office by the Irish vote on some question of imperial politics. ' Would there not inevitably be a bitter feeling in the Nuntry amongst the Tor' electors? Would there not be a feeling abroad that the Govern- . Trtent had not been fairly dealt with, and would, tins feeling not be likely to operate in ensuring - thatthe same party shouldbe returned to power with a still larger majority? If a Liberal Government Were turned out, the feeling would be pretty much lie sain; there would undoubtedly be a determii nation to get rid of the Irish vote as an all-impor- tant factor. But, how could this be done? it will bO asked; and our answer is—by having Home ute all round. Let there be four Home Rule Parliaments ; one for Ireland, another for Scot- land, a third for Wales, and the fourth for England --dealing simply with domestic affairs; and let/, :there be, in addition, an Imperial Parliament ' sitting at Westminster, to deal' with imperial a.,Mairs. The inhabitants of the four countries of fte United Kingdom would, of course, separately seieci representatives for their lici'me Parliaments; and as to the Imperial Parliament, that might be etrlPosed either of selected representatives from the 11°111° Parliaments, or by direct election from e various constituencies. In any case, it would kt each country on an equal footing, both ea, to me and Imperial affairs, and until this is dOne
there can be no end to the agitation for Home . . Rule.

The'latest information as to the new Local Government Bill is that it will, be introduced by Mr. RITCHIE, in the House of Comtnons, on Thurs- day week. Meantime there is,a, gooil deal of specu- lation as to its provisions; and it is announced, with an air of authority, that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN 19 to be taken into consultation: before it is lid before Parliament. It would seem that the Gov- ernment are anxious to avoid shipwreck 'ofer the measure; and, as the Liberal4Unionists are to be satisfied, there is reason to hope that the Bill will be framed on more democratic lines than might otherwise have been expected. It is thought that the pc:or-law union will be taken as the unit of area, though, if that be done, there will be serious interference with county boundaries. As a matter of fact, out of a total of 617 uniOns, there are no less than 182 that comprise parts of two or more counties. Warrington. Union is a case in , point : the bulk of it is in Lancashire but apart of it is in, Cheshire. It seems to be taken for granted that Local Boards will in part, if not entirely, be. knocked on the head. At a recent meeting of an association of Local Board clerks, it was resolved that steps should be taken for making a claim .for compensation in case of their being 4isplaced by the new bill. But the most vital feature of the measure is involved in the constitution of the new authorities. We know that if Ldd liaNno'ttit CHURCHILL could have his way, the representation of the ratepayers would be direct and democratic; and we would fain believe that the Liberal Union- ists twill not be faithless to their, creed as Liberals in this respect. Still; the Government is a Tory 'Government, and we find it difficult to conceive that they will sign' the death warrant of the county magistrates in the matter of county , government. Mr. Samuel SUTTON, clerk to ,the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority, read an iriteresting and instructive 'paper on County Gov- ernment, on Monday, in the course of which he suggested what he thought might be accepted as a sensible and honourable compromise. "11i is simply" he said, "the insertion .of a clause in the Bill providing that at the outset the justices of each county _have power, at '.general meeting called for the purpose, to nominate and elect cer- tain of their number to act as life members upon , the County Boards to be appointed under the Act. The advantages of this plan are obvious. In the first place, practical experience, combined with valuable advice and assistance to the new mem- bers, would be ensured. This is a very important' consideration, and there can be no doubt the sys- tem would be perfectly workable." Granted that the proposal would be workable, ate math con- sideration is—would it ,be satisfactory to the ratepayers? We think not. The fact is, it would be altogether out of harmony with, present-day ideas of representative government to pitch-fork men into office in this way. What would be thdught of a propo'sal to elect a number' of mem- bers of Parliament for life ? Wofild it not be dis- missed as invidious and' chimerical? And if the representatives`of the highest legislative body in tlie kingdom are to be i,ut through the siege of popula:-...: election, why should-any other course be taken with 'candidates for County Boards? Surely it will not be suggested that a member

of the County Board will be a more important personage than 'a member of Parlia- ment? What is really needed is the extension of the, principle of the 111micipal Reform Act of 035 to the counties. Than thil, after eliminating the aldermanic element, nothing could be better. It is due to remark that the only blot upon the Municipal Reform Act was made, as usual, ty the House of Lords. It WAS Lord LYNDHURST who damaged the Bill by making provisions for the election of aldermen.. It is true that the system his benefited the Liberals in that .it has enabled them 'in many cases to preserve the majorities they have from the first had in the Town Councils; but co-optative electidn is bad in principle, and as such it stands condemned. But reverting to county magistrates, as gentlemen of this class are forthe most part men of property, experience, and influence, it is a matter of course to say that, if they offered themselves as candidates for seats on Cminty Boards, they would be elected, unless there was some good reason why they ihould not be elected. If, with the advantages they possess to begin with, they could not secure the suffrages of their neighbours, they certainly ought not to be elected over their neighbours' heads. We direct attention to the question of the constitution of the new authorities because we regird it as of the ut- most importance. The Tories have a trick of holding the word of promise to the ear and of breaking it to the hope; and Liberals inust see to it that this, if they can help it, is not done in fram- ing the new Local Government Bill. .

Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley tind Wright's, which for strength is unequalled.—Advt.. A sister-in-law of William Thompson, who shot his brother-in-law in a church near Portadown, last week has been arrested on the charge of inciting to the crime. The Liberal Association of the Chichester division of• Sussex decided on Wednesday to contest the division, and a deputation wit, appointed to wait upon Mr. Wilfrid Blunt and request him to become a candidate DEATH SENTENCE .—William Arrowsmith was tried at the Shropshire Assizes, on Wednesday, for the murder of his uncle, an aged man named PiCkerill, at Press, near Shrewsbury, last November. The murder was a very cruel one, and was accompanied by plunder. 'A verdict of guilty was returned, and the prisoner was sentenced to death.

Lord Herschel! presided on Wednesday night at a house dinner of the National Liberal Club, and; in pro- posing success to the Liberal party, predicted that before long 'the Conservatives would themselves propose a measure of Home Rule equal, or perhaps superior, in its advanced views to the measure which they had so much condemned, _ .

_ LORD HABIT/401'0N AT IPswicii.—Lord Hartington on Wedirspay night addressed a crowded meeting of Uniomsta at Ipswich. He said it Vould be idle on his part to attempt to say, he saw at present any basis of a foundation upon which the once great Liberal party' could be reconstituted; therefore there was no alterna, tire for Liberal Unionists but to do all in their power to ,constitute it third 'party. They had induced the Conser- vatives to depart, from their old policy of obstruction to reform, and to take into account the growing want.g. in- terests, progress, intelligence, and requirements of the people of the United Kingdom. He contended that no device ;which included a separate Parliament could main- tain the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament in Ire- land: and held that all attacks on the Crimes Act had ,utterly failed. In ,no case had it been proved that the Act had been administered otherwise than with fairness , and justice. With regard to the extension of • local self- government tO Ireland, he said that Parliament was about to consider the extension of local government in England. and no harm or injustice would be done to the people of Ireland by their waiting until after ahother general election to see what was done in the sister country.—On Thursday morning Lord Hartington was entertained at breakfast in Ipswich Town Hall. Mr. Cuthbert Quilter, M.P., presided, and among the numer- ous company were the Mayor ad Mayoress, the Duke of Grafton', 'Lord Eltho, M.P., Mr T. W. Russpll; M.P., and Sir C. Dalrymple, M.P. Lord Hartington, respond- ing to the toast of his health, said some regret had been expressed that an attempt should be made to organise a .third party, and hopes were constantly expressed of compromise between the -Liberal party itself. He was afraid they were not at the point, of discussion upon the Irish question upon which the compromise was possible. The bulk of the Liberal party :were committed to the support of the Irish , party, and their extreme demands to the extent which seemed •to make any compromise ' rot all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley and Wright s cotton is the beat.-7 Advt. • •
" TOTJCIE AND GO." , • To-day, March 10th, the Prince and Princess of Wales celebrate their Silva- Wedding. Many happy returns of the day) and may they live to celebrate their Golden Wedding! •

The latest improvement in the ladies' improver is to ;utilise it for smuggling purposes. Two piing girls tried it on—the trick as well as the improver—eat Queenstown, on Sunday. They stowed away cakes of tobacco; and stowed away a cake too much, for they 'were suspected, and then searched. The result of their escapade was that they were called upon to pay a heavy fine, and forfeit the tobacco and the improvers. So the occasion was not improved after all.

It is amusing to observe how certain members of the House of Lords are bent on reforming them selves—as if anything whiph emanated from that reverend don't-touch-Int and do-as-we-please body would be likply to g to the root of the mutter ! It is no use tinkering, the worn-out kettle; best leave it alone% till it comes again .in collision with that people's pan—the House of Commons. It will then in all likelihood go to pieces, ; and Some- thing newer and better will take its place. _ _

In France the authorities appear to think 'adulteration is a more serious offence than we com- monly regard it in this country. Three Normandy Batter merchants have been fined and sent to pri- son for several months for sending out as butter a substance which contained from 10 to 24 Per cent. of margarine. Comparatively small fines are in- flicted in England, which the merchant or trades- man pays and 'goes on his way rejoicing-‘-and adulterating. Itpaysto adulterate, but if imprison- ment followed conviction it would not pay.

The annual report of Dr. Watkins, the Medical Officer of Health for the'Newton district, shows that the past year has been a pretty healthy one, the death rate being. 16.604 per 1,000. Tt was pointed out that thopails and rubbish boxes Were in a dilapidated condition. It seems that each property owner does that which he thinks right in his own eyes as to the sort of pail he provides; and the result is that some of the tubs will Scarcely stand on their own bottom. It would be better if the Commissioners would provide the pails, as is done in other towns.

There was quite a big gathering of Welsh people at Earlestown, on Saturday, to celebrate the feast of St. David, visitors being pieseet from all the surrounding villages. Welshmen when out of Wales do not, as a rule assert themselves as much as they ought to do. rule, ought to act together so as to make their influence felt on the question of disestablishment. It is a "shame," as some at the meeting on Saturday exclaimed, that the voice of four members of Parliament for Wales should outweigh, on this question, the voice of the twenty- six,whe demand the disestablishment of the Eng- lish Church in Wales. •

While making an appeal to the newspapers to refrain from discussing the nature of the illness of the German Crown Prince, the medical attendants have acted wisely in giving what information they can as to the present condition of the royal patient. It is inevitable that the public should follow the case with the deepest interest—so much depends on. the result—and, if they cannot get correct information, they are likely to speculate on what may prove to be incorrect. Let the doctors give the fullest bulletins they can; it will be the best means of satisfying the public wind, and will add *eight to their appeal.

It has been officially anaounced that the follow- ing'inembers of the House of Commons have, on the invitation of the Speaker, consented to form a panel for the provision of a Deputy Speaker in the absence of Mr. Peel and Mr. Courtney :—Sir John Gorst, Mr. J. W, Lowther, Mr. H. H. Fowler, Mr. Illingworth, and Mr. Craig-Sellar. It may be noticed that there is no representative of the Irish members, but that is not because the. matter was not taken into account. The Speaker, who . does not believe the nonsense talked about "Parnellism and Crime," asked Mr. McCarthy to serve, but for reasons personal to himself that gentleman de- clined the invitation.'

The Queen's letters to Miss Gordon, written on the death ,of General Gordon, shoW that her Majesty was, as she puts it; ill when she wrote. Gordon was heroic, but in the matter of the exe- cution of his mission to the Soudanese he was as misguided as he was heroic. He went out with words of peace on his lips, and, when the nativ,es refused to listen to hini, he declared war. In this he went beyjond 'his instructions, and paid the penalty of his error with his life. The "stain" ,upon England was in sending out a man with a. message of peace who was capable, on his own re- sponsibility, of converting it into a declaration of war. Admiral Byng was shot for less than that.

General Gordon was determined to have his own way ; he could have escaped, but he wanted to conquer. In his journals, printed from the original manuscript by Mr. 'Edmund Hake, he . himself 'wrote :—.• September 24. I altogether decline the imputation that the projected expedition has come to relieve me. is for myself, I could make good my retreat at any moment, if I wished. I came up to extricate the garrisons, and failed. Earle comes up to extricate garrisons and (I hope) succeeds. Earle does not come to extricate me. . . lam not the rescued lamb, and will hot be." The italics are those of General Gordon. They show that he perished in a task which he was not asked to undertake, and which proved beyondlis strength.

They nearly over-did it in the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday, when it was proposed that the Chief-Constable should have an allowance of £.50 per year, in lieu of the house which he is leav- ing in consequence of its "unsuitable condition." There was a good deal said about the house not being healthy,until somebody remarked that in all probability they would have to put a sergeant in. Of course, it would never do to immure even sk, sergeant in a really unhealthy house. What it comes to, in plain terms, is that the -unsuitable house is suitable for a sergeant, but not for a Chief Constable. Let us hope that the house will be made more habitable.

The Warringtoli Town Council is about evenly divided as to the question of taking down the wall in front of the Town Hall. It is not that many of the members do not think it would be an im- provement; the issue is whethepthe game is worth th¢ candle in these days of depressed trade and high rates. For the rates of Warrington are high with an average, for a score of years, of 5s IT.id in the pound. High rates, as Councillor Platt re- marked, have a tendency to frighten away manu- facturers; and, he might have added, to deter tradesmen from building big shops on the vacant land in Bridge-street. Let the rates be reduced first: it will be time enough then to talk about spending £4OO on an ornamental hobby.

The ratepayers will not be surprised that • there was a discussion, in the Warrington Town Council, on the qu,estion of the increase of the salary of the Inspector of Nuisances, and that the proposal was carried by a very narrow majority. Granted that Mr. Norman is a good officer, it must at the same time be stated that he is a lucky man, for, previous to this, his salary had been twice raised, being :25 per cent more than it was when he first became a servant of the Corporation. It now stands at 40 per cent more. Can it be said that salaries tlirougliout the town, or throughout the Corporation, have advanced at the sem) rate in the same period r And if not, will somebody ex- plain why an exception should be made in favour of the Inspector of Nuisances ?

'LOCAL NEWS

CAMDEN SIINDAT SCHOe/L, RUNCORN.—The service of song; entitled “The battle of lifer. was rendered in this school on Monday, before a goOd, audience. Mr. J. E. Frith presided, and Mr. S. Bayley' ably conducted. ; Supipsii DEATH At WIDNES.—Whilst, proceeding to- wards his home in Brytm-street; On Saturday morning, William Lawlor, aged 72 years; fell to the ground appar- ently in a fit. He was at once conveyed home, where he died half an hour later, before medical aid could be pro- cured.- About a month ago he was attended by Dr. Nealon for dysenteric diarrhcea, ; but for the last fort- night he had been without the services of a doctor.; having recovered from the attack, and not apparently suffering from any other ailment.. An inquest has not been deemed necessary.' - SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. -- At the Burial Bard ,Office, Runcorn, on Monday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest touching the death of ThOmas HOWeeroft, 66 years of age, a native of Lymm. On Saturday the deceased and other men were employed in ioading stone on a boat at the Big Pool, Runcorn. One of the men thinking that there was 'sufficient stone in the boat went to the part ivixere Howecroft had been en- gaged, and found Jinn lying dead amongst the stone. The deceased had suffered' from heart disease for some time post, ands verdict of 'Death from natural causes" was recorded. • -• •

1-ili-E-FT--0-1760AL WIPNES.-At Widries Pefty Session, on Thursday, Catherine Hynes, of Marsh-street; - Joseph Quinn (13), James Glynt (14), all of Water-street, were brought up on remand charged with having on the pre- vious Sunday, stolen a quantity of coal from a wagon be- longing to the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany en the canal bank. Hynes was also charged with assaulting P.C. Massey. The prisoners . pleaded guilty, and Quinn, who had been in trouble before, Was., sen- tenced to fourteen days' hard labour, and four years' de- tention in an industrial school. The otherprisoners were • fined lOs each.

TRANSFER DAY AT llnNeonx—The Runcorn Magis- trates, on Monday, granted the transfer of tile following licenses : Castle Hotel, Halton, from William Phillips to James Howard; George and Dragon Hotel, Egerton- street, from Wm. Jenkins to Henry Hughes ; the Mariners Hotel, Percival-lane, from Edward Page to Wm. Skinner; the Queen's Hotel, Waterloo-road, from Joseph Bancroft to Edward Page; the Foresters Arms, Canal- street, from John Ellis to Henry Forshavv ; the Three Crowns Inn, King-street, from Hannah Ravenscroft to John Blundell; the Wheatsheaf Inn, Bridge-street, from John Owen Bentiett to Robert Morgan; the Camden I Hoteli to Mrs. Davies from her late husband. ' THAT OF BOOTS AT RuNconx.-:-Mary Ann Morland, an elderly woman, was, on Monday,. at Ruacorn Petty Sessions, charged with having stolen a pair of boots, value 10s, the property of Andrew McQuinn. Inspector Millington deposed that about three o'clock on Saturday afternoon he saw the prisoner and another woman acting in, a suspicibus manner in Bridge-street He watched them into and out of a public house, and then followed thern into Nlersey-street, where he stopped them, and dis- covered that the prisoner had a pair of boots concealed under her arm: After some time she admitted she had stolen the boots from a shop on the canal side. The pri- soner was remanded for a kveek in order that inquiries may be made info her antecedents. . AN UNFORTUNATE IRISH FARMEIL-OR Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Silvester,Wlkite, a middle-aged man, described as a tramp, was charged with begging in VC Victoria-road, on Sunday. Constables , Field and ors- fold proved the elaarge, and said townspeople had com- plained that they had been annoyed by the prisoner. In reply to Mr. Lewin, 'the prisoner said he had been a far- mer in Ireland`, and had come over from Wexford to Liverpool about eight or nine days ago. On Saturday he walked frorq Liverpool to Widnes. He was penniless. Mr. Timmins said if complaints had not been %made against the prisoner he would have been discharged; but respectable people said that he had ahnbved them. The public must be protected, and therefore tlie prisoner would have to go to gaol for seven days' hard labour. If he had told the police that he had no money he would have been found lodgings.

.THE RATES OF THE R—UNCORN THEATRE.—Mr. W.' R. Waldron, of the Theatre Royal, Runcorn, was summoned before the Magistrates, on Monday, 'by the ,Runcorn Board of Commissioners for the improvement rate of £1 12s.—Mr. Waldron contended that he was not, liable for the rate and in reply to his questions, Mr. Barker, the rate collector, said this was the first rate he had de- manded from Mr. Waldron.—Mr. Waldron said this was the first rate that had been delnanded from him during the five years he,had occupied the Theatre. The rates had always been paid by the owner of the Theatre.—Bv Mr. Ashton: He was the licensee but not the lessee; he was a weekly tenant.—Mr. Brundrit (to Mr. Barker) Are the rates due from the landlord or from the. tenant? Mr. Barker: Tenant, sir.—Mr. Brundrit informed Mr. Waldron that he ought to have appealed to the Commis- sioners before allowing the matter to be brought there. He was the tenant of the theatre, and the magistrates would have to make an order upon him to iSaythe money lin a week. . ' "GASSES)" on DRUNK AT WiDNEs.—Before Mr. Tint- mis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick McCann, who was described as a labourer, of no settled residence. was charged with having been drunk in Vic- toria-road, on Saturday evening.—Prisoner 4replied that he had had some gas and whiskey. (Laughter.)—Mr. Timmis :.Do you say you were gassed P—Prisoner : Yes, sir.—Mr. Timmis : Where do you work ?—Prisoner: At Deacon's.—Mr. Timmis : Did you fall down 7—Prisoner: No, sri, but very near.—Mr. Timmis : And you got some blskey to cure you : Yes, sir.—Mr. Timmis : How many glasses did you have P—Prisoner : Three or four.—Mr. Timmis : And more, probably.—lt transpired, on further inquiries, that the prisoner was found drunk' at eleven o'clock, five hours after the prisoner had left work.—Mr. Timmis said under these circumstances the prisoner would have to pay a fine of 5s and costs, or go Ito gaol for 7days. Had the offence occurred directly after he had been "gassed" he would have been dis- charged. THE CONSEQUENCES OF A DRUNKEN FOREMAN. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Patrick Lawler, lately a furnaceman, who resides at the " Model,' was charged on a warrant with refusing to maintain his wife land family.—Mr. Tracey (relieving officer) said that 'prisoner's wife and four children became chargeable to the Union On the 20th February. The prisoner was re- cently employed at Messrs. Pilkington's works, where he earned 28s per week. He left of his own accord. The amount owing was £2 9s 6d. Prlsbner said he left vaork because his foreman was a drunken man, and went drinking with lyis (prisoner's) wife., Ile could not work fq such a person. He thought he could get work else- where, but he had failed up to the present.—Mr. Tracey:' That statement, I believe, is cOrrect.—Mr. Crossage (to prisoner) : That, however, did not excuse you leaving your children ;, but if you will promise to pay the money back, and in the meantime maintain your wife and family, yeu-will be discharged.—Prisoner promised, and was accordingly dismissed.. UNITED FREE METHODISM AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.— A very pleasing change from the ordinary service took place at the Zion Chapel, Oakland-street, Widnes, on Sunday evening, when the seryte,e of song, "From the Cross to the Crown," arranged by the Rev. J. Chisholm, of Liverpool, was rendered by the choir. There was a, good congregation. The musical portion consisted of hymns selected from Moody and Sankey's collection, in many of which the congregation joined with much hear- • tiness and apparent enjohnent. The readings were fro'm the Sacred Scriptures. but instead of one person being engaged to read, the following scholars performed that duty :—Misses E. J. Bettie'', M. H. Harrison, , Miss Betney, Miss Jane Betney, and Jessie Hughes; and Mr. J.. Bennett. This proved a very agreeable innovation. Appropriate recitations were also given by Master 'Alfred Betney, Miss C. Henshall, Mrs. Locke, and those previously named. Solos were capitally sung by Mrs. Locke, Miss A. Betney, Miss F. Causey, and Miss M. 11. Harrison: Mrs. Wilcocks and Miss Betney also gave a duet. Mr. John Betney ably conducted the choir.—On Monday evening, in the Sunday school connected with the chapel, the Rev. G. Ball gave a, magic lantern entertainment to a good andience. particular subject was illustrated, but a large variety of fine views were thrown upon the screen, and created gratifying interest. The Rev. E. Hall presided., on Tuesday evening Mr, Ball repeated his entertainment in Ellesmere-street School, Runcorn, and there was again a large and appreciative audience. Mr. Stubbs occupied the chair. DRUNKENNESS AND DEATH AT WO:WEL—Mr. S. Brig- house, the county coroner, on Wednesday held an inquest at the Rose and 'drown Inn, MOSS Bank. on the body of Patrick Caulfield, aged 27, who was a chemical labourer, who resided with his married sister, Mrs Neeley, at 60, Elizabeth-street. From the evidence of Mrs Neeley, and Mr. and•Mre Robert Coulter, it appeared that on Satur- day night, about eleveno'clock, the deceased went home in a state of drunkenness, and sat up talking with the witness until about one o'clock on Sunday morning. At that time he went upstairs, weiring his clogs, to go to bed. He was heard to stumble as he reached tlie top of the steps, and Coulter' who ran to see what was the matter, faw him fall with his head against the bottom of the stairs. He was removed into the kitchen, but died almost instafitly.—The foreman of the jury (Mr. It. Webster) said there was no doubt the man came by, his death accidentally, but drink had something to do with it. However, men wosld have drink, and men who, like the deceased, who probably could not get it during the week, did like to have a little on the Saturday.—Mr. Pre,scot (another juryman) said probably the accident would have occurred if t4O man had not had any drink. —Another juryman obs&ved that the deceased would have to work on Friday night and again on Saturday afternoon, and therefore a little drink would overcome him.—Several jurymen expressed 'the opinion that it was not usual for a man to go to bed in his clogs,—The Coroner : But you know men in this condition usually go to bed with their boots on. (Laughter.)—A verdict of "Accidental death "-was returned. THE: EVE SIGHT.—Mr. M. Arousherg, F.R.O.S. (of the arm of Aronsberg and Co.. the eminent ophthalmic opticians, of Liverpool and London) will visit Warrington at the Lion Hotel, Briclgesetreet, on Tuesday and. Wednesday, March 13th and 14th, for free cnnsultation on defective vision, and will scientifically test the eyes, and adapt, if requisite, their noted Plano-Paraholle Spectacles and Rye-preservers at strictly moderate charges. Their popular treatise on " The use and abuse of the Eyes" may also be had free on application at 40, Manchester-street, Liverpool.—Advt.

DRUNK.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Major Ha zlehurst, John Baddeley, a labourer' was fined ss, and costs ss, for being drunk in Fryer-strelet. The prisoner said he had come to get work on the Ship Canal, but it was shown that he had been turned out of one public-house and had stripped himself for a fight in the stvet. NEGLECT OF FAMILY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Majoi Hazlehurst„a sailor, Thomas Abram, was charged with neglecting to support his six children, who have been inmates of the Work- house since the 4th February. Mr. W. H. Linaker pro- secuted on behalf -of the Guardians,and Mr. Ward proved

the case. The prison of promised to' pay the ammint ex- pended by the Guardians, 4,2 7s 6, and to take the chil- dren fr..nn the house.—His Lordship adjourned the case 'for a' month to allow the prisoner an opportunity of carrying out his promise. 'ASSAULTING TIIS PL/CE AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Dawson, a middle-aged man, of Beaudilont-street, was charged with having been drunk in Church-street orithe sth instant, and also with assaulting and resisting P.C. Worsfold. It appeared that the prisoner, who was very•drunk, was knocking at the doors of houses as lie .walked towards Runcorn, and , the constable apprehended him. He then struck the officer several times on the sßoulder with an iron scraper. At the station four policemen wers, required, to. search . _ _ .

him. A fine of 53 'and costs was inioosed in each charge. ' HOME MrssioN SERVICES AT WIDNES.—The Rey. T. A. Fawthrop, of Dibsbury, delivered two .addresses on be- half of the Wesleyan Home Missions, in the Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday. There were large congregations, and the sum of £6 lOs was realized by the collections. On Tuesdayevenin; the annual meeting was held in the same place, when the Rev. S. T. House delivered .his popular lecture, entitled '6 Sunshine and Shadow of Life.' Mr. Roger Fog presided, and there was a good attendance. The Rev. R, .Burdon read the 32nd annual report. The amount contributed by the Widnes circuit last year was 23 13s. The collections amounted to 'about £5.

A HORSE RACE " FIZZLE " r RUNCORN.—The sport- ing inhabitants of Runcorn were in a state of great excitement on Tuesday, in consequence of a race to Chester that had been arranged between Mr. P. Smith, of Runcorn, and Mr. .T. Leather, of Ditton. 'he animals, which were each to be yoked to a gig contain- ing 30 stone in weight,' were to have started at half-past one, Mr. Leather from Wilson's Hotel, and Mr-. Smith from the Norton Arms at Halton. A large crowd assem- bled in Bridge-street at the time stated, but they had to) return home disappointed. It transpired Wet on the previous evening Mr. Smith's mare had met with an accident, and injured herself to such an extent that she was unable to carry out her owner's intention, and that the forfeit of £5 had been paid in accordance with an agreement drawn up. ' The stake was £2O aside. The news of the equine struggle for supremacy had ',spread throughout the whole route to the ancient city, and at Frodsham hundreds lined the roadway to see the speedy :teeds on their journey, and a great crowd had also gathered at Ermine Hfitel, Chester, prepared to see an exciting finish. It is needless tb say that they were dis- appointed. . THE OXFORD AND CAMBRIDGE BOAT RACE.-- Duringl the past week the "Dark blues have been under the tuition Of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, , t Mn. J. T. BRUNNER' AND THE LIBERAL VICTORY AT ST. HELENS.—Mr.J. T. Brunner, M.P. for North- wich, writing from the House of Commons regard- ing the LiberaLvictory in Windle Ward, says:— "The election of Mr. Martin will be an encourage- ment to every Liberal in St. Helens, no matter how poor he is, to make some sacrifice for the common good, and for that reason I congratulate Mr. Martin, and I congratulate St. Helens." MR. VD. SULLIVAN, M.P.—A copy of the verses entitled" We 're Brothers Evermore," which re- cently appeared in this journal, and which were suggested by the speech made by Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., at the Hyde Park demonstration, were for- warded to Mr. Sullivan at the House of Commons. Communicating with. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF SIR RICHAREi
BROOKE, BART.

Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory, near Runcorn, died at his residence 'on Sibturday morning it. Although Sir Richard had attained the patriarchal age of 74 years, the people of the neigh- bourhood were totally unprepared for his death, and when the circumstances became known, people of both high and low degree gave vent to their sym- pathy for the bereaved family. Mr. Octavqs Arooke, the youngest son of Sir Richard, having obtained an appointment on the Ship Canal works, had recently returned from. India. and in his honour a dinner party was held at the Priory leriday evening. Naturally the father took a ptominent part in the auspicious proceed- '.ings of the evening, and he retired to rest appar- ently in his accustomed state of health. For some time p2st, however, he has suffered somewhat acutely from heart disease, and about seven o'clock on Saturday morning he awoke and complained of a burning sensation in the breast. With all des- patch a messenger was sent for Dr. Car- ruthers, who has been his medical atten- dant, but before the aid of that gentleman could be obtained the Baronet had ceased to exist. During his long life Sir Richard had not taken a ,very active part in public life, beyond a zealous per- formance of his duties as a magistrate, being chair- man of the Runcorn Bench, and his occasional ap- pearance in the position of president at meetings held in support of the Conservative eause, to which he was devotedly attached. In recent years the state of his health ,bad prevented him from appear- ingin public so frequently as formerly, but he never- theless gave his patronage to many objects of public interest, He was the descendant of one of the oldett Cheshire families, and the inheritor of an ancient baronetcy, two facts that gave him importance in the county, and won him respect amongst the Community with whom his life was spent. The title was created in 1662, and the late Sir Richard, who was born in the year 1814, was the seventh baronet, having succeeded his father Of the same name in 1865. A man of command- ing presence;the late Baronet had been capt,ain and. Lieutenant-Colonel in the First Life Guards, and had also held the rank of Colonel in the Cheshire Volunteers. Of cl4il offices he had occupied the exalted office of Deputy-Lieutenant of the county. In 1848 he married Lady Louisa Duff, sister of the 4th Earl of Fife, who died In 1864. Of this union there were seven sons and three daughters. On December 21st, 1871, he was united to Henrietta Elizabeth! second • daughter of the late iSir Henry Mainwaring, of reoVer, and of this second mar- riage there was issue- two daughters. He' is succeeded by his eldest son Richard Mamas, Who was born in 1850, and who, like his late father, was formerly of the Life Guards. Again, therefore, there will be a Sir Richard at the Frio?, which is pregnant with' old time associa- tions. . _

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The remains of the deceased baronet were, by his own desire, interred at the Halton Cemetery on Thursday. Out of respect to his memory the windows of the whole of the cottages in the villages of Norton and Halton were darkened, and the villagers turned out in hun- dreds to show their regard for the.dead. At Runcorn flags were flying at half-mast on the public buikljngs, and a number of the places of business were partially closed._ It was desired that the funeral obsequies Should be conducted as quietly as possible, otherwise the demon- stration might have -been more marked. The gloomy procession departed from the Priory about eleven o'clock, and oonsiSted of the doctor's carriage (in which were Dr. Carruthers and Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to the estate), the hearse, four coaches, and seven private carriages. In the first coach were the Dowager Lady Brooke, Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. (the eldest son), the Ron. Last-piles, and Mr. Artituß Brooke (brother) : in the second Mr. Optavius 4rooke (son), Miss Brooke, Miss Winifred Brooke, AEA Lilian BroOke (daughters) ; in the third, Miss Mainwaring, Miss Maud Mainwarirtg, Mr. Brooks Cunliffe, Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton (Arley in the fourth, Mr% Close, Mr. -11. ' Close; Mrs. Close, Mr. F. and Mr. A. Dixon, The private carriages were sent by the follow- ing :—Mrs. C; Hazlehurst, of The Gagange, Run-

I corn; Th• 110411, if I m Daresbury; the Rev. G. Heron, o{ erfron all; Mr. B. B. Chadwick, J.P., Run- ; corn ; Mr. EV -Warburton, of Arley Hall; Mr. Jones, I The Oaklands, Daresbury ; and Mr. R. H. Wood, Halton. At the lodge gates' at Halton the tenantry of the late baronet met the cortege, and preceded the hearse to the Parish Church. Amongst the tenanto were Messrs. John . Weir, Walton; T. J. Weir, Kekewick ; F. Weir, Norton; C. Percival, Norton; C. Baguley, Norton; T. Hewitt, Aston Grange; John Baguley, liaßwood ; Joseph Baguley, Stockham • J. Finch, Astmoor; W. Humphreys, George Bradshaw, George Johnson. The vicars of Hal. ton and Runcorn (J. Lockwood and A. Maitland Wood) and the choristers and a detachment of the 2nd Cheshire Volunteers met the mourners at the gates of tile church- yard, and, chanting, led the way into the sacred edifice. The solemn service was fully choral, and Was conducted by the clergymen named. The order of procession from - the church to the cemetery was as follows : County magistrates, volunteer.officers, the tenantry, gentlemen of the neighbourhood,. the choristers, the clergy, the coaches &e. The magistrates present were the Rev. E. A. P. coaches, Messrs. J. Brundrit, James Reynolds, A. Thomas, a.nd H. Reynolds. The Volunteer detachment consisted of Colonel Ashton; Major Hazlehurst, Captain Woolley, Lieuts. Wigg,Lightburn, and Ashton. Amongst the gentlemen from Runcornwere Dr. Steele, the Rev. W. Preston; Messrs. W. Whittaker, J. W. Lightbum, P. Smith, R. Lea, W. Timming, W. Lea. and W. Shaw- (missionary), with Mr. G. Lyster, of the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board, Liverpool. The body, which was • enclosed in a 'polished oak coffin with silver furniture, was borne to its last resting place by the keepers of the estate, namely, George Hargreaves, Henry liuckley, George Rigby. Henry Clare; • John Woodward* Jos. Dun- Calf, John Hollland, and Geerrge Millar. The plate on the coffin bore the following inscription:—" Sir Richard. Brooke, seventh baronet, born 21st December, 1814, filed 3rd Muck, 1888." The grave was beautifully lined with , moss. Affiongst others, wreaths had been sent by the Earl of Lathom, Miss Wilbraham, Mrs. R. Tomlinson, Miss Edith Lyon, Mrs. Emerson (Knutsford),,Mr. and Mrs. W. Timmins, Mr. R. Cunliffe, Mr. Evans Mr. Howard, the servants at the Priory, Runcorn Coheerva- tive Association, and Runcorn Habitation of the Prim- rose League.,

div.head: MAIFISTERIAL REFERENCE.
div.p: MAIFISTERIAL REFERENCE.

Before business commenced at the Runcorn Petty Ses.• sins, on Monday, Mr. John Brundrit, who presided, al- luded to the sad event, and said Sir Richard Brooke dur- ing his lifetime was a leading man, and had filled many thigh offices in the county, and he was sure they would an miss him. He had held the position of Colonel of the Volunteers, and Fes connected with the local corps. Sir Richard had also acted as High Sheriff of the county and as Deputy Lieutenant, and had given satisfaction by the able manner in which he had fulfilled the duties of those offices. Early in his life he was placed on file Rommis- sion of the peace, and until recently had occupied the chair on that bench and had always taken the greatest interest in everything appertaining to the business of the county. On behalf of his brother magistrates and the townspeople, Mr. Brundrit wished to tender to the family of the deceased baronet their sincere sympathy with them in the heavy bereavement they had been called upon to endure.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, as a gen- tleman practising in that court for the past twenty years, , endorsed what had been said, and spoke of the late baronet's courtesy towards the members of the bar, and the officials of the court. All the time that Sir Richard had visited that court he (Mr. Linaker) could not call to ,1 mind any unpleasant scene—in fact; he was .straight- forward and kindly towards all with whom he came in contact. Be wished to endorse, on behalf of the bar,. what Mr. Brundrit had said with reference to tendering their sympathy to Lady Brooke and family in their be- reavement.
PINNER TO WIDNES FOOTBiLL

In commemoration of their vihory over Aspen, the holder&of the West Lancashire Cup, the mem- bers of the Widnes football team, and the reserves and committee of the club, together with a number of friends, were entertained to tea on Thursday evening by two earnest and enthusiastic supporters of the club. About fifty persons sat down to an excellent repast. which was served at Anderson's Railway Hotel by Mr. and Mrs. Anderson. After- wards the company'adjourned to a lower room. Mr. H. A. Richards occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. Roger Wilcock (Liver- pool Old Boys), J. H. Smith G. n. Plumpton, W. Kiddie, J. E. Farrell, J. Bingham, C. Hemingway, T. Ashall, J. A. Brown, W. Grice, A. Raton, W. Ire- land, F. Sampson, W. Bray, S. Bingham, J. Tallon, and Lecomber., The evening was spent in a convivial manner, but during an inter- val Mr. Wilcock pronosed the health of the Widnes football team. In apologising for the absence of Mr. I'arry, secretary to the West Lanca- shire Union, Mr. Wileock said that gentleman had been prevented from being present because he had that evening to perform the painful task of meeting a representative of Aspull to get the cup which Whines was so anxious to win. (Applause.) The team were very enthusiastic; he did not know • tvhether they were going to win it—(cries of "We are that")—but at any rate they would have She credit of dispossessing the original holders, and that was in itself a great achieveraent. (Hear, hear.) Several charges of rough play had been made, but the people who made those charges, had but a dim notion of the difference between vigorous play and rough play. As a frequlat spectator of the play of the Widnes teain he had always taken the opportunity to • disprove the accusation most stoutly. He spoke in high terms of praise of both the conduct of the players and the six thousand spectators on Saturday, even under the ad- verse decisions of the referee, and to the friendly spirit displayed by Aspull under their defeat. He urged the Widnes team to do all in their power to win the cup, as such a feat would draw attention of the most prominent clubs in Lancashire and beyond,and they wouldget muck L better fixtures. As an instance, Warrington before win- ning the cup were nobodies in the football world com- paratively speaking ; and afterwards they succeeded in meeting some of the best clubs in Manchester and dis- trict. Widnes would also find their position improved, 1 and they have a much better opportunity of getting their best men in the county teafn.—The toast was drunk with much enthusiasm, and Mr. Smith, the captain,' responded in a neat speech, during which he remarked that if the team would plaz with combina- tion and determination there was not muck reason to doubt that the cup would be brought to Widnes. (Ap- plause.). As to the accusation of rough play, they were most unjust, and as he had often observed, to play a winning game they must play a pleasant game. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Ireland, in terms of eulogy, proposed the liealthof the donors of that entertainment, which was received most "enthusiastically and suitably: acknow- ledged. The toasts of the health of the Chairman, Mr. Wilcock, and the Press followed, the representative of this journal responcljng to the latter toast. During the evening songs were given by Messrs. J. G. .Kiddie, Gor- don. Brady, Ireland, Farrell, Smith, Leech, Pennington, and Hughes, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. Mr Harnson,presided at the piano.

Joseph Houghton, William Royston, and William Appleton were ap- pointed representatives of the Council. / NARROW ESCAPa.—On Monday afternoon a cow , was being driven from Bradley Hall to a sale. at the - Eagle and Child, Warrington,. and 'when near Tunstall's-row; Latchford, it was seized with para- lysis. A woman named Hamblett obtained a bucket of water and was in the act of crossing the road to carry it to the animal, when tlie cow got up and at- tempted to toss her, but only succeeded in knocking herdown. She was wearing a thick plait Of hair at the back of her head, which prevented the cow's horn from injuring her. She, however, received a severe she-ck to the sYstem. The. cow afterwards charged its driver and knocked him down, but the man re- ceived no injury. It was subsequently brought in a cart to Warrington. DEATH OF A WAnnINGTA RAILWAY GUARD.— Our readers Will regret to hearof the death of Mr. John Osborne, a well-known Warrington Railway guard. A. few weeks ago the deceased started from War- lington in charge of the 8-33 train, and upon ar- riving at Broadheath he was, discovered to have burst a blood vessel.' By the instructions of Mr. Hope, stationmaster, Dr. Gotland was sent for, and . the train went on to Manchester under the charge of the senior porter at the station. • Upon the arrival of the doctor deceased was found to have lost a considerable quantity of blood, and as his weak condition rendered it extremely necessary that he should receive prompt medical attention he was immediately removed to the Altrincham Hospital. A few days ago as Ile appeared to be better he returned to his residence in Liverpool- road, but he' shortly afte,rwards died. The body has been interred at Dansthble. The deceased was 53 years of age, and was , w,ell-known and much respected in Warrington. A man who vras formerly a night-watchman refers to ;t as his "late ocitunatioa." "_Co.ue here, Johnny, and tell me what the four seasons are." Young prodigy: "Pepper, salt, mustard, and vinegal."- - -
