RUGBY RULES. WARRINGTON "A" TEAM v. NEW BRIGHTON OLYM- PIC lsr.—The first fixture between these teams was brought to a conclusion on the Wilderspool ground, on Saturday, before a Moderate number of spectators, when a most enjoyable game was witnessed, although the visi- tors proved to be no match for the Warrington "A " team, whose splendid passing was the chief feature of the encounter Hockey kicked off for New Brighton at 3-30, Thornley charging down the ball, and from a scrimmage in mid-field Whittle threw to Evans, who passed to Sanson, but the ball went wide anctrolled into touch. Neat passing between Antrobus, Whittle, and a long kick by Samson took p*ny to the New Brighton 25, but Hockey relieved with a good dribble, Whittle arrest- ing his progress. After exchange kicks between Kent, Benson, and A. Venables, Daniels secured and put in a strong rim, being brought down near the line by Ed- wards. Passing between Whittle, Antrobus, Daniels, and Evans shortly afterwards took place, the latter player getting in a good kick, and Stoneman mulling the ball, Molyneaux rushed lip and grounded the leather over the line, Isherwood kicking a goal from the place. Hockey re-started from centre, and kicks were ex- changed between Evans and W. Venables, the ball even- tually going into touch in the visitors' quarter. Warrington worked the ball into the New Brighton 25, where Holmes broke away with a good dribble, and had hard lines in not, scoring, the ball being kicked clean frbm under him, a minor point being. registered. From a line out Whittle secured, and after a short run dropped at goal, the ball just going under the crossbar, a dead ball accruing. Half time was now called, the score standing—Warrington one goal and five minor' points to New Brighton Olympic nothtrig. On change of ends Whittle restarted, the ball going into todch. The same player afterwards passed to Antrobus, who suc- ceeded in grounding the ball over the lino, Isherwood's kick at goal failing. Shortly after the kick off from centre Whittle passed to Evans, this player making a strong run, but was collared by Titterinton near the line, another minor point being added. Warrington continued. to have the best of the game, scoring two more minors, and on call of no side were victorious by two goals, two tries, and nine minor points to New Brighton nothing. Teams: Warrington—Full back, Warburton; three- quarter-backs, Daniels, Evans, and Sanson ; half-backs, Whittle and Antrobus (captain) ; forwards, E. Dillon, Molyneaux, Thornley, Donohue, Tones, Bate, Holmes, Beard, and Isherwood. New Brighton Olympic: Full back, Stoneman; three-quarter-backs, A. Venables, Kent, and W. Venables; half-backs, Higson and Ed- wards ' • forwards, E. Gardner, Shaw, Titterton, Lowe, A. Gardner, Hockey, Campbell, J. Bull, and J. Stones-

worth. BIRKKTREAD Panic V. Runcoftw.—Unusual interest was centred in tnis return match, at Runcorn, on Saturday, the meeting. virtually resolving itself into a fight for the championship of Cheshire, as on the first occasion the game between these clubs ended in a draw, each side scoring a goal. Both teams were fairly represented, though the Park suffered everely through the absence of Blain, his substitute at full back being of very little use, D. A. Bingham also being absent from their forward ranks. Stubbs had not sufficiently recovered from an injury to his shoulder received in the Eccles match three weeks ago to don the jersey, whilst Cawley was given a rest on this occasion, W. Riley, who took his place, playing a remartcably fine game. Speakman's " last ap- pearance" in the team previous to his Australian tour was marked by a brilliant exhibition on his part. Woods showed that, although being off colour of late, his old full back form is returning ; whilst H. Hughes, Whitby, and T. Davies worked like Trojans. The horne vanguard , played a fine combined game, the Birkenhead forwards being little behind them in this respect. Black was seen to great advantage, and L. M. Holden fairly excelled himself. Black won the toss, and W. Hughes kicked off against the wind. The home forwards, on the loose, - rushed ahead to the Park 25, Holden saving gal- lantly. Lockwood retaliated, with a nice dribble, but H. Hughes stopped him and some clean passing be- tween W. and H. Hughes, him, and W. Riley was exhibited, little ground, however, being gained. Holden made his mark, and F. Ker's kick was returned with ad- vantage, but Black immediately landed the ball into touch ten yards from the Runcorn line, Woods having eventually to save. After the drop-out, play raged in neutral ground for a time. Then Clarke Game through with a good dribble, Whitby further improving the posi- tion, and Black just rushed up in time to save. Drop- ping out, Lockwood, Cowen, Craig, and A. G. Wood in- vaded Runcorn territory. Wainwnght staved the rush, but Holden passing to Ferule, and the latter enabled Black to threaten the home lines. Davies tackled the Birkenhead captain, and Speakman ran well to centre, , whence the home forw.ard,s dribbled towards the Birken- head citadel, H. Hughes worming his way through and grounding near the touch line. Woods's place kick failed. After kicking out, Lockwood was the means of the leather reaching the Runcorn 25. Woods relieved, and F. Ker was tackled before he could :return, even play ensuing in midfield. Lockwood, Cowen, A. G. Wood, and Moodie showed the way to Runcorn quarters. Davies stopped the rush, but was badly shaken in the attempt. H. Hughes relieved the pres- sure' and after a period of even play Han- cock got in a good run and pass to Riley, and the latter, having a deaç course, grounded in a good position, but Woods failed to improve, this bringing about half time. Facing about, little advantage accrued to either side for mome me;ti then Black got Over behind the posts, after a good run, but the point was not improved. A couple of free kicks to the Park, and then Wainwright was con- spicuous with a couple of fine runs, and carried play in front of the Birkenhead posts, Gayter eventually strug- gling over the line. Woods landed a goal from the easy place, and immediately on re-starting Speakman got in a grand dodgy run, the Park conceding a couple of touch- downs. After Taylor Wood'had exhibited his dribbling powers, Alardice made a "fair catch,", but little advan- tage accrued, soon after which Speakman again dashed off, winding up with a brilliant try between the posts. Woods was not successful at the place, and after another touch-down to the home sidc'the game ended in a win for Runcorn by a goal, three tries, and five minors, to a try and one minor. Teams :—Birkenhead : F. Ker, back; J. A. Black, R. K. Fernie, and A. D. Jones, three-quarter backs • L. B. Ker and L. M. Holden, half backs; P. H. Lockwood, A. G. Wood, J. Cowen' N. Allardice, C. Craig G. Rome. R. P. Moodie, S. M. Jones, and W. T. Wood,, forwards. Runcorn: T. Woods, back; T. ,H. Davies, H. C. Speakman, and W. Riley, three-quarter backs; G. Whitby and H. Hughes, half backs • W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, J. Dolan, G. T. Wainwright, W. H. Broady, J. Clarke, F. Hancock, E. Andrews; and J. Gayter, forwards.

WAP.RINGTON V. COVENTRY. Fresh from their victory over Moseley, the iVarrington team jourtreyed to "the city of three spires " on Monday afternoon to bring their list of fixtures with the midland clubs to a close. The teams differed slightly from that which performed so creditably against Moseley, Barnes and Warren being absentees, the former havivg been placed hors de combat by an injury received on Satur- day. However, a fair team was mustered, •and at 3-30 both fifteens entered the enclosure. There was a fair attendance of spectators, and brilliant weather Pre- vailed. Warrington having lost the toss, the Coventry cap- tain dkided to have the sun at his back, and Frank Turner set the ball in motion. A good rue from the kick by Goodrick invaded Warrington ground, but this was soon neutralised by an effort on the part of Jolley. Davies superseded this by a kick into touch at his opponents' quarter flag, and shortly after, the home team, by lucky kicking, scored a dead ball. Frank Turner dropped out, Coventry replying. Povey came through the pack to half way, and Littlewood and Frank Turner carried the . , oval to the home team's line. Handles and Dillon shone individually vithstnart work,but all efforts to score were frustrated by the smart defensive play of the Coventry ' team. Davies looked like scoring here but H. Rother- ham brought about timely relief by a tinge punt be half way. A drop at goal by Jolley registered a minor to Warring,tori, and from the re-start, pretty passing by the visiting backs again forced the Coventry men back. The " wirepullers " tried hard to get over, but art obstacle was found in Rotherham. Jolley replied to the last- , named player's run, and Davies, Jolley, and Massey in- dulged in some neat passing. Littlewood and Hayes rendered useful service, and a smart and neat pass from Davies to Fair. Turner enabled the latter to make a good run to within a few yards of the line, where he was held, but he transferred to Ashton, the latter grounding the wrong side of the line. This was indeed hard lines for the visiting team, and the Coventry men relieved to half way. Ashton showed up with a smart dribble,Good- rick saving the rush. The latter got in a good kick to Speakman, he replying with interest. Exchange kick- ing by H. Rotherham and Davies was nOw witnessed, and after some play of a give and take nature, half time was called with the score one minor each. Restarting from centre, Nevins replied to Ha,ncox' kick off. Stuart tactics by Hugh Rotherham took the leather to Warling- ton quarter flag, but by splendid combination the visit- ing forwards forced Coventry to act on the defensive. From a tough scrimmage on the Coventry line, Read re- lieved to half way, and Warrington were compelled to re- sort to the tactics adopted by the home team just pre- viously. - However, the forwards broke away splendidly, their screwing in the packs earning for theft' high praise. Speakman was to the fore with smart work, and a good run by Massey placed the home goal in jeopardy. Povey responded to a neat dribble of the Coventry forwards, and smart following- up by Eyes and Adamson prevented Hill returning. Judicious kicking by Speakman and un- selfish passing by Davies gaited ground. Jolley and Massey now had a chance, but Hancox relieved. From , a pack in midfield Davies passed to Massey, who punted to Read, the-latter making his mark. This availed his side little, for Massey by a grand kick landed the oval in touch at Coventry quarter flag. The home team rallied, and they had a chance, but Littlewood and Frank Tur- ner by a grand combined dribble three parts the length of the field, had hard luck in not grounding. H. Rother- ham stopped their career close to the line, and a pass

from Hancox to Read enabled the latter to relieve, Jolley checking him. The home team was placed again on the defensive, through the fine play of Dillon. Fair. Turner, and Povey, and Hill saved from a drop at goal by Jolley. Passing by the Coventry backs neutralized an advantage gained by the Warrington forwards, and after Randles had missed a chance of scoring., the whistle was blown for no-side, Warrington having two minors to their credit, whilst Coventry had one. ' The game was a splendidly colitested one, each side striving their utmost to gam the mastery. The drib- bling, tackling, and screwing of the scrimmages by the Warringtonians quite, non-plussed tbe opposing team. Jolley at centre played a strong game, -01*.st Davies at half performed in a manner that cannat be too highly spoken of. The forwards all played a splendid game, their combination being grand. Individual distinction is out of the question. On behalf of Cov- entry, H.*Rotherharn, Hancox, Boyle and Hill were the pick. The following were the teams: Warrington—Full back, W. Nevins; throe-quarter backs, J. T. Massey, J. Jolley, and Fair. Turner • half backs, W. Speakman and T. Davies; forwards, If. Ashton Frank Turner W. Littlewood, W. Dillon, W. Hayes, V. Povey, W. Bandies, ,C. R. Adamson and R. Eyes. Coventrv—Full back, Hill (captain)t; backs, Read, "Goodria,H. Rotherham, and Mason ; half backs, Hancox and Riley; forwards, K. Rotherham, Boyle, Sergeant, Richardson, Oxboro', Illingsworth, Bennett, and Ward. Referee, Mr. H. Hill, Coventry.

div.head: ~.75aRRINGTON V. MOSEBEY..
div.p: ~.75aRRINGTON V. MOSEBEY..

The famoubVestLancashire organisation made their firs appearance in the Midlands on Saturday, when they en- countered the well known Moseley team. This they did with credit, winning a good game by one goal and eight minors, to three minors. Both teams were strongly re- presented, Barnes Making his reappearance having re- covered from his, injury received at Halifax, but the muddy state of the ground rendered good play difficult, and it was after the advertised time-3.30 —when A. Smith, as captain of Moseley, set the oval in motion. . . .

For the first few minutes the visitors were conl- - to rest in their twenty-five, but when the work had really commenced, it was soon apparent which team had really the best of it, as regards combination. War- ren gob away from a pack, but a pass forward spoiled the chance. A rush headed by Dillon took the game tio half-way, and Randles ond •Speakmin a,dded to this smart dribble by short ,runs to the Moseley twenty-five. The home team relieved, but Jolley, by a timely kick, forced them back. Barnes almost got in after 11, good run, but Hasluck brought timely relief by a smart kick to midfield. Ashton dribbled to the line, and from some loose play Massey sesured, and taking his drop, the ball- struck th,e uprights on the outside. Nevins replied to the drop-out, and, for a while, play rested at centre flag. Massey put in some sterling work, and from a pack at Moseley 25, Warren passed to Barnes, who punted, and following up smartly, prevented the Moseley skipper from returning. Jolley again forced the home team to save by a good run to the line, and exchange kicking from the drop-out by Ha.sluck, Warren, and Mansell found ptay in Moseley territory. Davies and Speakman almost got in after a fine effott, but the home team were playing a grand defensive game. Mylius relieved, but Ashton and Hayes took the leather over, the ' former being knocked into tolach-in-goal when on the point of grounding, only a minor accruing. Pretty passing from the drop-out by the visiting backs was applauded, and A. Smith by a good kick neutralized the advantage gained. The Warringtoniatts tried hard to score a major point, the latter being almost landed from a fair catch of Fair. Turner's, his brother's attempt striking the post. How- ever, fortune favoured them shortly after, for Barqes, by a splendid run, was held on the line, and after DaYies had tried ineffectually to ~oxound,Warren passed to Barnes, . who was not slow to add another to his already long list of dropped goals. Soon after restarting from centre, the , visitors looked like again scoring, Dillon, Povey, and Frank Turner rushing to the line, R. Smith saving. Barnes intercepted some passing of the Moseley backs. Try as they would, the home team could not pass the half-way flag, but no apldition to the score was made, Warrington having the lead by 1 goal 4 minors to Mose- ley nil. Frank Turner restarted the second half, and no return being made, a scrimmage was formed on, the Moseley Tines, l. Smith saving. Fowler dropped out, Barnes replying with a grand runt. half way. • From a pack at midfield, Fair Turner headed ,a rush to the Mose- ley lines, and almost got in, being held by Mylius and A. Smith. The succeeding pack found Moseley again sav- ing. Little relief was brought by the drop out, and it was marvellous how the Moseley men kept the Lancashire team from scoring. Some rather severe play was now witnessed, and Warrington were placed at a great disad- vantage here, losing the services of Barnes, who was compelled to retire. The visitors were thus playing fqur- teen men, Davies going half., whilst Speakman went centre. A good run by Minshall forced Nevins to save. Frank Turner dropped out, and Daviesand Warren forced the home team to adopt the defensive. Jolley, by a grand run, added another minor, and a similar point was added to the Moseley score, after a good run by A. Smith. The Warringtonians, although shorthanded, had all the best of the game, and were unfortunate in not scoring more , than they really did. However, only minor points were added, and after 70 minutes' hard play, Warrington de- • feated the second Midland club (Rugby being the first one) by the score already indicated above. The ground was sadly against good football, and in- terfered with those characteristics that have marked Warrington's successes. Nevertheless, all the Warring- ton team played a determined game, and they must be complimented on Satuislay's success. Of individual play, !Dulles was the best of the backs; he was playing a splendid game imtil he got hurt. His ill-luck seems to cling to him, for after an absence ef a month, he made his re-appearanoe on Saturday; only to receive another check to his successful career. Both Jolley and Massey played A sterling game, whilst Nevinsas hill back played smartly. The halves were on a par, both passing unsel- fishly, and never letting opportunities miss their grasp. All the forwards played well, and it is impossible to dis- tinguish any individual. On behalf of Moseley, Smith, FlasloclTNicoll, and Pnwler were the pick.' The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full back, W. Nevins; three-quarter backs J. Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and J. T. Massey; half backs, Warren and Speakman; forwards, 11. Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, W. Hayes, W. Dillon, W. Randles, R. Littlewood, T. Davies, and W. Povey. Moseley : Full back, R. Smith; three-quarter backs, A. Smith (captain); M. Smith, E. L. Mylins' and Haslock ; half backs, Man- sell and Lea; forwaTds, Lycett, Nicoll, Rogers Dawes, S. Smith, Acton, Fowler, and Jackson. Referee, Mr. Gill, Lelmington, who gaye general satisfaction. WEST LANCASHIRE CUP. WIDNES DEFEAT THE CUPHOLDERS.

Not since Runcorn met Warrington at.Widnes 'three years ago has there been such excitement over a football match aMidnes as there was on Saturday, when Wid- nes met Aspull in the first round of the West Lancashire and Berder Towns Union challenge , Cup. Both. teams were confident of victory, and the rem* was one of the most determined struggles ever witnessed on the ground. Aspull are at present the holders of •the cup, and although they had a month ago suffered 'a crnshing de- feat at the hands of Widnes, they were then without several of their best players, and had afterwards dis- played fine form. In addition, they had undergone a course of training. On the other hand, the Widnes team is now better than at any period of its history, and the present season's record is one to be proud of. With about three exceptions victory has crowned their efforts; and with the whole team in good health and condition there was nothing to cause their supporters a moment's 'uneasiness. Half an hour before the commencement of the match several thousands of spectators had assembled on the field, and the enthusiastic partisans on both sides were to be heard wagering their money very freely as to the result of the game. Special trains were run from Aspull; there were hundreds of visitors from Warring- ton by the ordinary trains; and there would be no less than 6,000 spectators on the ground when the teams faced each other as follows : • Widnes: S Bingham, back; Farrell, Parkinson, and Plumpton, three-quarter backs; Barker and Wilkinson, half backs; Kiddie, Woods, Barber, Hardman, J. Bing- ham, Hughes, Gandy, ,Pennington, and Smith (captain), forwards. • Aspull: Pilkington, back; Bullough, R. peddon, and Morris, three-quarter backs;' Hulme and Cartwright, halfbacks; Hesketh, Bramwell, James Lindsay, John Lindsay, Monks, Grundy, Croston, Haydock, and J. Seddon, forwards. The Widnes men, dressed in white, presented .a much smarter and more athletic appearance than their rivals, who were attired in dark blue jerseys, but both teams were heartily cheered by the assembled thousands. Smith, the Widnes captain, losing the toss, kicked off at three o'clock, with a slight breeze a;gainst him, and a strong sun shining in his eyes. For a while the ball remained in mid-field, then the home team, who had the -advan- tag,,e in the scrimmages, and on the loose, rushed the ball into their opponents' quarters, and after a stiff de- fence Kiddie grounded the ball over the line, after a smart combined dribble. The referee ruled, hdwever, that Kiddie was off-side, and he disallOwed the poebt. More scrimmaging ensued, and Farrell getting hold, some neat passing took place between Barker, Parkin- son, and Plumpton, the latter player falling when just on the line, and an almost certain try within reach. Aspull now repulsed their opponents and dribbled to the half flag, and Hulme, by a lucky flying kick, caused the home quarters to be invaded, and some stubborn play tool place. The splendid combined play of the Widnes forwards quickly asserted itself, and Aspull had toretire to their gwn quarters. The capital following up of Wid- nes was very noticeable at this point. A series of scrim- mages took place in Aspull twenty-five, and Kiddie and. J. Bingham transferred play to the line where the latter passed to Farrell, who placed the ball over the line. The try was disallowed for passing forward. Shortly afterwards Parkinson had to retire, having had his leg seriously in- jured, and about ten minutes later half-time was called, no score having been made on eitfier side. During, the second half Aspull played four three-quarters, J. Seddon being drafted from the forwards. Widnes made no return to the kick-off, and the ball was scrimmaged in the home twenty-five. Parkinson again took his place at three- quarters amid tympathising cheers. Play was even .for

div.head: YHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCII 10,1888. THY I SHlttiftWAL WdilkSl AND ROW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND TriF. DISTRICT.'
div.p: YHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCII 10,1888. THY I SHlttiftWAL WdilkSl AND ROW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND TriF. DISTRICT.'

some time, then Plumpton Obtaining /Sol/session frodi dribble made a fine-run to the Aspull line, but was brought down by Morris when becoming dangerous. Play was now mostly in Aspull quarters,. but try as they would the home team could not overcome the stubborn defence of the visitors. Getting the ball in the loose at the centre, Wilkinson made a splendid run through the thick of his opponents, and grounded the ball over the line. just as he was tackled by Pilkington. Another Aspull player went to the assistance of Pilkington, and together theydragged Wilkinson back into play. The referee for the third time disallowed the appeal for a try. Some exciting play took place on the line; and Aspull were compelled to con- cede a minor to clear their territory. Parkinson shortly afterwards made a fair catch, and Plumpton at- tempted to place a goal from, the place, but failed. As only about a quarter of an hour remained, Widnes played with yedoubled vigour, and at Last their persistency was rewarded, Kiddie from a scrimmage dribbled over the line near the flag and obtained a try, amid the greatest excitement. Hats were thrown into the air, and deafening cheers were given for some minutes. Plurnpton failed to add the premier point- from a difficult position. Aspull salire now completely penned, and from a capit,al drop at goal by S. Bingham; conceded another minor, and Widnes were declared .the winners by I try and two minors, or six paints to nil. Throughout the game the home team showed their superiority to their opponents. Although some pretty back play was occasionally shown on both sides, the play was chieflii; forward, and in this department they played with a aash and judgment that was a treat to 'witness. If we were to single out any who were excep- tionally prominent amongst a good lot we should mention Kiddie and Hardman, the latter frequently gain- ing much giound by his ' splendid following up. The backs also displayed capital form, and deserve equal praise. For the loosers Ilulme played by far the best, but R. Seddon, J. Seddon, and Cartwright played well, " Curley " looked too well after Bullough to allow that noted player accomplishing anything. The •Umpires were, Widnes, Mr. Flufton ; Aspull, Mr. J. Brindle; Referee, Mr. Beswick of Swinton.

NO. B.—FROM STOCKTON HEATH TO LATCHFORD LOCKS. ' -Prior to digressing into an account of the -pro- posed diversion of the Warrington and Altrincham Railway we traced the intended c'ourse of the Ship -Canal, through the hamlet of Lower Walton peat Tom Paine' Bridge, on the Chester-road, and up to the point where it crosses the Stretton and North- wich-road near to St: Thomas' Church, at Stockton Heath. Here, as we pointed out, the short remnant of the Runcorn and Latchford , canal, Tanning be- tween Stockton Heath and the Mersey at Howley will have its connection with the Ship Canal by means of a lock, the greater waterway taking its undeviating course in the direction 'of Manchester. From the southern side of Twenty-step Bridge, at Stockton Heath to a: point close to the southern side of the railway Crossing at Latchford Station the Ship Canal will run in a straight line across the fields, intersecting footpaths and roadways in its course. A favourite Sunday afternoon's stroll for many Warringtoniang is, after reaching the Saracen's Head, public house at Wilderspool, to turn off to the left along 'the narrow lane which leads to the bank of the Latchford canal, pass over the canal, either by the over-bridge or the draw - bridge, and then: follow the footpath which leads south through the fields and after go- ring some distance turn off either to the left and come out near the Baptist Chapel, in Wash-lane, or continue straight ahead and so reach the main road between Stockton Heath and the Dog and Dart public house, at Grappenhall. When the Ship Canal is made, however, a pedestrian who desires to enjoy rural sights and sounds will have to •betake himself in another direction, for this particular footpath is one of those which will be scooped up by the relentless steam digger and as no. provision is to be made for carrying the footway over, the 'broad expanse of the canal will be an .effectual barrier to, farther progress. The next roadway on which the canal will impinge is Ackers- lane, through which it strikes at a distance of about one hundred and fifty yards to the south of the Baptist Chapel. At this point the limits of devia- tion of the canal do. not include any residences as for some distance on either side there is open coun- try. A swing bridge will be provided to carry the, roadway over the canal. As people familiar with the locality know, at the present time when a; per- son pastes the level crossing in Wash-lane, he may, by turning sharply to the left, along Common-lane, reach Grappenhall-lane, but in the future the roadway in this direction will be closed at the point where Common-lane, is to be crossed by the canal, which from Ackers-lane cuts straight across the ground, lately the scenes of the achieve- ments of the Latchford Cricket Club, and another field. As a sort of compensation for the road that is to be , closed, a new road will be made from Ackers-lane. and will skirt the southerly banks of the canal till it reaches the remaining portion of Common-lane, lying on the southern side of the canal. It follows, therefore, that if a person at Waah-lane railway, crossing desires to. reach Gran- penhall-road, or Enutsford-road,'which lies still farther away in the same direction, he will, after the Ship Canal has been made, have to go straight ahead up Ackers-lane till he comes to the canal, over which he will cross by the swing bridge, and then turn to his left along the neW road till he reaches tlie remaining portion of the upper reaChes of Common-lane. ANOTHER NEW ROAD, &c. It is only a comparatively narrow space of open field which separates Common-lane from Grappenhall-road, and through this space the canal continues its straight course, breaking in upon the latter road just on the south side of the station and between it and the house of Mr. S. Gas- kell. Seeing that Mr. Gaskell's residence stands in such close proximity to the station, it Might be expected that it would be numbered amongst those which are doomed to disappear. But this is not the case. Were the limits of deviation to maintain their usual distance from the intended channel of the canal,* they would undoubtedly include this residence, but at this point they abruptly incline inwards and having, so to speak, come round the building they regain their ordinary distance from the prescribed course of the canal. As in the case of other thoroughfares that at Latchford station will be carried over the canal ,on a swing bridge. The southerly end—that is to stay the end nearest Grappenhall,—of this swing bridge will be the start- ing point of another new road—the longest of .the new roads we have yet had occasion to refer to. Starting here the new road will be continued in a parallel line with the canal to Morris Brook farm house, immediately in front of which it Fill, run, and directly afterwards join the present Warring- ton and Thelwaltroad. • Following. the route of the canal from near Latchford station, we find that it cuts through Knutsford road close to, but still on the south side of the present level crossing, and hereabout the limits of .deviation for the canal and the new road already mentioned include the house, situate farther along Knutsford-road, formerly oc- cupied by the late Major Cartwright, and now in the possession of Mr. W. Fell. Another swing bridge will be placed on, Knutsford-road, but Cross- lane, the next roadway eastward from Knistsford road, is, as we mentioned in a previous article, to be closed altogether, and consequently no provision of *the nature of a bridge is required. What with the canal and the new railway, the embankment of which will have reached a considerable height, the neighbourhooa of Cross-lane will be very largely alterdd, and 'here the limits of deviation include pretty nearly all the habitations—which are not numerous—on this connecting roadway between Knutsford-road and ThelwallTl6ane. THELWALL LANE AND LATCHFORD LOCKS. Thelwall-lane is the next highway to be inter- fered with, and. it will be first encroached upon al- most opposite to Cedar Lawn, the residence of Aid. Pickmere, which, together with the gardens and, outbuildings, will be entirely swept away. The half- dozen or so of }leases on the opposite side of the road to Cedar Lawn all come within the limits of deviation, .and will most probably bean taken dovvph as the canal is marked to cut through the site of the one furthest 'east, which is specified as being in the occupation of Mr. R. W. Hawthorne. At this point the canal will begin to widen out so as to form Latchford Locks, and it, will continue to widen till it reaches something like double the width of its ordinary channel, when it will, commence to close in again till it re- turns to its ordittary channel on the Thel- wall side of Morris Brook 'farm. Through- but, the whole length of these locks the present §ite of the Thelwall road will be demolished add will form part Of 'the bed of the canal, and it is provided that the Canal Company rnay'stop up and extinguish all rights of way on the Thelwall road froni about sixty yards on the Thelwall side of Cross-lane, or rather more than that distance on the Warrington side of Alderman Pickmere's residence to about one hundred and fifty yards—measured along the road—on the Thelwalil side of Morris Brook farni. It will thus 'be seen that for a length of something approaching a mile the present Thel- wall road will cease to be a roadvvay, and will, in fact, for the greater part of /the distance entirely disappear. In the future, therefore, in order that a person may reach the villaue of Thelwall from War- rington he will, when near the Post-office at Latch- ford, instead of turning to the left, as at present, have to proceed Straight ahead along Knutsford- road, cross the canal by the swing bridge at the far- ther side of the present level crossing and then turn' to his left along the new road, which, as we have explained, is to be made from Grappenhall-lane to the remaining part of Thelwall-road on the southern side of the canal, and thence on to Thelwall. The existing road in that direction is separated from the front of Morris Brook farm house" by a rather spacious garden, but the new road will be imme- diately in front of Mr. Darbyshire's residence, and will run over what is at present the site of some out- buildings. . -

CARNARVON HARBOUR TRUSTEES AND THE SHIP CANAL.

During Tuesday's sitting of the Carnarvon Harbour Trustees, under the presidency of Sir Llewelyn Turner, Mr. J. Menzies proposed that, in view of the advantage that would accrue to the trust by the extension of the narrow guage railway to the harbour, and the construc- tion of quays under the provision of the company's Ex- tension Bill, 1885, the trustees should ,contributo £l,OOO towards the costs of such quays, which would beerected on their estate, subject to the quays becoming' the pro- perty of the trust, and being carried out in accordance with plans approved of by the harbour authorities and further, that that authority undertake to open and close the bridge to be made across the harbour bvj the com- pany. Mr. Menzies said that he believed that by the opening of the Ship Canal a much larger proportion of

Sates would be shipped than at present, and in order to retain their legitimate trade and give reasonable facilities the present quay space, already limited, would be totally insufficient-,a difficulty which could easily be, obviated by transferring a part of the trade to the opposite side "of th harbour, and thus increase their wharf rents and dues. For the same reason he anticipated a material in- crease in coals and other merchandise forwarded by sea and loaded direct into the railway trucks. Mr. Menzies read a letter which he had received from Mr. W. A. Dar- bishire, quarry proPrietor, Nantlle, supporting the pro- posal.—The Chairman pointed out that insteserof con- tributing, the harbour authorities might expend £l,OOO upon the proposed new quays. He agreed that the opening of the Ship Canal would have a very beneficial effect upon the slate industry of North Ivas, and con- sequently upon the shipping trade.—Mr. Newton thought that in such a case the London and North-Western Rail- way Company would reduce their rates—Mr. Ap Hu Williams did not consider that the 'company referred to could compete with the shipping interests in the transit of slates to Manchester after the canal had been opened. —The Hon. C. H. Wynn pointed out that the London and North-Western Railway Company would certainly develop the sea traffic from Deganway, in which case Camarvon should endeavour to steal a march upou them by aiding in extending. the Narrow Guage Railwayto the town. He seconded Mr. Menzies proposal—Even- tually the resolution was adopted after having been slightly amended. .

- THE NEW BILL. , The Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which authorises the acquisition of additional lands at Ea.stham and Frod- sham, will pass unopposed through the House of Lords, no petitions having been presented against it within the time limited by the standing orders.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The West Lancashire Rugby Union Committee met at the Goat Hotel, Liverpool, on Saturday evenifig, when the draw for the second round of ties was made, with the following result :—St. Helens Recreation v. Wigan, at St. Helens; Pemberton v.• Widnes, at Pemberton; Litherland v. Walkden, at Litherla.nd ; Tyklesley v. St. Helens, at Tyldesley. • Runcorn still retain the proud title Of "Champions of Cheshire." Birkenhead Park visited the old town on Saturday fully prepared. to "do or die," but they had to retire most decisively vanquished on their merits by one goal, three tries, and five minors to one try. and one minor. In the first half the Park made the pace at a terrific rate, but even then the locals more than held their own. In the second half the visitors had .ctearly shot their bolt. and Runcorn, aided by their splendid staying powers, were easy winners at the conclusion of the game. The game was a most enjoyable one from , start to finish. It was of that open character that spec- tators love to see, and the passing on both sides was at times very pretty, and equally effective. Unfortunately 1 Davies got rather an awkward throw, and dislocated his shoulder in such a manner that his presence in the arena need not be expected again this season. To-day Runcorn meet Rochdale Hornets at Rochdale, 9,nd "Pat' Woods has been chosen to fill the post left vacant by Speakman, and ha is looked Upon in many good quarters as no unworthy follower of that fine player. That he may prove to be sois the wish of all. It would be scarcely correct to say that the people of Widnes went wild on Saturday evening, but they gave many evidences that they were bubbling over with joy. And had they not good reason ? • Aspull, the holders of the West Lancashire Cup, came to uphold their title to )he possession of the trophy, and had to return to their native heath, not as proud conquerors, but as losers in a fair fight. Of the match on Saturday, it cannot be said that the score is a correct indication of the game. For at least three-fourths of the time played the Widnes men were in the territory of their opponents, and on numerous occat sions experienced hard lines in not scoring, whils- Kiddie, Farrell, and Wilkinson were unfortunate in hav- ing tries disallowed. Putting aside all feelings of par- tisanship, it must be said that the first try obtained by Kiddie was quite fair, and ought to have been allowed; but the referee no doubt acted according to his honest convictions, and his decision was and must be accepted. Fsrward, the winners played in magnificent style, never allowing their opponents to become really dangerous, and the only fault that can be found is that they did not give the backs sufficient work to do. Had more use been made of the good men behind the scrimmage, the score, we opine, would have been heavier. The visitors, how- ever, were pointless, and it would be ungenerous to cavil when victory was so gallantly won. Aspull were so decisivelrbeaten forward that their backs did ndt get nauch chance to show bilieir prowess, the most prominent man being HuLme,who played a sterling game. It is satisfactory to note that although the excitement was very high, the spectators behaved in a most friendly and sportsmanlike manner, and there was not the slight- est complaint.

div.head: TTIP., EXTENSION OF ST. PETER'S • PARISH.
div.p: TTIP., EXTENSION OF ST. PETER'S • PARISH.

On Thursday evening a public meeting of the parishioners of the old parish of Warrington, con- vened by the Rector and churchwardens, was held in the National Schoolroom, Church-street, the objdet for which it was called being to protest against the proposed alienation of the district bounded by Battersby-lane, Orford-lane, and Lyth- goes-lane, by annexing it to the parish of St. Peter's. --The chair ws.s occupied by Councillor N. B. Per- cival, the Rector's warden, and there was a good at- tendance.—The Chairman, in explaining the object of the meeting, said that the parishioners of the district in iiiiestion were strongly averse to being included in the parish Of St. Peter's, and wished ,to 'remain as they were. They hoped that they should not be too late tq prevent the change. The Crossley-street and Hamilton-street schools wete flourishing, and parish work was 'tieing well carried on in the district, and there was no justification for such a change being made.- -Councillor R. W. Francomb, the people's warden, pro- posed "That this meeting expresses 'the astonishment and indnation of the parishioners of the Warrington Parish Church That any scheme involving the alienation of so large a portion of this parish should have beenpro- jected, and carried to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, against the express wish of thc Rector, and without con- sulting the feelings of those whom it seeks to transfer to anothq parish." He -was, he said, much surprised when he heard that it was proposed to take that portion of the church parish and annex it to St. Peter's parish. He could not see thehecessity for it. and thought that it wbuld be much better for the people of St. Peter's to work up their own district—Councillor Wright seconded the resolution. He failed to see, he said, what benefit St. Peter's was to gain by the aliena- tion, which would mean an addition to St. Peter's of about ninety acres of land, and a large population. Any clergyman who wished to do his duty would have suffi- cient to do in St. Peter's parish without such an addition. He looked upon it as a ver3- unfair proceeding to at- tempt to take a portion of the old parish, without hav- ing obtained the consent of the Rector or of the parish- ioners--Mr. T. Cawley advised the meeting to pause be- fore they adopted such a, resolution as the one proposed. The scheme had been put forward ' by men who had the interests of St. Peter's at heart. —Mt. John Roberts also 'spoke against the resolution, and spoke of the difficul- ties that had to be encountered in connection with the new parish of St. Peter's. They had a. right to ask the old parishioners to give wait, a little. The permission of the Rector had been asked more than, two years ago, but he had always opposed the scheme tooth and nail. After a little further discussion the resolution was adopted by a largo major- Cannell then proposed—" Resolved, that in deference to the strong feelings already expressed by the parishioners, and particularly the unanimous opposition thereto offered by the residents of the parish immediately affected thereby, this meeting respectfully, but firmly, requests Sir Gilbert Greenall to Withdraw the offer made to St. Peter's, in .so fax'as it affects the -aliehation of any. portion of the rectory parish of Warrington." He thought that' the attempted alienation was a mean ana contemptible trick. Mr. W. Brooke ' seconded the resolution and spoke at length on what had taken place in connection with St Peter' parish. parish. He thought that the extension was abodt as cruel and un- righteous a thing as had ever beeh perpetrated.—The resolution was carried.—lt was also resolved, on the motion of Mr. Woolaeott, secon,ded by Mr. Brundrett, '; That this meeting resolves itself into a committee, with power to add to its lumber, to memorialise the Bishop of Liverpo.ol, and the Archbishop of York, against the scheme, a copy of such memorial to be forwarded to the Privy Council.—The meeting then terminated.

Tiu SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC.—A most alarming outbreak of small-pox was discovered on Wednesday night in the (irimshaw Park district of Blackburn and a further dis- covery of nine cases was made on Thursday morning, all of which ,have been removed to the hospital. One woman, who was takenill on Wednesday night, died on Thursday moruing.. The people in the town are full of consternation ancialarm. There are now 22 cases. Shef- field returns for the week indicate that small-pox still fights very strongly there for the upper hand! During the seven days reported upon 21. people died in that town of the disease, though the greatest efforts are being made to cope with the epidemic. " Sayo-Lnu," or Linseed Soap, cherishes the cuticle. 64. post free. Ray Bros., Ld, Stockport.—Advt. •

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton) pre- siding ; Aldermen Burgess, Pickmere. Holmes, Chandloy, Webster, Harrison; Councillors Greening, Barker, Wright, J. Pierpoint, Heaton, Platt, Black- hurSt, J. Shaw amen, Jolley, Taylor, Percival, Ashton; Francomb, Dixon, W. Pierpoint, Hutchinson, Fleming, H. Roberts; Mqssrs. J. L. Whittle (deputy town cleric), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor.) I • THE LATE COUNCILLOR JOHN BROWN AND MR. RICHARD RAN. _ _ _

The MAYOR said that before proceeding with the busi- nesi,of the,Council, it was his painful duty to refer to the recent death of two gentlemen who had been con- nected with that Council—the late Mr. Richard Kean, who, although not a member of the Council Itt the time of his death, had faithfully served his native town both as a Councillor and as an Alderman of the borough for many years. As most of them sat with him, and knew him as a most active and useful member of the Corpora- tion:for so long a time, it was only natural that they should feel deep regret at. hearing that he had taken his final departure; and they would all sympathize with his family in the loss they had sustained. (Hear,hear.) Mr. Councilor Sohn Brown, whose remains were interred at Grappenhall that morning, was and had been a member of the Corporation continuously since 1878 until the time ' of his death; and he (the Mayor) thought he might say that no member of the Cbuncil rendered greater or more valuable service, or devoted More time to the benefit of the town than Mr. Brown did. (Hear, hear.) Hts loss would be very much ,felt, and he begged to move the following resolution :--"That the Council receives with regret the announcement of the death of Mr. John Brown, one of the Councillors of this borough, which took place on the Ist-March, and desires to express its 'appreciation of the valuable services rendered by him to the borough during a period of 16 years, and its heart- felt sympathy with his widow and family in their bereavement."

Alderman HOLMES, in seconding the proposal, said the members of the Finance Committee Would feel Councillor Brown's loss very much; to them it would be very serious. (Hear, hear.) • Aldermen WEBSTER and Sultans supported the motion, which was carried.
ALLOWANCE OF £5O PER ANNUM TO TILE CHIEF CON- _ STABLE.

- The MAYOrt moved " That, in consequenhe of the un- suitable condition of the house occupied by the Chief ConstablA he be at liberty to leave the same. and that in Hell of house rent; Coals, gas, and taxes, an allowance of £5O per annum be made to him." He thought it was a very reasonable proposition. (Hear, hear.) As they all knew, Mr. Hunt had not enjoyed very good- health of late, which fact he attributed in a great measure to the unsuitable condition of the house in which he lived. It should be understood that the £5O really only meant an addition of £25 so far as the ratepayers were concerned, as £25 out of the £5O was repaid by the Gov- eminent.

..... Alderman HARRISON said he had great pleasure in seconding the resolution which had been proposed. He did not think there was an officer of the Corporation more worthy to be recognized in a matter of that kind than Mr. Hunt. (Hear, hear.) Alderman PICKMERE supported, the motion. As had been already observed, the £5O would not ell be paid by the ratepayers of Warrington, but a• moiety would be paid by the Government. Even if that were not the case he should have voted for the whole £5O to support such an efficient officer. Mr. Hunt had been a gobcl officer for many years. and he hoped the Council would unani- mously support the resolution and allow the Chief Con- stable what he asked for. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Ilemusox w I think he .has not esked for it.

_ .Ahlerman PICENEHE Well, What we ask for. Cobncillor BOLTON also supported the proposal. • Alderman CHANDLEY said there was only one remark ' he wished to make. They were very unanimous in' wishing to consult Mr. Hunt's convenience, but it ought not to go forth that the place was such an unhealthy one—(hear, hear)) because it would put the Watch Committee in a very difficult position. In all probability they would have to put a sergeant in the house, and it would seem a very injudicious thing to put a man in a house which wAs notoriously unhealthy The fact was the house was not at all unhealthy, but when a man reached Mr.; Hunt's age he required a greater amount of ,fresh air than in his youdger.days. Councillor .Tottev also supported the motion. Councillor Pr...vir, speaking in support of the motion, said the request had not come from Mr. Hunt, but; on the contrary, had been pressed upon him time after time, and he was glad to see that the Chief Constable had at last consented to it. Ile thought the Corporation could congratulate themselves upon having a very able and worthy officer in Mr. Hunt—(hear, hear)—who during the time lie had been in the force had done his Work well. (Hear, hear.) ' The motion was then put to the Council and cannel unanimously. •' .
THE SALARY OF THE INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES, PROPOSED INCREASE., _

Al&Mail BURGESS moved the following iwsolution : " That the Committee, having regard to the important and increasing duties which have from time to time been 'imposed upon the Inspe,ctor of Nuisances under the fol- lowing Acts of Parliament, in respect of which no remu- neration has been allowed to him, it is resolved that he be paid the following sums per annum for his services As Inspector under The ContagiouS 'Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, £4; as Inspector under' .the Dairies, Cow- shedS, and' Milk-shops Orders of 1885 and 1888, £4'; as Inspector under the Sale of FOod and Drugs Acts, 1875 & 1879, £4 ;as Inspector under the Canal Boats Acts, 1877 and 1884, £4; as Inspector under the Margarine Act, 1887. £4." Mr. Norman's salary had been raised twice since his appointment. His salary on appointment was £124, which, in September, 1877, was increased to £143, and in 1880 to £156, at which figure it now stood. From the 31st May, 1877, .on Which date he was appointed, to the present time there had been a large accession to the population in this borough; but there had not been a corresponding increase in the direction of assistance in the Inspector's. department. • It was time a, third inspector had been apPointed, but in reality he received no remu- neration for his services ; his work was to 'superintend the scavenging, and the only assistance which he ren- .dered to Mr. NormAn was at night time 'in the inspection of lodging-houses. They thought that Mr. Nortvan was a very efficient officer, and discharged the duties of his office exceedingly well. • The Committee had no feeling in the matter beyond believing that the best interests of the town and ratepayers would be served by the action they were advocating: (Hear, hear.) Councilloi FRANCOMB seconded the motion., He be- lieved that in Mr: Norman they had an excellent, officer. Perkaps the Corporation did, not know sor much of his. labciurs as the Sanitary Committee. He had a lot of very difficult and almost dangerous Work to ,perform, and he always did it well. (Hear, hear.) • Alddrman PICKMERE.—Were those appointments all, made since his last advance in salary? • Alderman BURGESS.—Yes. • • Alderman PICKILERE.—And he has never received any- thing_ on account of them? , Alderman BudoEss.-,—Nothing whatever. Councillor BLAcicuunsr asked whether Mr. Norman had not been already paid for 'his extra duties, because he found that the increasers which he had reteived had been made 'when those , particular Acts of Parliament were passed? Not only se, but two assistants had been appointed. Mr. Norman commenced at £124 a year, and his salary was now £156; which was quite ample for services rendered. He was no doubt a good officer, yet they might' pay a good officer too .11, and he begged to move, as hn amendment, that the application for an in- crease of salary be not entertained. • Councillor JOLLEY believed that Mr: Norman was as efficient an offieer as that Corporation could have, and he believed also that he had two good men under him= one of whoine received £95 , Per annum and the other £B7 12s, so that altogether the Council were paying £314 12s a year for sanitary officers. That sum, he con,- sidered, was sufficient, and he should not vote for any advance at all. An application had been , made by another officer to the Finance Committee, and the Com- mittee came to the.eotoklusion that they could not enter- tain the proposal, for an increase of salary. , Cduncillor FLEMING supported the amendment, because he believed that the officer in. question was

having quite as large a salary for the work as he was entitled to. (Hear, hear). Councillor W. PIERPOINT in supporting the amendment, said Mr. Norman was as good a man they could possibly have for the work, and he believed that a mart ouAlit to be paid for his libotris,-aiirar the proper time he•, did not think he should hesitate to support the proposition in faiiour of increasing the salary ; but the reason he had in his niirid for not supporting it on the present occasion was that he thought in the present condition of sanitary matters in 'Warrington, seeing the ig,norance•which they as a Council were In. and having waited so long for , , statement of account—(hear, hear)—from the. Com- mittee, which would enable them to form an opinion of what' that Committee was doing—he was not in a position to vote for anything until a report was sent in, • either good, bad, or indifferent, (Hear, hear). 'Alderman Harms supported the amendment. He did not wish to pass any censure upon the inspector in the slightest degree, but he did think he was amply paid for the work which he did, and, takingante account the fact that during the last twelve months an assistant had been appointed, he thought the expertes of that depart- ment were quite Sufficient without an advance of salary. (Hear, hear). There were two other' applications on Committees of which he was a member, both of which were declined. •

Alderman WEBErrign supported the resolution, and said that seeing that since Mr. Norman's appointment a great increase had taken place in the amount of work, he thought it only fair that a reasonable sum be paid him for extra work.

Alderman PicxxEßE agreed with the last speaker that extra moiry should be paid for extra work. He thought that if they imposed fresh duties on an officer they ought to pay him for them. Everybody else was paid for work of a 'public character; and they did not do it for love of the Council (Laughter, and hear, bear.) ' Councillor BOLTON supported the amendment, remar- king that if Mr. Norman's salary was to be increased, those -of some other officials should be reduced. Alderman CILANDLEY supported the resolution. i Councillor H. ROBERTS, n supporting the resolution, said that at the time of Mr. Norman's appointment there was the same number of inspectors employed as now, and 75 per cent. of Mr. Norman's new duties were ad- ditional to what he performed when appointed. (Hear, hear.) _

, Councillor GREEN, in speaking against the proposition, said they had other officers of the Corporation who, since their appointment, had had additional duties im- posed upon them, and if the present proposition were sanctioned they would at once have applications from those other officials for similar increases in salaries. (Hear, I-nr.)

Counci,llor, Dixox spoke in favour of the proposition, and remarked that economists had sprung up that night with great rapidity. (Laughter.) • Coucillor WRIGHT thought it would bp false economy not to grant the increase which was asked for. ' Alderman BURGESS, in replying, said that Mr. Norman only received 2s. 2d. or 2s. 3d. a week more ttian his predecessor and late chief, Mr. William Heaton. He had filled the office for thirteen years, and in the mean- time there had been an increase of 13,000 in the popula- tion of this borough, which naturally entailed a great increase in the duties which devolved upon him. Mr. William Pierpoint had asked for a statement from the Sanitary Committee. (Hear, hear). One day he would have that stattment, but that would be when it suited him (Aldermah Burgess)—(laughter)--and he would try to make it in such a way that it would be satisfactory to that Council, and that Mr. Pierpoint would regret having spoken as he had that evening. (Hear; hear, • and laughter). The MAYOR said heintended to support the resolution. Tde proposition was then put to the meeting, the vote- int being as follows ::-For r The Mayor; Alderman Pick- mere, Webiter, Ha,rrisori, Burgess,' and Chandley ; r Councillors John Pierpoint, GrErening, Wright, Heaton, Francomb, Dixon, and Henry Roberts. Against: Alder- man Holmes; Councillors Jolley, William Pierpoint, Fleming, Green,, Ashton, Taylor, Bolton, Blackhurst, Hutchinson, and Percival. ; The .resolution was accordingly 'declared ' carried. there being 13 votes recorded in favour a it. and 11 against.

ELEUTIVE AUDITORS. • The DEPUTY. Towx CLERK announced that Mr. John Harrison and Mr. J. L. Tunstall had been elected elective auditors of the borough; and that the Mayor had appointed Councillor Greening to be his auditor for the ensuing twelve months. enorese) MEMORIAL TO THE _WATERLOO HEROES.

The MAYOR read a letter from the Lord Mayor, asking for the co-operation of his 'Worship in the effort he was making dto aid the fun i now being raised to erect a me- morial n the new cemetezy at Brussels to thst•Britist4 officers and Men who fell during the Waterloo campaign, and were burled in Belgium. The Brussels municipality .had generously offered a•site' for the proposed monument, and it wal thought that the memorial, including its per- manent maintenance and guardianship, will cost about £3,000 in addition to the amounts already received. The Mayor intimated that he would have an account opened at each of the banks in the town, And would forward -any subscriptions the members of the Council desired to give.

. . THE ROYAL SILVER WEDDING. - The Council agreed, on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman • Buttorss, to forward to their Royal Highnesses the. Prince and, Princess of Wales a congratulatory address on the attainment of their silver wedding, which was Worded as follows :—" We, the Mayor, Aldernien, and Burgesses of the Borough of War- rington, beg very respectfully to approach your Roy-al Highnesses and to offer our sincere and heartfelt con- gratulations on the auspicious occasion of your Royal Highnesses' silver wedding. Your Royal Highnesses' mar- riage ha-bee'n blest with an affectionate and happy ,family, and every domestic and marital felicity has been vouchsafed' to you and we pray that God in his infinite goodness may, be you, to grant to your Royal High- nesses many years of health and happiness to live in the enjoyment of the sincere affection and .profound regard of a great and loyal nation." , - WATCH COMMITTEE. • This Committee recommended that • the teUders of Messrs. :John Hammond and Co., and of Messrs. lUns- worth Bros., t 6 supply various articles of police cloth- , ing, be accepted. There as not much in the amounts of the tenderS re- ceived, and the committee thought that it was best to ' give the Preference to townsmen. • The MAYOR. in answer to Cr. Dixon; said the Watch Committee had under consideration, the representations made to them; by a deputation, on the temperance 4ues- tion. .If they had anything to prdpose they would bring it forward at the next meeting, Alderman WEBSTER said that the Watch Committee cnmmunicated their views to the deputation, arid Coun- cillor H, IlorsEnrs, as one of the deputation, said that grey were perfectly- satisfied, with the reception. they got from the Watch'Cofnmittee., , The minuteswere then approved. nr.c DILIDGE-STREIV PROPERTY. In proposing their adoption; Councillor Pr.:Arr said that the Committee had had several inquiries with regard to -the land in Bridge-,street, and the MAYOR remarked that he knew there were many:peoPle Who should be desirous of taking shdPs in Bridge-street if someone WoUld 136 inducedtoin- vest money on the land. fl THE PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. ` _ _ _

In prop—o—is adoption of the. i:e-lx;rt of ihiA ''coni- mittee. Councillor WEIHHT said that it was The. intention of the committee to proceed, at as early a period as ,pos- sible, with the paving of private, streets. • They never made Streets at a less rate per yard than they were do- ing at present, and they felt that they were acting in the interests of the ratepayers, .and the property owners' also. The proposition haying been seconded by Council- lor HUTCHINSON. the minutes were approVed. • sCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes were confirmed on themotbn of Alder- man ViTgasTEn; seconded by Councillor J. SHAW•GREEN. They contained the report Of the Inspector that 91 cases had. been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 89 cases for 186 children. Sixteen cases had been taken before the magistrates, whe,n fines were inflicted in twelve cases, two warrants ordered, one ordered,to be whipped, and one dismissed. The average attendance at the Public Blementary Schools during the month of Jandary was 6,94; last year, 6,528; increase, 376.

div.head: SANKEY-STREET WALL AND THE BATH.
div.p: THE SANKEY-STREET WALL AND THE BATH.

At a meeting of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Com- mittee it was resolved "that it be an instruction to the, Borough Treasurer to include in his next estimate Of ex-, ' penditure by this Committee' a sum of £4OO for taking down the wall in front of the Town Hall, also the sum of £l5O for asphalting the walks in the gardens, and also the sum of £175 for providing a supply of water for the Baths." The Committee also reported that, having had a conversation with Mr. Chapman, of Salford, and hav- ing considered his offer to undertake certain alterations to the Baths well for £l2O, they were disposed to accept his offer if he will guarantee to provide 200 gallons of water per minute, and tenter into an agreement to that effect.

The MAYOR in moving the confirmation of the minntes; said he hoped the resolution with reference tie the removal of the wall would be agreed to. it would be an improvement' in every way, and would do a great deal to relieve the crowded condition of Sankey-street. (Hear, hear.) With reference to asphalting the walks je the gardens, he did not think there could be two °Pinions; as the walks were at the present time inn very disgrageful condition—(hear, hear)—while with regard to the Bathe Mr. Chapman was prepared to give them a guarantee. Alderman PICIEMBRE seconded the motion.. Councillor DrxoN moved an amendment to the effect that the minute that it be an instruction to the Boron Treasurer to include in his next estimate of expenditure a sum of £4OO for taking down the wall in front of the Tolini Hall be not confirmed. He contended that the rates of the town were very heavy at present, and the .expenditure contemplated should be avoided. , Alderman Burgess and Councillor Heaton expressea the opinion that Mr. Chapman would not for the 5aL,02 stated be able to produce a contiauous supply of 2,Ve gallons of water per minute, and the latter gentleruce suggested that the pump should be kept going for e, week without stopping as a test. A rather protractee discussion on the subject followed, in which Councillor Bolton; Alderman Webster, Alderman Pickmere, Cone" cillor Barker, Councillor Platt, Alderman Harrisoc, Alderman Chandley, and Councillor H. H‘oberts tool' part.

Councillor PLAIT seconded the amendment with ference to the proposed expenditure of £4OO on th removal of the wall. The passing of the minutes won} not commit the Council to remove the wall, but it was long step in that direction, In the present state of tb rates—which were frightening away manufacturers- they should be careful not to spend £4OO on what b should call a fad, though perhaps he was wronr, in dojo so. The removal was not a necessity, ,andbthe rate should be considerably lower before they applied £l° for the purpose. • Referring to thg Sankey-street wall, .Councillor ROBERTS said he diR not consider its removal a necessit at the present time. If the affairs of the town we; Iprosperous, and the rates comparatively low, he show not begrudge those who seemed to have an idea that tt •alteration was desirable the. possibility of carrying out, but £4OO was nothing like adequate to do what v 4 II required. What was to become of the land between tl Wall and the ,front of the Town Hall? They could n' do the work creditably for less than £l,OOO or £1,500. Alderman FlorAiEs and Councillor PERCIVAL supporte the amendment.

• Connelllor JOHN PIERPOINT 'iipported the passing the minutes, thinking that there would be little or cOst beyond the £4OO. He contended that it was agP shaint that such a handsome building as the Town 11 should be hidden by a blank wall. councillor BOLTON said he should vote for the rem°, of the wall, as he considered it would be a greatimpro' ment to the Town Hall, He did not think they rg spend the .whole of the £4OO. •
- COURCiIIOr GREENING was of opinion that the go° sense of:th9 Council would be shown if they refused t pass the minute.

Councillor JOLLA( supported the passing of lb minute, because he thought the wall had been a grea. eyesore for many years, and. also " because the inhabl tants were anxious to see it taken down. Alderman Haaarsoa said it wash a reproach to t. common sense and intelligence of the Council, in 10 opinion—though it was using strong Language to say,9 —to have an ugly Wall like that standing before la, Town Hall, blocking it but from public view. The Iv?' was an innovation. It was not in existence when how was built, when George the Third was King; ' When Bank Hall was built there was no wall at the /roll but there were pillars and chains, and the house all grounds were visible to the public. The wall was tall. in the days of one of Lord Winmarleigh's andestors,! prevent children trespassing on the front ground. Borough Survey-or could manage to do the work for than £4OO, L4OO, but that amount would do it handsomely. Alderman BURGESS said that the wall which is nel standing was' built by Lord VVinmarleigh, then Coloo 'Wilson-fatten, and maintained that the ground in fra of the Town Hall was not a recreation ground wile they made it so. The recreation ground was on 03 otherzide.
Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT said the wall which Wilson-Patten built fell down some 30 or 40 years (Laughter). '

Coimcillor licrrcinmsox said he had great pleasure 0 supporting the uroposition as he thought it very desir able that the alteration should be carried out. Alderman Bunauss said he found that so faras land in front of the hall was concerned ho had been error, as the major portion of it was set apart for re' creation. .• The MAYOR said the propogition was simply an instrnE tion to the/ Borough Treasurer to include in his estic_na,t: _ _

the sum of £- 4-0-070-r- trlieTtri:PoS-e's-VaZ;ajTl,'a—at,l)l resolution was simply to obviate any alteration in treasurer's estimates. The Council then divided, with the 'following 'result --For the amendment—" That, that portion of the utes having reference to the wall in front of the TO Hall be not confirmed."—Aldermen Holmes, Webster and Burgess ; Councillors Platt, Greening, Withal' Pierpoint, Fleming, Giten, Blackhurst, Dixon, PerCiVai and H. Roberts-12. Against: Aldermen Picklueret Harrison, and Chandley ; Councillors Joßn PierPoi° Barker, Jolley, _Wright, Heat da; Bolton, Taylor, Ashton Francomb, Hutchinson, and the Mayor-14. The minute&were then adopted. MISCELLANEOUS. The 'Markets Committee reported a total income £254 19s 10d. The minutes of other committees contained nothing of importance, were passed, and was resolved that the new bye-laws relating to juverli.L trading approved by the Council at the last meeting 1' confirmed. .1

div.head: WELSH .GATHERING AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: WELSH .GATHERING AT EARLESTOWN.

In commemoration of •St. David, the patron saint of Wales, the Welsh residents of Earlestoivn held 'their annual festival, which partook of the character. of an Eieteddfodd, in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom an Saturday evening. The three Welsh religious bodies in the • district—Wesleyans„Cal- vinists, and Independents were well represented, and there was a very large attendinice. The ar- rangements had been carried out by an energetic ,committee comprising Vq Messrs. J. Parry, T. liams, H. Williams, J. Davies, R. Owen, T. Williams. Morris Watkins, R. 0. Roberts; D. Owen; E. Morris, and T. Pierce, and with Mr. L. T. Foulkes at their head as secretary, their efforts to make the...affair a success were well rewarded. There were competi- tions in various subjects, eompriling stocking knit- ting, antimacassar work, map drawing, hand writ- ing, choir and glee singing, essays, Sze. Nearly the whole of the meeting was conducted in the Welsh vernacular. The proceedings commenced, with tea, of which about 400 'persons partook: The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mesda,mes Williams (Tamworth-. strut), Profit, Williams (Viaduct-street), Parry, Grove, Williams (Queen-street), Owen, Watkins, Jones,,Pilliriger, Jones; Misses Profit, Williams, Hughes, L. Hughes, Owen, Davies, and C. Profit. After tea the room was crowded with an enthusiastic audience, there being many present from Ashton, Golborne, Haydock, Tyldesley, Skelnersciale, and the suirrounding neighbourhoods. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Griffith Ellis, M.A., of Bootle, and there were also present on the platform Rev. J. O. Williams (" Pedrog "), Mr. John Evans (" Cynog- fab"), of Manchester, and Mr. L: T. Foulkes (secretary). The proceedinga opened with d pianofote solo by Miss K. Williams, of St. Helens (pianoforte prize winner in the 1884 National Eisteddfod it Liverpool), which was exe- cuted in a masterly manner. The Chairman next addressed the meeting, and said he occupied that position owing to the unfortunate acci- dent which occurred to Mr. John Parry, one of the most popular men in Wales, and he was sure they all sympath- ised.deeply with Mr. Parry, who, he *was glad to say was gradually recovering from the elects of the accident, and they hoped he would soon be able to resume his post in the present agitation on the question of the tithe rent charges in Wales. • (Applause). He expressed his sym- pathy with the great national awakening that was taking i place n this nation. He coMmented upon political ques- tions affecting Wales at the presenp time and said they were well awar9, that there was notliinr, more popular witliWelsh audiences than the cry of Home Rule 'for Wales, but he could net agree with the cry in the form which it took amongst their leaders: (Hear, hear.) He believed as firmly as any One that Wales knew its own 'wants better than anybody else and that Wales ought to be allowed to pronounce upon legislatiOn intended for Wales. He considered it a disgrace that Wales should send 26 out of 30 members in favour of Disestablishment and yet the voice of the remaining four outweighed the ' voice of the 2t3." (" Shame.") It was a shame. (Ap- plause.) On its own wants Wales ought to be allowed to be its own jirdge, but they did not want a Welsh Par- liament. What they wanted was than when Wales pro- nounce in constitutional terms beyend dispute, Parlia- ment should yield. (Hear, hear.) That prineiple pre- vailed in regard to Scotland and why should it not be applied to Wales? (Applause.) It was well known what Home Rule for Wales would mean—they would dispense with all the present abuses in 12 months. . The Church would he disestablised, there would be a land law, and land reform, the mine royalties would be settled and the publican and a good. number of other sinners would also be settled. The Radicalism of Wales could not be said under a bushel, and it was known that when they fought for Home Rule they fought for the removal of every existing abuse at one stroke. (Applause.) He conclud,ed by expressing the hope that that meeting would be a national gathering and he handed over its charge to " Pedrog "-(thd Rev. J. O. Williams.) • The Rev. J. 0. Williams (" Pedrog."), of Liverpool, then briefly 'addressed the meeting in the Welsh ver- maculan—Miss Davies afterwards rendered in excellent taste the Welsh' air "Ash Grove."—Mr. L. T. Foulkes read the results of the competitions in knitted stockings and antimacassars, handwriting, and best,rnap of North Wales, the two latter being confined to children under 12 years of age. The adjudicators were Misses Davies, Watson, and Williams for wool work, and Misses Davies, Williaffis, and K. Williams for writing and snap draw- ing. The prize for stocking knitting was gained by Mrs. Williams (Tamworth-street), and for antimacassar Miss Profit; handwriting Master George Profit, and map drawing Thomas If. Watkin (Wargrave-road.) The nelct event was a glee competition, the piece selected being " Gwllthyn,' sang in Welsh. s The competing choirs were the " Lathorn," from Skelmersdale, and Tyldesley choir. • The adjudicator was Mr. John Evans (Cynog,fab), of Manchester, ,who awarded the prize to• the Tyldesley choir, the, cohductor being Mr. D. Davies (Tyldesley.) , ." Hos Llifon," of St. Helens, then gave, with much effect, a Welsh song, which was evidently appreciated by the audience. Miss Owen gained a well- de.soried encore for the careful manner in which she sang "The Children's Home," and in resPonse she re- peated the last verse. Mr. J. Evans (Cyno,gfab) then sang sang; a song in Welsh, which was said to, be his own composition. " Pedrog" afterwards adjgdicated upon the best .translation from English into Welsh of 10 lines of Portia's speech in the "Merchant of Venice," the prize being divided between Messrs. W. and R. Hughes -(brothers), of Warrington. The next item was a choral com Petition on the Congregational hymn tune, Llangan," by choirs of not less than twelve, and not more than Eixteen voices. The competing choirs were Skelmersdalefryldesley. and Earlestown. It was at once manifest that 'tyldesley were far and away the best, their rendering of the piece being most careful and studied. The prize was accordingly awarded to that •choir. Miss Williards, of St. Helens, who possesses a beautifully rich and, clear voice, then sing in Welsh, "My father's cotta.ge," and in response to an encore, gave " The fall of Jordan." Mr. Robert D. Roberts, of Earlestown, gained the two prizes for. the best essay in Welsh on "The Sabbath; its Divine ordination and right observance for the benefit •of mankind," and also , for the best ode,on "The Welshma-n from home." Miss K. Williams again sang with excellent taste, in Welsh, "The soldier's wiferafid, receiving an encore, sang in English, "Spirit of spring. The concluding item was a grand choral competition, tha piece selected being the Congregational Requiem, " Wylwy-n-Wylwvn " ("Weep- ing-Wailing"), for choirs of not • less than 25 voices, the competing choirs being Skelmersdale, Tyldesley, anti Earlestown, and the prize £2,, and a conductor's baton.' Again the Tyldealey choir were i.iccensful in carrying off the palm, their training having evidently been conducted in a most masterly manner.— The proceedings all through were of a most enthusiastic character, and the committee are to b congratulated upon the success of the gathering.

Much of the failure of vacations and the disappointment of leisure comes from the habit of giving.the mind only to one subject.
