• "AT IT AGAIN !" Sir,—What a god-send those few retiarks of Justice Grantham anent drunkenness, in Liverpool, last week, have been to the "Fkdders-General of the Universe"—the Good Templars, Local Optionists, and all that ilk! Why, one cannot now pick up a daily paper without coming across samples of their screeches of delight! And they are so candid that they don't mention the little fact that when Mr. Addison, Q.C., waited upon his lordship to show him where the publicansha,d been slightly 'wronged, he had the manliness to "take some bark." it was not to be expected .they would; for they are so eager to propagate anything to the detriment of that particular class that they always forget the first rudiments of • fair play, and fairly run a-muck at the trade, like a skittish . bull at a red rag. One would think that they are the only philanthropists in creation, and that perdition is the end of all who are engaged in dispensing beer and

spirits. I wish I could swallow their professed motives. I remember once asking a spouter of teetotal twaddle if he had never tasted a glass of ale, and he said "yes, but he aropt it because it became expensive'!" In other words, he would have had it if he could. • Nov, I shall not say all are "tarred with the same brush -'" I believe some of them are genuinely anxious to do good; but I will say that they goabout their work in a most offensive , manner. They will meddle with interests as sacred asl their own; they will interfere with as honest a calling' as their own; and they ,do always forget that there are , two sides to every question. Their choicest motto seems , to be "Give a dog a bad name, and then hang him,"l regardless of the fact that the law of the land is as much im the side of the publicans as on theirs. And fancy a l 7 landlord getting fair play where mpatit teetotaller is ob . on the bench, and has to adj on his ease! As soon expect a hungry hawk to a lame sparrow alone if he should chance to see it. Their prejudices are so strong, their minds are so biassed and warped, and their feelings so saturated with bigotry against this class, that it is next to impossible for them to be impartial. But, to the writer, who hates to see a drunken man or woman as mfich as an`vone living, their will-ye nill-ye meddling with other peciple's concerns is the most disgusting sight I know, and undoubtedly prompted the lines of a cele- brated poet, who wrote thus : And its oh! that some splenetic folks I could name. If they must deal in acids would use but the same, In their innocent graphical labours! In the place of the virulent spirit wherewith— like the polecat. the weasel, and things of that kith— They keep biting the backs of their neighbours! BELLEROPHON. Warrington, March 15, 1888.

WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. I Sir,—Your correspondent seems to have been amused at my previonsletter, and suggests a frame or a glass case. Why not Like the bull by the horns by framing it and hanging it in his shop for the benefit of his custo- mers ; for lam not so blind that I cannot see that it is his own interest and business which he is attempting to defend in this correspondence. He gives the price at which he can purchase various articles; the price at the stores being a penny or twopence in the shilling more. It is quite true; I have proved it myself. I went into a shop in one of the princiyal streets of War- rington a short time ago, in the window of which I had seen a sample of sugar better in quality and cheaper than I could get at the stores. But sir, judge of my dismay when-told by the assistant that they did not sell sugar alone: I must • purchase something else or they could not sell me sugar at that price. It is the same with the other articles he has named, sugar at one shop, flour at anOther, soda at another, and so on through all, his list, losing 5 per cent on one article and making 35 on aaother. It is a positive fact which a "Looker-on" cannot deny, that it is the practice of many tradespeople to sell some article at little or no profit to induce trade in other artichn. Of course it is imposition and not quite honest. It is throwing dust in the eyes of the public—giving with one hand and taking away with the• other, but it draws custom, you know, and we must do something or we should very soon have to shut up shop. You may 'sometimes see a genuine sale of old stock, where some- thing Cheap may be had, but there is not that eternal round of "selling off below cost price," Sze. Is it in this way they pay enormous rents for palatial-looking shops and the wages of employee? Co-operation is free from this, and many other objec- tionable features. It has its market ready made; there- fore it has no need to puff to command custom. Its do- ings are open and above board. The members can attend the quarterly meetings (and peep behind the scenes), an so express approval or otherwise of its transactions and • management. He Gays it. and says it fearlessly, that the working- man does not see it to his interest to join the stores, un- less he is like mvself, blind and will not see. His know- ledge of the working-man is as limited as his knowledge of other things. 95 per cent. of the menabers are, like myself, working-men, but we are not blind to the tricks of trade, and we are not likely to be caught by men of the " Looker-on " class, whose sole object is to get their pound of flesh. He says, again, that if the tradesman could get ready money for all lie sold, instead of giving such long credit, he could sell- cheaper still. • The remedy is in his own hands; let them combine on the same principles as co-operators, namely, ready money' and pure goods. If it be so difficult a matter already for the private 'tradesman to earn a living (and it is quite evident that "Looker-on" belongs to that class), well, the sooner be turns his talents and attention to an occupation more in demand, the better for himself and everybody else. For him to oppose co-operation because it is detrimental to his interests is only repeating the mistake of those people who, a few years ago, so strenuously opposed the intro- duction Of machinery, because it would throw them all out of employment they thought. The machinery won the day (as co-operation will do). and yet these people people get a living still. Remember the fable of the ,old man, the boy, and the ass. We can never hope to please all ; let us, therefore, choose the least evil or rather the greatest good.—Yours,
A MEMBER

• THE ROYAL SOCrETY OF LITERATURE. Sir,—ln justice to the• Royal Society of Literature, if -not to Mr. R. A. Naylor, I must ask you to let 'tie, as 1 secretary to the society, remove an erroneous idea, which a paragraph in your impression of March 3rd is calculated to create. The conditions of en&ance into this society by no means depend either upon the wil- linfriesS,' as you state, to pay an entrance fee and sub- scription, or even upon the actuality of paying the same, put include the execution of some litetary work, or the possession of some degree or diploma, the nomination of three Fellows—the approval frequently withheld—of the council, the suspension of a name for two months fdr general question, and finally ,a. ballot taken at meeting of the society, when a. very few black balls would suffice /to exclude a candidate! To run these gauntlets is, without doubt, somewhat more difficult than "to pass the Ist standard" "or to write a letter to a news- paper." At the saille time I must ask you to remember that not any Of the learned societies act upon any other system than that I .have indicated in their mode of election. When gentlemen have arrived at the mature age and standing at which they usually aspire to enter such so- cieties, they must be judged, not by the narrow standard of examination, but by their intellectual appearance upon the great stage of the world. I believe that Mr. R. A. Naylor has so appeared in a somewhat higher literary character than -even that of / "the writer of a letter to a newspaper," and so he has now had the honour of being admitted into the ranks of an historic society, which has net only numbered many of' the greatest literati of the presentt-centuri among its Fellows, but which has the / Queen for it direct patron—which had the late Duke of Albany for nine years as a Fellow and Its president— which consists, not only of literary men in a professi plat sense, but also of scholars and dilettanti supporters of 'literature, and in which are now enrolled the learned Duke of Devonshire, Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, the Duke of Northirnfberland, the Lord Chancellor, Dr. Sohn Evans, president of the Society of Antiquaries, the Lord Bishop of Durham, acknowledged to be the inost learned prelate on the bench; Sir Henry Rawlinsore the great Oriental scholar; the Marquis of Ripon, late viceroy of India; Sir Charles Newton, of the British Museum, one of our greatest authorities in classi- 'cal antiquities' the ',Waiter of St. John's College and /present vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge; and the encyclopedic Sir Patrick Colquhoun, who is xitev the- president.—Yours obediently, • E. GILBERT HIGHTON, M.A.' Cantab et Oxon, Barrister at Law, F.R.S.L., and Secretary of the Society. [Notwithstanding Mr. Highton's letter, we still maintain that "the essential qualification is for a • fellow ' to be willing to pay three guineas entrance fee, and a sub- scription of two guineas annually." We ask the secre- tary for proof of his statement that one of the condi- tions of entrance into the society/ is "the execution ot some literary work, or the possession of some degree or diploma." We have looked through the "regula- tions and conditionefor the admission of fellows," but do not find a single reference to literature, literary work, or diploma. The main point is cash. "sweet cash," "to be paid in advance," as section Z points out. What can be thought of the value of the qualifi- cation when we find that "members of the Royal' Family, upon signifying their wish to become Fellows, shall be admitted without ballot, upoe entering their names in the book of record ef signatures " Perhaps the secretary ll explain Pow it happens the list of Fellows doee not include Tennyson , Browning, Swinbume, MOT. ris,Herbert Spencer, Matthew Arnold,G A. Sala, John Morley, and a host of others of world-wide fame? As to Mr, R. A. Naylor, his chief literary distinction seems to be his haying quoted Job (Wrongly), and assigned the quotation (wrongly) to Shakespeare.-4D. Ex.]

MANENT RELIEF SOCIETY. Sir,—All members of the e.bove society should know that the annual meeting takes place on the third Satur- day in March', at the *ming and Mechanical School, Rodney-street, Wigan, wben some very important ques- tions will be brought up for discussion. It will be re- menibered that, at special meeting held in December last, a resolution was passed in favour of raising the codtributions a halfpenny per week, together with the Inasters' per centage, and although it was passed by a large majority, I may say that I emphatically opposed it, on the 'ground that them were other sources to which the Board of Management might reasonably appeal for aid, without further intruding upon the employers and employed, whose multifarious payments are hard and difficult to maintain. I suggest that the president and the other officials at the head of the society ought to be invited to appeal respectfully to the landowners of the vicinity, to certify if they will generously, contribute aminally to its support, as they would be memorably reyrardid by the good work the society is doing, and by receiving the congratulations of all sensible people. My reason for making this suggestion is , because they are greatly indebted to the members of this society to the getting of their coal mines. The society has a member- ship of over 40,000;and they produce something like 112.000,000 tons of coal per annum, on which the Aland- owners receive, in the shape of mine royalties, a sum equal to at least 6d per ton, which amounts to £300,000 per annum. Now, if they would contribute at the rate of but one halfpenny per ton (which is certainly not excessive) the society wouldbe richer by £25,060 a year, which sum, together with the members' contributions and the masters' per centage would not only provide for the fatherless children and widows, and disabled mem- bers, but it would provide and maintain a Superannua- tiereFund, in conjunction with the society, which is an object of necessity. Then there is the question of disablement Day. It was thought when the contributions were raised that the 5s which was taken off the first week's pay in 1884 would be refunded, but it is not yet returned, a fact which the Board of Management will have to explain. There is also the question of economy. It is some- what ridiculous to find that there is so much - money spent every year in clerks' wages, travelling expenses, office cleaning, Ikc., all included in the duties of the gene- ral secretary, a man who, in spite of these "piping times " of competition is "passing rich" on £3OO a-year. Next, there is the question of medical treatment, a question most vital to the interest of not just the mem- bers alone, but of the society as well, and though it is a question that is left to the local agencies, that does not say but what the Board of Management shouldinterfere, if the local agencies fail to appoint doctors in compliance with the wishes of the members. At present there are scores of members residing a distance of four miles away from the doctor that is appointed to act for them, While at the same time they have a doctor residing and practis- ing in their very midst, and acting for members of • this very society, though they work at other collieries. In conclusion, I would advise the members generally to take more interest in the society, and consider it as their own, for as it is composed of all sorts and condi- tions of Mtn, it may be expected that there willobe.here and there a black sheep; and undoubtedly there am many in receipt of relief that do anything but comply with the rules. But, as a method of checking imposi- tion, I would suggest that if there be any guilty of breaking the rules they should be summoned before their committee, and be -dealt with as they think fit. The reporter (whether he or she be a member of the society or not) should be. remunerat€ol with a reward of ss, but I would not'be so strict with those that are crippled. I would give them an extension; in fact, I would allow them to earn a trifle honestly if they could. These are questions of importance, which I hope will be duly con- sidered.—Yours truly,

div.p: Biltinge, February 28, 1888.
' THE UNION OF THE DOXIES.

Sir,—l am perplexed. From a class of studies where- in facts were allowed due weight, before which, opinions and mere beliefs must give way, I have lately been con- sidering subjects wherein the beliefs and religious opinions of modern society form the chief element. And lam perplexed. For, whereas, in the one study I find opinions`founded upon facts and giving way when they were adverse; in the other, the opinions appear to be formed and maintained irrespective of the attitude of the facts,—it the facts do not agree with the opinions, sci much the worse for the facts. Is there any cause for wonder then at the perplexity resulting from this sudden change of moral and intellectual atmosphere? If some nineteenth century physician would follow the precedent of good Sir Thomas Browne, and give us a modern " Religio Medici," it would serve' as a measure of the immense change two, centuries have wrought in Un- religious opinions of Englishmen. Now, whence • and why, this change? The statements of the bible, the only source of these opinions, are the same now as then; so we must look outside the scriptures for the source of this great change in the mode of regarding and interpreting them. This external influence has been the adverse evidence of physical facts, rendering the literal acceptation of the language of the bible impossible. And this Isosefiing of the strict bonds of literal rendering' of the text has had its influence upon the acceptation and the teaching of other parts a scripture riot directly affected by the invalidating evidence of physical phe- nomena. For Men finding some of the literal statements of the Old Testament incompatible with well ascertained and established facts, proceed, perhaps unconsciously, to ' construe the rest more according to their own inclin- ings than is warranted by the text. Hence we have the great divergence of modern doctrine from the iron- bound teaching of John Calvin. Now I cannot regard Calvinism otherviisethan'in the main a logical induction from the text of scripture. Horrible as some of Calvin's tenets were, they do find their justification in the weeds if not in the then undiscovered meaning of scripture. Hence, if Calvinism was a logical outcome of a literal rendering of the text, what ,place are we to give to modern religious thought, with its broader and humanly more acceptable views, its lax rendering of the text, and its acceptance of a scientific hypothesis directly opposed to systematic religion? ' Ilinaw nothing better illustrative of the illogical elasticity of modern religious thought and its great declension from the cold-blooded rigidity of Calvinisni, than the way in Which professing Christians have accepted the doctrine of evolution, whilst professing a ' belief in the doctrine of specific creation. Now, while it is easy to understand a •reasoning mind accepting one and rejecting the other, it is beyond my power of con- ception to imagine a man capable of believing in the truth of both. Evolution and our systematic religion are essentially and 'diametrically opposed to each other, accounsing for the appearance and condition of man as we find him to-day by utterly antagonistic theories and methods, wide as the poles asunder. The latter demands a belief in the sudden creation of man as a perfect being who fell from a state of beatitude to his present inferior posation:. Evolution on the other hand declares man is the highest form of vertebrate existence on earth, to have been devfloped by natural laws, and through un- nunibered ages, from the lowest to the highest form of organised life. As an onlooker, I can only marvel at the immense receptivity of the modern religious mind which can 'take in and assimilate such antithetical •doctrines., And while I marvel, I wonder whether this mongrel belief knot resting upon two stools and so will come to theground. As we cannot serveboth God and mammon, so these two doctrines are alike incompatible. Indeed I think no sane mind—not c,onf used and stultifiecity early (so called religious) teaching, could accept and retain so incongruous a mixture. But with all this we may console ourselves that the essentials of true religion are not inthe• slightest detrimentilly affected by these specu- lations and discoveries of men, but only the bark—the outward and worthless husk—that is abraded, thereby exposing the valuable grain the better to view.— famine.,,' Penketh, March sth, 1888.

LEctunE AT KINGSLEY.—Last evening week, a meeting of Liberals was held at the National Schoolroom, Kings- ley, when an instructive address was delivered by the. Rev. W. Mellor (president of the Crewe Liberal Associa- tion), on "The Irish Land Question" and "Home Rule." Mr. S. Woodward, vice-chairman of the local committee, presided. Several of the leading points in Mr. blellor's discourse upon the Irish agrarian problems were further exemplified by the lecturer's recent travels in Ireland. At the conausion of the address, a vote of thanks to the speaker was mowed by Mr. B. Kniveton, seconded by Mr. W. Gerrard, and carried. OPENING OF A TRAMWAY AT llELSBY.—Hitherto, Messrs Guest and Son have ritperienced much difficulty in con- veying the stone cut from their quarry, ivhich is situated at a considerable height on Helsby Hill, down to the railway, as the blocks of stone are perhaps larger .than can be taken from any quarry in this part of the coun- try. Iga,ny obstacles have been in the way of construct- ing a tam line to carry the stone to the railway, but during the last month the necessary land has been 'pro- cured and the work completed ; and the other afternoon Mr. Councillor Farish, of Chester, who is also a resident of Helsby, opened the much-needed tramway, which is about half a mile in length. It is also hoped that when the Manchester Ship Canal is completed they will be able to extend the tram line to its banks, so as to be able to ship the stone to any place that may be required. At the conclusion of the ceremony,the workmen were enter- tained by their employers to a knife and fork tea, and the rest of the evening was spent in a ovinl manner.

A FRODSITAM FARMER'S DispurE.--In the Nisi Prius Court, at Chester Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Stephen an action was brought by William Ellison, farmer, Kingswood, near Frodsham, to recover 28 4.s from Sarah William Davies (widow), farmer, Helsby, damage done by trespass on hay grass at Vrodsharn Marsh. Mr. Marshall (instructedby Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, Frodsham) was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Clement Higgins, Q.C. (instructed by Mr. Jos: Burton, Runcorn), was for the defence.:—Mr. Marshall, opening the case, said his client was the occupier of between ten and eleven acres. The crops on the land for the previous year had been 22 tons, but last year it was not quite so •

• good. % The defendant, who occupied the 'adjoining field, cif% her hay before the plaintiff cut his. She then turned, her cattle in to the land, and her fences not being in very good order the cattle trespassed on Mr. Ellison's land, and practically spoilt a good crop. The valuers he intended to call would place the damage done it from £25 to Ea which was the nett loss after all expenses. had been paid.—Mr. Higgins, submitting his case, did not deny that some damage li)acl been done, nor that his client was liable, but the liability was nothing like the amount claimed. This field was open to other people's cattlebesides Mrs. Davis's, so that she was not liable for the whole of the damages—After hearing evidence, the jury found that the amount £l2 10s paid into court was sufficient to satisfy the cause of action, and the Judge directed that judgment should be entered for the defen- dant, with costs from the date of payment into court.

TliE 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH
FAREWELL TO HARRY SPEAKMAN.

On Wednesday mortflng Mr. H. C. Speakman. de- parted from Runcorn to London to join the Austra- lian football team, of which he is. one of the selec- ted members. Although sorry to lose his valuable sArvices as three-quarter back, the townspeople, are delighted that Speakman's merits have been recog- nised, and are confident that he will not fail to shine even amongst the smart men of which the team is composed. In a list of the players published " Harry " as he is best known is thus described "H. C. Speakman, three-quarter back (Runcorn, Cheshire) • age 24; height 5fC. 84 inches; weight 11 stone Has played in best county matches for three years. Is a brilliant man and never loses his head To mark their dense of kis,part seryices and his present position the: club desired to give Harry a benefit match, but the Rugby Union, when consulted, promptly put their veto upon the pro- ject, and some other means of making a contribu- tion towards his heavy expenses for an outfit were adopted. Subscription lists weredistributed, and it is gratifying to state that a tostimonial amounting to over EPA was quickly raised, and has been handed over to Speakman. After the match, on Saturday, in which Speaktnan played a magnificent game and scored a try, the members of the team and several of the committee of the club assembled in the large room of Mr. Riley's Coffee Can to wish Harry good bye and bon voyage. ,Mr. H. Chadwick, of the Widnes Alkali Works, under whom Speakman was employed, was also present: The prOceedings commenced with a capital tea, prepared and well served by Mrs Riley and assistants. Rill justice having been done, Mr. W. Wright. an old veteran took the chair, and said as they were all aware they had met to wish Mr. Speakman God speed. He hoped Mr. Speak- man would be as successful for the Austra- lian team as he had been for the Runcorn club. (Hear, hear.) If he should happen to come back, he hoped he would not do anything that would hinder him from again taking the position of centre three-quarter with the old club.. (Applause.) He had been a great help to thenl in times past, and thew were all sorry to lose him. (Hear, hear.) He did not like praising him before his face but he had the hearty good wishes of them alt. (Applause )—Mr. H. Hughes (capeain) also expressed regret at the club losing Mr. Speakman. He only hoped- that he would play as well in Australia as he had done in England, and that he would be a credit to himself, and an honour to the old clith of which he had been a member so long. He was sure he took with him all their good wishes, and they would be glad to see him back towards next October ready for the' fray again. (Applause.). During last season he had been spealeing of retiring, but he (Mr: Hughes) trusted 124 -would be like many others, that when he saw the teams at work he would want to be in harness again. (Hear, hear.) They all wished him a pleasant voyage, ' but he haa better prepare for sea sickness, and engage some person to write up his diary for the first few days. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. J. E. Langshaw (secretary) said he was glad to say alew words about their friend, Mr. Speakman. He had been a credit to the club in every sense of the word. He joined the second team, and gained honours there, and four years ago, having fought his way into the first team, he took the position of centre three-quarter, and had held it ever since. The manner in which he had conduc- ted himself en the field had always been marked by courtesy and propriety. (Hear, hear.) He invariably kept his temper, and if he chanced to get knocked down savagely he was up again quickly and in his place. He did not go grumbling and growling at anybody. He was very sorry indeed that Mr. Speakman was go- ing away. He would leave a plac4 that they should not so easily fill. When there was some doubt about their captain also joining the Austra- lian team, and Wainwright wished him to write for him an engagement, he began to get alarmed, and won- der how poor Runcorn would fare. He was glad that nobody besides Mr. Speakman was going to Australia, and if he played as well for the Australian team as he had done for the club, he would not disgrace Runcorn. He wished him a safe voyage across, and a safe journey homeagain. '(Applause.) Mr. C. Pownall, in a few genial remarks, mentioned several Runcorn friends Mr. Speakman would meet on his travels, especially referring to Mi. Farrie Bate at Rockhampton, who was one of the captains of the club, and was a great help when they first started. The health, of the guest of the evening was then drunk with much enthusiasm, and Mr. Speakman, in respond- ing, said he could not thank them too much for the way in which they had referred to his connection with the Runcorn Football Club. When he had played for the flub he had always tried to do his best, and when he re- turned from Australia—he expected he should have to do so, as a'return ticket had been taken for him—he would do all in his power to forward the interests of the club. (Applause.) The evening was spent in a pleasant con- vivial style, songs being givenlly Messrs. C. Pownall, E. Lunt, A, Howard, Turnbull, Faulkner, Wainwright, Langshaw, &c., and before *separating the company joined in singing "Auld lang syne."

DEPARTURE OF A NEWTON FOOTBALLER FOR AUSTRALIA: INTERESTING PRESENTA- TIONS. The selection of "Sam" Williams, of Newton-le- Willows, as one of the team of Rugby footballers to represent the United Kingdom in the first visit of any such company to the Australian colonies is con- sidered. a great honour by the supporters of hot', the Rugby and Association codes in tVe district. The honour was well deserved, for the abilities of Wil- liams as a first-class player may be guaged from the fact that during the season just concluding he has officiated as the captain of the Salford P.C., one of the strongest and best organisations in the North of Eng- land. As our readers will well know, Mr. Williams' home was New Hey farm, Newton, and he formerly played with the old Newton Rugby Club. For'some time past he has occupied a responsible position under the firm of Messrs. Bostock and Co., packers, of Manchester, though it was customary for him to return home each week end. A lengthy article on his brilliant football. career since his connection with the Salford F.C. recently appeared in these columns, and the facts then stafed need no repetition. "Sam's" geniality and thoroughly honest conduct on the football field mace him a general favourite with all who celiac:in contact with him, and front h, fellovi. players, and his personal friends, including many in Earlestown and Newton, he was the recipient of" their hearty good wishes, accompanied by varioui tokens of their.respect. The members of the Salford F,C. last week presented him with a splendid travelling trunk and dressing case; while the employees of Messrs. Bot 4 tock and Co., of Manchester banded to him a vallable gold breast pia and a pair of goidaleeVe links. The latter gift was accompanied with the following communication: Mr.. Sam Willianas,—l have very great pleasure on be- half of your fellow-workmates in presenting you with a gold breastpin, set with marls ;'also a pair of gold sleeve links of chaste design, QR your leave of absence, for time, to engage in the manly spdrt -of fobtbalt-Lat tfle` Antipodes. We presr.nt these gifts as a small-token of the esteem and respect in which you are held by your fellow-workmen, wishing you health, strength, and an enjoyable out. God speed you and bring you safe back again is the earnest wish of all who have subscribed their mite. I remain, on behalf of your fellow-workmen, yours sincerely, WILLIAM GRINDLEY FUREMAN."—MT. Williams has been at home during the earlier part of the present week, and on Wednesday morning, accompanied by several Wends, proceeded to Manchester, ,where he joined a portion of the Australian team.

The Lancashire and Cheshire players bound for Aus- tralia left_the Central Station, Manchester, at neon on that day and caused a vast number of football bnthu- siasts to assemble on the platform. The crowd was so great that it was only with the utmost, difficulty that the tourists could approach their saloon carriage, and as each player pushed his way through the barrier he was recognised and cheered to the echo. The crushwas so great that the train was delayed a few minutes, but when it steamed out of the station, long hearty cheers were raised all along the line of spectators. The men appeared to be in the best of spirits, and on the arrival of the train at Nottingham an immense crowd had as- sembled, and the players who were decorateil with red, white, and blue colours, were heartily cheered. Thu full strength of the team dined together at the Manches- ter Hotel, Aldersgate-street, London, in the evening, a complimentary and congratulatory' banquet being held in their honour, and on Thursday they proceeded to Gravesend and embarked 'on the s.s.'Kaikoura for New Zealand. , •

POACITEIIS AND POLICEMEN.—At the Chester Assizes on Wednesday, James Swindells and Edwin Bailey were sentenced to eight years' penal servitude for assaulting two police officers at Sale last November, The prisoners were part of a gang of poachers whow the officers en- countered. In another case of assault arising out of alleged trespass on preserved land near Tarporley, Mr. Jiktice Wells said gamekeepers had no right to take the la W into their own hands, and he gave effect to a recom- mendation of the jury by merely ordering the prisoner to enter into his own recognisances. A committee of the Cabinet, consisting of Lord Salisbury, Mr. Smith, Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Lord Cross, and Mr. Ritchie, held a meeting to-day to consider the Local Government Bill. They were all dressed rin deep mourning. WRECK OF A BARQUE : Loss OF 12 LIVES.-012 Thurs- day night, just before twelve o'clock, the iron barque Lanoma, of London, went ashore in Chesil West Bay, near,Weymouth, and became a total wieck. Twelve of the crew were drowned, six others being saved. The vessel was bound from Tasmania with wool, hides, &c.

div.head: LAST NIGET'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGET'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—SaveraI local Scotch bills were read a second time, and the Lord Chancellor introduced a bill for the revision of statute law which was read afirst time. he Pluralities Acts Amendment Bill, which gives increased power to the bishops to require ministrations irk Wales in the Welsh language passed a second reading. The County Courts Consolidation Bill passed a third reading, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at 2-5 p.m. VOLUNTEERS All ALDERSHOT.-Mr. E. STANHOPE', re- replying to Mr. I4aors, said that no available quarters at Aldershot had been refused to officers aecompanying their regiments at Easten. THE DEATH OF THE E3IPEROR OF GIIRMANY.—MT. W. SMITH, with feelings of the deepest regret, informed the House that a telegram had been received announcing the death of the Emperor of Gormany.—Sir,W. HARCOURT, on the part of his side of the house, expregsed the deepest' sorrow at the announcement. • THE NATIONAL DEBT.—After a new writ had been issued for Merthyr Tydvil, the House went into Committee on the National Debt Acts.— The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said that his proposals would tend materially to lighten the bur- dens of the country, and to raise its credit and increase its resources. (Cheers.) He proposed to keep in the hands of Parliament power to pay off the dissentients at such periods and in such manner as Parliament might determine. He proposed to act entirely in harmony with the precedents set before him, endeavouring to follow successful conversipns on parallel lines, and he would ask the House to give the Government now similar powers in order that they might achieve similar results. The right hon. gentleman then made reference to Mr. Goul- bourn's scheme in 1844, and said it was mainly on the I lines of that precedent that he should invite the House to act. He also spoke of similar finabcial operations conducted by Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Childers, and laid down as conditions for successful conversion tha,t assent should be presumed in he absence of dissent, and that the power should be given. to pay off dissentients in such a manner as Parliament might direct. div.head: DEATH
div.p: THE DEATH
OF THE
GERMAN EMPEROR.
(CENTYAL NBWB TEILBSR&M.)
FRIDAY.—The Emperor William died at half- past eight o'clock this morning. J.
SCENE IN THE CHAMBER OF DEATH.

A Renter's Berlin telegram dated Friday, 11-20 a.m., says :—According to descriptions from eye-witnesses of the Emperor William's death, His Majesty during the last few-hours before the end was entirely free from pain. Shortly after eight o'clock this morning all the members of the Imperial House staying in.the Palace, as well as the court Ilignitaries, the generals of the army, and the Cabinet Ministers, were summoned to the chamber of the dying monarch, who was in a half sitting position on his camp bedstead. The members of the Royal Family gathered round the bed, and the room was crowded. Prince William, standing nearest to the Emperor, half bent over the couch and earnestly watched the Emperor's last moments. The fact of His Majesty's death was received towards half-past eight this morning. Both the Reichstag and the Prussian Diet have adjourned. The remains of the late Einperor now lie covered with a white cloth, on the bedstead in the Imperial chaMber, surrounded by candles. The expression of the face is extremely peaceful and placid. Dense crowds are stand- ing in sorrowful silence in front of the Imperial palace, which the members of the Royal family left, shortly after ten o'clock. Divine service will be held in the Mortuary Chapel-this evening, when the choir of the Cathedral will perform the choral parts of the service. SAN RENO, FRIDAY AFTRNOON.—The Crown Prince will leave at eight o'clock to-morrow morning for Berlin direct, via, the Tyrol. He will travel by special train. _ .

VIENNA., FRIDAY ATEnwoox.—A special despatch to the "New Free Press" states that the Emperor of Ger- many died w4th his hand in that of the Empress. An hour before his death he exclaimed "I am a man of peace; but if Russia will force me to war I will faith- fully range myself hn the side of my ally Austria." The Imperial remaips will be interred at Charlotten- .. berg.
THE CROWN PRINCE PROCLAIMED EMPEROR OF GERMANY;

A Central News telegram from Berlin states that the Crown Prince of Germany has been proclaimed Emperor under the title of Frederick the First of Germany and Frederick the Third of Prussia. . BERLIN, FRIDAY, 1-10 P.M.—Prince Bismardk entered the Reichstag at 12-35 p,m. to-day and communicated to the House the fact of the Emperor's death. The Imperial order for the closing of the session, the last official docu- ments signed by the deceased Monarch were laid on the table by the Chancellor, who proposed that the House should adjourn. Prince' Bismarck further informed the Reichstag that the new Emperor Frederick 111, would leave San Remo to-Mayrow. • SAN REMO, FRIDAY, 9-10 A.l.—The 'Crown 'Prince passed a fairly good night. His Imperial Highness was rathei restless during the early part of the night, but slept better afterwls, , SAN REMO, FRIDA EARLY 1110minio.—The Crown' Prince and Ps mesas wilt leave here without delay, travel- ling by way of the,Brennef. Their Imperial 'Highnesses proceed to Charlottetiblirg. They will be accompanied by Sir Morel Mackenzie.

div.head: EXCITEMENT IN LONDON. *
div.p: EXCITEMENT IN LONDON. *

The news on reaching members of the West-end Clubs, caused a revival of the excitement of Thursday evening'. The German Emba.ssy'Was speedilybesieged by inquirers. The flags on the public offices and other prominent buildings around Whitehall and Pall Mall were hoisted half-mast high, and the blinds drawn. • Count Hatzfeldt, the German Ambassador, had not received the fatal news up to a quarter-past ten, but it was then forwarded to his private residence:

div.head: OFFICIAL INTIMATION.
div.p: OFFICIAL INTIMATION.

The Prince of Wales received a telegram' from Prince William of Prussia, an,d another from Sir Edward Malet, stating that the Emperor William died at half-past sev,en on Friday morning. Count Hatzfeldt received official intelligence of the fact just before noon' and the flag was immediately hoisted on the embassy. The Queen sent Prince Henry of Battenberz to inquire for confirmation of the news. • THE 'ENGLISH COURT IN MOURNING., • The Queen received an official announcement of the 'Emperor William'S death shortly after nine o'clock on' Friday morning. TiakCourt has been ordered ,to, go into mourning for a montß. All State ceremonies are post poned. Her Majesty dressed on Friday in deep black ;The prince of Wales, Prince Christian, and Prince Henry of Battenberg will probably attend the funeral. The Queen has been in communication with the Princess Royal, to whom many telegrams of condolence have been, sent. The Queen returned to Windsor on Friday.; SPECIAL SERVICE. ' A 'special service will be conducted to-morrow (Sun- day) in the German chapel, ' St. James's, at which the Prince of Wales, Prince Christian and other members of the Royal 'Family are expected to be present. Count Ijatzfeldt will also attend, together with representatives of most of the Foreign Embassies and Legations.. STATEMENT_ IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

in the House of Commons:cm Friday afternoon, Mr. W. H. Smith, immediately after questions, rose and said :—I think It vKell to inform the House that her Majesty's Government have received a despatch from her majesty's ambassador at Berlin announcing the death of his Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Germany. I make this communication to the House believing that it is one which deeply interests the House. and knowing that the House and the country will join in the sorrow which is afflicting the whole people of Germany: (Sym- pathetic cheers). Sir W. Harcourt: In the absence of my right hon. friend the member for Midlothian, I have only to express the entire concurrence -of this side of the House in the sentiments expressed by the right hon. gentleman. (Hear, hear). S. THE FIRST UNFOUNDED REPORT.

A tremendous sensation, was excited on Thursday evening by announcements from Berlin that the Em- peror harpassed away. His 'Majesty, whO'' had been in a semi-comatose condition, fell into a deep swoon, and this was mistaken for death. Reports of his death were instantly printed and cgculated in Berlin. In a short time, however, the Emperor regained some degree of consciousness, and a little food was given to him. At nine o'clock he was "in a state of torpor." The report of the Emperor's death was implicitly believed in Court circles in London. The Queen countermanded various festivities which had been arranged in honour of the "Silver Wedeline of the Prince and Princess. of Wales, and the" Court Circular" announced that the Priny
'fiadrciaded t theVerinan Embassy to express condo- lence. Later in the evening, however, on receipt of news from Berlin, the State dinner was given at Buckingham Palace.
A REGENCY APPOINTED.

BERLIN, TIIIIIISDAY.—The following Imperial rescript address to Prince William, dated November 17, 1887, is promulgated to-day "Considering the uncertain state of my health, which compcls me temporarily to abstain from the transaction of affairs, and in view of the illness and prolonged ab- sence of my son the Crown Prince, I charge your Royal Highness in all cases where I believe representation to be necessary in current Government business, and especially in the signing of orders, with the said representation, without a special order being requisite on every separate occasion —Berlin; November 17, 1887. (Signed) "To His Royal Highness Prince William.". THE BULLETINS.
" WILHEL3f.

The following bulletins were issued during Thursday : BERLIN', THURSDAY, 10-40 A.M.—The following bulle- tin is issued this morning :—" The Emperor has passed a very restless night, and is very weak. (Signed) VON LAUER." 12-30 P.M.—The published assurance of the physicians in attendanc‘ that the somnolent condition of the Em- peror is not the result of the injection of morphia con- firms the belief that the crisis is imminent. _ _ _

8-25 P.M.—The Emperor swooned shortly after five o'clock, and remained unconscious Alan six. Ills Majesty then fell into a quiet sleep, which lasted until seven. Wine and liquid ,nourishment are administered from time to time.

9 P.3f.-A bulletin announcing that the Emperor still lives, and that oil the whole his condition is store tran- quil, has reassured the people of .Berlin, who were thrown into a state Of great excitement by the report published in extra editions of the evening papers that His Majesty had passed away.

The German Emperor, William 1., King df tPrussia, whose ninety-on 4 years would have been completed on the 22nd March, ,had indeed reigned.not muchinore than half the time of our own Queen, but he continued to reign at fourscofe and eleven years of age. He not only reigned, he also ruled, attending to every particular de- tail of the control of his Empire and his kingdom with a minute care that would be remarkable in a man of seventy,butin a man of ninety-one was passing marvellous. He was the second son of King Frederick William 111., fifth Prussian monarch, but he was born on March 22nd, 1797, in the last year of the reign of his grandfather, who presented him for baptism. His, mother was that noble Queen Louise, to whom, perhaps' more than to any soldier or statesman, must be traced the recreation of the kingdom and the triumph of the Empire. He was weakly in childhood and early youth, yet he was made a soldier before he was ten; he made field-works by the time he was fourteen, and he pursued his studies and observed domestic discipline so well that when he was eleven his mother could write of him that he, was , "simple, honest, and intelligent." Good man,though. he was who was familiarly called Fritz Germany will sorely miss the grand old Sovereign who had seen six generations of his own family, who by a score of years had exceeded the term allotted to mortal man: but who, six feet in height, with a martial and a noble air, and with the kindly look which mani-, fested his imperturbable amiability, recalled the long ago when he, his elder brother, and his brother-in-law, the Czar Nicholas, were called the three handsomest men in Europe.

div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.
• THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL (Continued front page 6.) FROM EASTHAM TO FRODSHAM. BY LOOKER-ON.

The canal works are divided into ninesections of 4} miles each, and the first of these, stretching from East. ham to Ellesmere. Port, is the, one where the greatest quantity of plant and the largest number of men are at present employed. The transformation which has taken place here in three months time is astounding to any person who has been used to travel in the neighbour- hood. Here, besides the Ship Canal, three huge locks are to be constructed, side by. side, on what is now the river bank, and on the ground which has hitherto been a very pleasant stretch bf meadow land, on which the men and officers of the First Cheshire Engineers have on different seasons camped out. There has now been erec- ted in this short period quite a village of houses for the Workmen, and these may rightly be called a "navvy Town." There are already employed in this Ist section 1,000 men, 12 locomotives, with some hundreds of tip waggons, seven steam navvies, and three steam cranes. Work has been started at both erids of the section and railways now extend the entire length of q miles. Store- houses are completed, and carpenters' and blacksmiths' shops hive risen up with • magical rapidity on the river bank, and powerful steam saw- mills are likewise in full swing. Notwithstand- ing all that is being done, the able foreman here speaks regretfully of the crowds of poor fellows seeking work, who pour in daily, only to be disaPpointed in their sea&h for work. The value of the plant of all descriptions for carrying on the work in this locality is estimated at £lOO,OOO. . The work on this section should be pretty easy, for the test cutting, 60 feet deep, reveals that the first 20 feet down are of a loamy soil of the softest character, with a bed of easily worked red sandstone below it. It is satis- factory to learn that for the first and second sections, which extend to Ince,, the land already acquired by the Company has been bought at a figure below the Parlia- mentary estimates. In the neighbourhood of Pool Hall Mouth, about', two miles from Easthatno there are likewise a gopd number of Men employed. At Stanlow Point, and across the river Gowey, some 200 men are at work removing the top soil with spades and barrows. A large quantity. of timber, barrows steam cranes, and pile driving machi-, nery have arrived at the wharf Igtere by barges. • Coming th the wood which skirts the shore near Ince , Hall, it is found that a number of Men have been set to work this week, felling tikiber' removing soil, and going through the preliminary work necessary in making the canal. Near Frodsham Marsh are some 200 or 300 men at work, and the change which has taken place here dm.. i tug the last fortnight s very striking. Embankments have been made, a locomotive has been, got on the line, and a steam navvy will be at work in a few. days. Every available lodging • has been taken up, and many of the men have to walk several miles to and from their work. Navvies' huts are being erected, and men are working night and day, so as to get them ready as speedily as possible. It should be added that large• quantities of material of various kinds are daily arriving at the wharf Close to the line of canal and at Ice station,- about a mile away. Altogether the quiet scene has become a very lively one.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

From. this section steady progreSs must be reported this week. A walk from the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele to the 'Big Field at Norton reveals a state of busy activity that cannot but vastly astonish the persons who tramped.over the land but three short months ago. Running through the centre of what was recently fine agricultural land, is a line of railway metals, upwards of a mile in length commencing a short dis- tance wide of and Love the works just mentioned, and ending at Norton in .an almost confusing series of branch lines. Six locomo- fives are constantly employed iemoving the clay and soil as it is excavated by three steam navvies at the rate of about three tons each per minute, and the spoil bank on the marsh is already assuming prodigious proportions. Of the bridge erected across the canal, and 'extending far, on to the opposite side,, by Messrs. Kirk-, I ham and Co., nothing can now be seen of the supports 'On the land. Clay has been " tipped " until the spaces underneath the top have been filled in, and the loco me- Jives when once across the, canal, seem to be running upon a \ solid , foundation of earth. A line of rails has in fact been laid from the bridge to the spoil bank, and that which erstwhile afforded but treacherous fopting for man, now bears an engine puffing merrily al3ng with a train of waggons behjnd it, In the neigh- bourhood of the depot several tanks have been erected fox the purpose of holding water to supply thest engines and from these tanks pipes have also been laid to the steam navvies, and prept.ratiop.s are being made to still further extend the system of water pipes. The cuttings in which the navvies are at work, at a depth of 20 feet, have been visibly lengthened since last week, and the view of them from near the depot is quite panoramic in effect. Another navvy is in course of being fitted up, and goubtless will soon commence its labour of, destruc- tion. . ,

div.head: .WESTON. ,
div.p: .WESTON. ,

The depot here is now fast approaching completion. The buildings are assuming a habitable appearance, and it is anticipated that within a brief space the offices and workshdps will be occupied. The huts are also being steadily erected.

THELWALL. • As time goes on thii scene in connection with the canal works near Thelwall assumes an ,even busier aspect. By the side of the road a little past/Morris Brook farm what.appears to be quite a hamlet of wooden erec- tions is springing up, but none of these biiildings are really intended for human habitation. The largest struc- ture of all is rapidly approaching completion, and, being provided inSide with several brick fireplaces and chim- neys, it is evidently intended to partition it into various compartments, and to use it as an office. The material on the' ground is continually being augmented by the fresh additions conveyed by the many vehicles which ply between Warrington and Hid scene of operations: The gigantic framework of more than one steam navvy of the "American" type is to be seen lying alone the line, and yesterday a num- ber of mechanics were busily engaged in erecting one of these great instruments of industry. Adwe mentioned last week, several locomotives are on the giound, and these are now actively engaged in enlarging the already, imposing heaps of "spoil." It is quite safe to predict that at the present rate of pr.ogress this particular sec- tion of the canal will soon be one of the busiest, and, as

' The total assets of the Company have been raised from £6,811,954 to £7,867,103, being an increase of £1,055.149 dur- ing the year. ORDINARY BRANCH. The number if Policies issued during the year was 37,450, assuring the sum of £3,903,635, and'producing a New Annual Preminm Income of £192,109. The Premiums received during the year were £535,131, be- ing an increase of £138,191 over the year 1886, t. The claims of the year amounted to £158,257. The num- ber of deaths was 1,071, and 39 Endowment Assurances matured. The number of Policies in force was £11,451. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The Premiums received during the year were £3,058,501, ' being an increase of £147,206. The Claims of the year amounted to £1,204,823. The num- ber of Deaths was 142,665. The revision of the Tables of the Industrial Branch (in all eases in favour of the Assured), which was alluded, to last year, has been much appreciated by the Policy-holders. The effect has been to add more than £30,000 to the amount paid in,the year for Claims, owing to the increased benefits thus afforded. the projected Latchford Locks lie in' close proximity to Morris Brook farm house, there will be ample employ- ment for all the machinery and apparatus that is being se fapidly brought together. • • BARTON. At Barton additional workmen continue to find em- ployment, and teams aie engaged carting away the rock found in this portion of the Weaste section. This rock will be utilised for the erbction of the wall dividing the Trafford estate from the canal works. Greater activity has prevailed this week on the Barton section, the offices at Peelgreen having been beseiged by navvies seeking employment. Many of the men's names have been taken., and large quantities of railway rails, timber, bariows, &c., have been deposited in the meadows of Salt Eye. It is stated that a good number of men will be engaged on this section on Monday. RIXTON. At B,ixton four •steam navvies are at work, and the progress they have made in the short space of time is remarkable. The engine shed to hold 14 engines is com- pleted, and the offices are finished and occupied by the contractors. The stables, carpenters' and smiths' shops are almost completed, also toe huts • so they are called, but they will outvie many cottages, being both roomy and well built. Under the vigilant superintendence of Mr. Buxton, the contractor, who is doing all the woodwork and erecting all the buildings here, nothing is being spared that tends to make the places comfortable and homely, and considering the recent state of the weather, it is wonderful how such an amount of work has been done.. Sheer Itock has been transformed from a quiet picturesque field to a hive of industry. Five engines are at work removing the soil, some hundreds of tons being emptied every day. A-NEW MISSION ROOM. . On Wednesday evening, a mission room was opened at Irlam, ty the vicar, the Rev. Dr. Martin, who has al- ready taken active steps to provide for the ministerial wants of the navvies employed on the Irlam section of the canal. ACCIDENT AT lionas GREEN. On Wednesday afternoon, Arthur Jackson, a labourer, was working on the Rixton section of the Ship Canal at Hollins Green, when he was knocked down by a truck, which passed over his right leg. He was at once taken to the Infirmary at Warrington, where it was found necessary to amputate the injured limb. The operation was performed by the house surgeon, Dr. Smith. •

• OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT:I • 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The Stock Exchange during the east week has been in the throes of a semi-panic, resulting in still further decline in prices all round. One, of the most noticeable features of this decline has been the class of securities affected. It would hardly be thought that the serious illness or even death of the Emperor of Germany ought to have any direct influence on home rails, yet such has been the case, and in nearly every instance there has been considerable decline. ' For the second time this year South-Eastern Deferred Stocks have gone below 100, and Brighton A's are at the lowest figure touched for some months, hull and Barnsley have also'shown a fall after a long-continued maintenance of premiums. The divi- dend of the North British Railway has been declared at the rate of 4 per cent per annum on the ordinary stock, and on the announcement being made there Was some heavy selling on realizations. The announcement by Mr. Goschen of his conversion scheme has caused a small relapse in Consols. The city financim do not take at all kindly to Mi. Goschen's proposals, and are not likely to do anything to facilitate them. • The most active markets at the present time are-mines, and for the moment diamonds have relegated copper 'to quite a secondary position. The dealings in De Beers ana other diamond shares have, however, become a mere gamble with the Hatton Garden dealers at the back. After some wide fluctuations prices are still firm, but the public are not doing anything,with them. They will be wise in eping clear of the present diamond gamble. Indian gold mining shares have eMperienaed some de- mand, and prices are becoming firmer, and will after the present disturbed • state of the mairket go still better. Mysore gold on Wednesday went up 1, which, although' since partly lost on realisation by holders soon returned tO best prices. Don Pedros have also been better during the week, and with the sale of a part of their property to a new company under the title of Don Pedro Segundo, ought to go better. Not long since they were dealt in at over £2, with every probability 'of evbn going higher. With regard 'to the new company! it Acquires an excel- lent property adjoining the original mine, and is in the fortunate position of being able to commence work, at °nee.
